 National foreword
 This document is part of the series of Eurocodes. Eurocodes have reference numbers from EN 1990 to EN 1999 and are regarded as a consistant set of design rules. Eurocodes assume the use of a number of parameters to be determined nationally, denoted Nationally Determined Parameters (NDP), given in a corresponding National Annex (NA). Eurocodes can only be used for the design of structures together with the NDPs applicable in the country where a structure or product is to be used.
 Therefore, this document can only be used as a basis for design of structures or products to be used in Norway together with the NDPs given in the Norwegian NA. This document specifies recommended values for the NDPs, but these cannot be used as replacement for the NDPs.
 NAs are in principle informative. According to § 10-2 of the Technical Regulations to The Planning and Building Act (pbl), it may be assumed that the requirements in The Planning and Building Act and the Technical Regulations are met, provided that methods and execution are in accordance with Norwegian Standard. Use of Eurocodes assumes that the corresponding NA, with the NDPs, is used as basis for the design. Consequently, the NAs shall be considered as normative.
 Information on the Eurocodes is found on www.eurokoder.no.
 December 2014

Below is a structured, detailed description of the relevant portion of “Table 3.1”—in particular its ninth row (the last column)—suitable for ingestion into a RAG‐style vector store. The surrounding context (EN-style clauses 3.1.4 and 3.2.4) indicates that this table belongs to a set of material‐law parameters for the concrete stress–strain relationship.

1. Table Identification  
   • Title (implied): “Table 3.1 – Parameters for the Concrete Stress–Strain Model”  
   • Purpose: to list characteristic strains, stresses, and empirical coefficients used in the parabolic–rectangular approximation of the concrete compressive envelope.

2. Column Layout (typical for this table)  
   1. Parameter name/description  
   2. Symbol  
   3. Empirical expression  
   4. Numerical limit or range  
   5. Units and notes

3. Ninth Row (Parameter ε_c1)  
   • Parameter description: Initial ascending‐branch strain limit for concrete under uniaxial compression. This defines the strain at which the parabolic curve transitions to a flat (rectangular) branch in the stress–strain diagram.  
   • Symbol: ε_c1 (expressed in “per mille,” ‰)  
   • Empirical formula:  
     ε_c1 = 0.7 · f_cm^0.31  
       – f_cm is the mean cylinder compressive strength of concrete (in MPa).  
       – The exponent 0.31 reflects the experimentally observed dependency of strain on strength in normal and high-strength concretes.  
   • Upper bound: ≤ 2.8 ‰  
       – Originally the table entry read “< 2.8 ‰”; the amendment replaces the strict inequality “<” with “≤” so that the calculated ε_c1 may attain exactly 2.8 ‰ at the very high-strength end.  
   • Units/Notes: Strain in ‰ (parts per thousand). The bound applies irrespective of curing time or age, so long as f_cm is defined at the relevant reference age t₀.

4. Rationale for Amendment  
   – By allowing ε_c1 to reach 2.8 ‰ (rather than be strictly below it), the standard ensures continuity at the upper limit of practical concrete strengths, avoids an unnecessary gap, and aligns with rounded laboratory observations.  
   – This adjustment is consistent with parallel updates in clause 3.1.4 (notation changes φ_k → φ_nl) and in clause 3.2.4 (notation for k⁠= (f_t/f_y)_k), streamlining symbol consistency across the document.

5. How to Vectorize/Retrieve  
   – Key embedding terms: “ε_c1,” “initial ascending‐branch strain,” “0.7 · f_cm^0.31,” “≤ 2.8 ‰,” “stress–strain model,” “Table 3.1 amendment.”  
   – Potential retrieval questions:  
     • “What is the formula for the first compressive strain ε_c1 in EN Table 3.1?”  
     • “What upper limit does the standard place on ε_c1?”  
     • “How was the inequality for ε_c1 modified in the latest draft?”  

By capturing both the numeric expression and the precise change (< → ≤), this description ensures that anyone querying the vector store about ε_c1 will retrieve not only its definition but also the fact that the amendment broadened its permissible maximum.

The figure is a longitudinal sectional sketch through a flat slab with an enlarged (drop) column head. Its purpose is to show the geometry of the critical (“control”) sections for punching‐shear checks when the depth of the head, h_H, is such that the horizontal projection l_H of the shear‐transfer surface exceeds twice the total slab depth (that is, l_H > 2·(d + h_H)). The key elements and dimensions are as follows:

1. Overall geometry  
   • A horizontal slab of uniform thickness d (the effective depth to the tension reinforcement) is shown in solid outline.  
   • At midspan of the sketch there is a downward projection—the column head—of additional thickness h_H below the slab underside. The combined thickness of slab plus head is therefore d + h_H.  
   • Directly beneath the centerline of the head is the supporting column, indicated by a dashed vertical box of width c.  

2. Loaded area and control planes  
   • The shaded or hatched region at the center (column head footprint) represents the loaded area, A_load.  
   • Punching‐shear control sections must be taken at a perpendicular (in‐plane) distance r_cont from the perimeter of the loaded area. Two distances are distinguished:  
       – r_cont,int: the interior control‐section radius (or offset) measured from each face of the column head toward the slab edge (for “internal” sides).  
       – r_cont,ext: the exterior control‐section radius measured from the outside faces of the loaded area (for “external” sides).  

3. Shear‐transfer surface  
   • From each control‐section line on the slab underside or head bottom there is a dashed line drawn down‐and‐in toward the column. These lines represent the critical shear‐transfer “frustums” along which punching shear is checked.  
   • All these sloping lines make the same angle θ = 26.6° with the horizontal. This angle locates the surface of potential shear‐failure and is determined by the standard relationship tan θ = 0.5 (approximately 26.6°).  

4. Left and right halves: external vs. internal faces  
   • On the right of the column (labeled A – “external” face) the slab extends freely toward the slab edge. The control section is drawn at a distance r_cont,ext from the column head, and the dashed shear‐plane slopes back at 26.6°. The horizontal projection from the slab underside back to the column face is denoted l_H, and it is explicitly noted that l_H > 2 h_H.  
   • On the left (labeled B – “internal” face) the slab adjoins another panel on the opposite side of the column. The same construction applies—control section at r_cont,int from the column head, a sloping friction surface at angle θ’, and the same requirement l_H > 2 h_H.  

5. Dimension call‐outs and notation  
   • “d_H” denotes the vertical distance from the slab top down to the critical control‐section plane (i.e. d + h_H, measured at the red dots on the slab top).  
   • “θ′” marks the same inclination angle of the shear‐transferring surface when drawn from the slab face or head bottom up to the slab top red‐dot location.  
   • The red dots on the slab top indicate the points at which the horizontal offsets r_cont,int or r_cont,ext are measured from the loaded‐area perimeter.  
   • The footnote box “θ = 26,6°” reiterates the fixed angle of inclination of all shear planes.

––– begin figure description –––

• Two heavy continuous horizontal lines:  
  – The upper line (thicker) represents the bundle of reinforcement bars to be anchored.

• On the left side, a dimension arrow pair spanning from the left end of the bar bundle back to the concrete line indicates “≥ lᵦ,rqd.” This is the minimum required development length measured from the concrete face to where the bar bundle must extend.  
• Moving rightward along the bar bundle, a second dimension arrow pair marks “≥ 1.3 lᵦ,rqd.” This shows that at least 1.3 times the required development length must be provided in the central portion of the bundle for widely staggered arrangements.  
• At the far right end of the bundle, an arrow labeled “E” points back toward the concrete; this dimension “E” denotes any additional extension beyond the 1.3 lᵦ,rqd segment if called for by design or detailing rules.  
• Directly below the bar bundle, two small vertical lines and a bracket enclose a segment of the bundle and are labeled “A – A.” This marks the location of the cross-section view.

Cross-Section A–A  
• A single horizontal line at the bottom of the section shows the top surface of the concrete element.  
• Above that line sit three small circles in a triangular (staggered) pattern. Each circle represents a single bar in the bundle, illustrating how bars are offset laterally to reduce concrete splitting and improve embedment.  
• No hooks are shown here; these are straight bars embedded into the concrete cover.  
• The section label “A – A” is printed beside the view to correspond with the bracket in the elevation.

2.  Table 2.1N “Partial factors for materials for ultimate limit states” (Normative)  
    •  Location: Clause 2.4.2.4 in Section 2 (“Basis of design”) under “Verification by the partial factor method.”  
    •  Purpose: Specifies the γ-factors (partial safety factors) to be applied to material strengths when verifying ULS.  
    •  Structure:  
       – Two “Design situations”:  
         • Persistent & Transient (normal and long-term loads)  
         • Accidental (exceptional or extreme events)  
       – Three columns of partial factors:  
         1. γC for concrete  
         2. γS for reinforcing steel  
         3. γS for prestressing steel  
    •  Values:

       – Accidental:          γC = 1.20; γS(reinf) = 1.00; γS(prest) = 1.00  
    •  Notes:  
       – These factors are “basic values” recommended for national adoption.  
       – Fire design uses different values (see EN 1992-1-2).

3.  Table E.1N “Indicative minimum strength class for durability” (Informative)  
    •  Location: Annex E (“Indicative minimum strength classes for durability”).  
    •  Purpose: Guides the designer on the minimum concrete strength class (fck) recommended by exposure category in order to control carbonation, chloride ingress and other degradation mechanisms.  
    •  Caption update: “Indicative strength class” → “Indicative minimum strength class.”  
    •  Typical structure (illustrative—actual country annex may vary):  
       – Column 1: Environmental exposure class (as defined in Clause 4.2 / EN 206-1), e.g. XC1, XC2, XD1, XS1, XA1, XA2, XA3, etc.

       – Column 3: Indicative minimum strength class (e.g. C20/25, C25/30, C30/37, C35/45, C40/50).

    b) Determine material properties (fck, fyk, fpk, etc.) from that class and from Sections 3–5.  
    c) For ULS checks, apply Table 2.1N partial factors to obtain design strengths (fcd, fyd, fpd).

The table under consideration presents the nominal unrestrained drying‐shrinkage strains ε_cd,0 (in ‰) for concretes made with CEM Class N cement, as a function of concrete strength class and ambient relative humidity.  It is extracted from Clause 3.1.5 (Creep and shrinkage) of EN 1992-1-1 “Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures – Part 1-1: General rules and rules for buildings.”

1. Table Structure  
  – Title (implied): “Nominal unrestrained drying shrinkage values ε_cd,0 (in ‰) for concrete with cement CEM Class N”  
  – Rows: each row corresponds to a concrete strength class, given by characteristic cylinder strength f_ck (MPa) and corresponding characteristic cube strength f_ck,cube (MPa). Five strength classes are tabulated:  
   • 20/25  
   • 40/50  
   • 60/75  
   • 80/95  
   • 90/105  
  – Columns: each column represents a level of relative humidity (RH in %), from drier to fully saturated: 20 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 %, 90 %, 100 %.  
  – Cells: numeric values of ε_cd,0 expressed in thousandths (‰), indicating the expected mean drying shrinkage strain under unrestrained conditions.  

2. Data Highlights  
  – Shrinkage decreases markedly as RH increases: for a given strength class, the greatest shrinkage occurs at RH = 20 % and reduces to zero at RH = 100 %.  
  – Higher‐strength concretes generally exhibit lower shrinkage: for RH = 40 %, ε_cd,0 falls from 0.58‰ (20/25) to 0.25‰ (90/105).  
  – The rate of reduction with rising humidity is more pronounced in lower‐strength mixes.  

3. Intended Use in Design  
  – These tabulated ε_cd,0 values form the basis of Expression (3.9) to calculate time‐dependent drying shrinkage ε_cd(t) = β_ds(t, t_s) · k_h · ε_cd,0, where β_ds is a time‐development coefficient and k_h accounts for section size.  
  – They support serviceability limit‐state checks for cracking and deflection, and contribute to long-term deformation assessments.  

4. Relationship to Durability Annex (Annex E)  
  – Annex E includes “Indicative strength classes for durability” (Table E.1N) that link exposure classes (e.g. XC1–XC4, XD1–XD3, XS1–XS3, XA1–XA3) to minimum concrete strength classes.  
  – As per the user instruction, in Table E.1N (and its caption) the wording “Indicative strength class” should be revised to “Indicative minimum strength class,” emphasizing that the tabulated strength is the lower bound required for adequate cover and concrete quality under each exposure condition.  

5. Paragraph Context (Para 2 of Clause 4.2/4.3)  
  – Clause 4.3 “Requirements for durability” notes that cover quality and concrete strength must be chosen in relation to environmental exposure. Table 3.2’s shrinkage data thus complements durability provisioning by quantifying one mechanism (drying shrinkage) that can affect cracking and cover performance.  
  – The adjustment of Table E.1N’s caption underlines the principle that listed strength classes are the minimum acceptable for protection of reinforcement and the control of shrinkage‐induced cracking, in combination with minimum cover values from Clause 4.4.  

By capturing both the quantitative shrinkage strains and their dependency on environmental humidity and concrete strength, this table informs the serviceability design checks and interacts directly with durability provisions (Annex E) to ensure that concrete members remain crack‐controlled and protective of embedded steel for their intended service life.

Below is a structured, self-contained description of the input table suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store. It includes its context, purpose, column definitions and values. In addition, any reference to Annex E.1N (not shown here) should use the caption “Indicative minimum strength class” in place of “Indicative strength class.”

1. Table Identification  
   • Number: 3.3  
   • Caption: “Values for kh in Expression (3.9)”  
   • Location: Clause 3.1.6(2) “Creep and shrinkage,” immediately after Expression (3.9) for drying shrinkage development.

2. Context and Purpose  
   – In Eurocode 2 Part 1-1, total shrinkage strain εcd(t) for uncracked, hardened concrete is calculated by Expression (3.9):  
     εcd(t) = βds(t, ts) · kh · εcd,0  
     where • εcd,0 is the final drying shrinkage (mean value);  
           • βds(t, ts) is a time-development factor;  
           • kh is a size-dependent coefficient that reduces the assumed free-shrinkage strain in larger members.  
   – Table 3.3 provides the recommended values of kh according to the member’s “notional size” h0 (mm), defined as h0 = 2Ac/u (twice the area over exposed perimeter).

3. Column Definitions  
   • h0 (mm): Notional member size – twice the cross-sectional area (Ac) divided by the perimeter (u) exposed to drying. Represents a geometric measure of section thickness.  
   • kh (–): Dimensionless reduction coefficient for drying shrinkage. Applied to εcd,0 to account for reduced free-shrinkage in thicker sections.

4. Tabulated Values  

   | h0 (mm)    | kh (–)  |  
   |------------|---------|  
   | 100        | 1,00    |  
   | 200        | 0,85    |  
   | 300        | 0,75    |  
   | ≥ 500      | 0,70    |  

   – For a notional size of 100 mm, no reduction applies (kh = 1,00).  
   – As h0 increases, shrinkage reduces: at 200 mm kh = 0,85; at 300 mm kh = 0,75; and for h0 ≥ 500 mm kh = 0,70.

5. Usage Notes  
   – Use the table in conjunction with Expression (3.9) to determine εcd(t).  
   – If a section has multiple exposed faces, compute h0 using the total exposed perimeter.  
   – National annexes may modify kh values for local practice, but the values above are “recommended.”  
   – When preparing or indexing Annex E.1N (durability table), its title and caption must read “Indicative minimum strength class for durability” instead of “Indicative strength class.”

The image is a schematic stress–strain diagram for normal-strength concrete, intended for use in structural analysis (see Eurocode 2, Clause 3.1.5).  It consists of:

Axes

• Vertical axis (ordinate) labeled σc (compressive stress in concrete).

Curve  
• A bold, smooth curve originates at the point (0, 0) and rises non-linearly to a peak, then descends.  
• The ascending branch represents increasing concrete stress with increasing compressive strain, up to the maximum mean stress fcm at strain εc1.  
• The descending branch shows softening beyond the peak: stress falls from fcm to a lower stress level fcu at strain εcu1.

Key points marked on the curve  
• Filled circle at the origin indicates the start of loading.  
• An open (hollow) circle on the ascending curve at σc = 0,4 fcm marks the point used to define the secant modulus Ecm (approximately tangent slope at zero).  
• Open circle at the peak defines the ultimate mean stress fcm at strain εc1.  
• Open circle on the descending branch indicates the stress fcu at ultimate strain εcu1.

Tangent and modulus  
• At the origin, a light straight line is drawn tangent to the curve.  
• The angle α between this tangent and the horizontal axis is shown. A label “tan α = Ecm” identifies the initial (secant) modulus of elasticity of concrete, Ecm.

Caption (shown beneath the sketch)  
“Schematic representation of the stress–strain relation for structural analysis (the use 0,4 fcm for the definition of Ecm is approximate).”

Context notes (from Eurocode 2):  
– fcm is the mean 28-day cylinder compressive strength.  
– Ecm is the secant modulus of elasticity between σc = 0 and σc = 0,4 fcm.  
– εc1 is the strain at peak stress; εcu1 is the ultimate strain at onset of crushing.  
– The diagram underpins section 3.1.5 where non-linear material behavior of concrete is introduced for analysis of reinforced and prestressed sections.

This figure is typically referenced when determining concrete section resistance under bending, axial load or combined actions, and when evaluating deformations or redistribution of internal forces in limit-state design.

The figure is drawn from Clause 3.1.7 of Eurocode 2, “Stress-strain relations for the design of sections,” and is captioned “Figure 3.3: Parabola-rectangle diagram for concrete under compression.” It combines a compact algebraic definition of the design stress–strain curve with a graphical sketch showing how the simplified model compares with a more realistic stress–strain response.  

1. Above the graph appears a two-part, piecewise formula for the compressive stress σc as a function of the concrete strain εc:  
   - For strains from zero up to the strain at peak design stress (0 ≤ εc ≤ εc2),  
     σc = fcd × [1 – (1 – εc/εc2)ⁿ]  
   - For strains beyond the peak up to the ultimate crushing strain (εc2 ≤ εc ≤ εcu2),  
     σc = fcd  
   Here fcd is the design compressive strength, εc2 the strain at which that strength is reached, εcu2 the ultimate strain at failure, and n an exponent that depends on concrete strength class.  

2. The coordinate axes of the plot are labeled:  
   – Horizontal axis (abscissa): “εc,” the compressive strain in the concrete (strain increases to the right).  
   – Vertical axis (ordinate): “σc,” the compressive stress in the concrete (stress increases upward).  

3. Two vertical dashed lines mark the key strain thresholds:  
   – A line at εc2 (the strain at which peak stress occurs).  
   – A line at εcu2 (the ultimate crushing strain beyond which the model no longer applies).  

4. Two curves are sketched on the same axes:  
   – A smooth dashed line rising from the origin in a gentle convex-upward curve to the characteristic compressive strength fck (at strain εc2), then turning into a horizontal plateau at fck up to εcu2. This represents a more realistic, actual stress–strain behavior of unconfined concrete.  
   – A heavier solid line showing the simplified “parabola + rectangle” model used for design: a parabola rising from zero to the design stress fcd at εc2, then a horizontal flat line at fcd up to εcu2.  

5. Key constants and parameters are indicated in small call-outs or expressions adjacent to the axes or lines:  
   – n (the exponent in the parabola)  
   – εc2 (strain at peak stress)  
   – εcu2 (ultimate strain)  
   – fcd (design stress level), compared with fck (characteristic strength) in the realistic curve.  

6. The caption centered beneath the drawing reads exactly:  
   “Figure 3.3: Parabola-rectangle diagram for concrete under compression.”  

In context, this diagram and the accompanying formula define the idealized compressive stress–strain law adopted for cross-sectional design in Eurocode 2.  The solid parabola-rectangle shape simplifies calculations while conservatively capturing the essential behavior of normal-strength concrete under axial compression.

  – Begins at the origin with a straight-line (elastic) slope.  
  – Reaches the characteristic cylinder strength f_ck on the stress axis at a strain ε_c2 (sometimes referred to as ε_c1 in other parts of the code).  
  – Continues nearly flat (plateau) at σ = f_ck up to the ultimate compressive strain ε_cu1, beyond which crushing occurs.  

3. Design (bilinear) approximation (solid line)  
  – Also starts at the origin on the same initial slope, but diverges downward:  
    • It reaches the lower, design compressive strength f_cd (f_cd = α_cc·f_ck/γ_C) at a slightly smaller strain ε_c3.  
    • From that point onward, the stress remains constant at f_cd until the ultimate design strain ε_cu, where the material is assumed to fail.  
  – Thus the bilinear model replaces the actual curved peak and plateau by a two-segment polygon: an ascending straight branch and a horizontal top branch.  

4. Annotations  
  – f_ck (dashed-line peak) is marked on the stress axis.  
  – f_cd (solid-line peak) lies below f_ck on the stress axis.  
  – ε_c3 is shown at the junction of the two solid segments.  
  – ε_cu is the terminal strain of the solid line.  
  – ε_cu1 (terminal strain of the dashed curve) is aligned vertically with ε_cu for comparison.  

5. Design context  
  – The bilinear curve is the basis for cross-section design in ultimate limit‐state checks.  
  – f_cd and ε_c3 reflect partial factors (γ_C) and long-term effects (α_cc) required by the partial‐factor method (see Clause 2.4).  
  – This idealization ensures a conservative but tractable representation of concrete’s non-linear compression behaviour.  

Note on Annex E: In Table E.1N and its caption (Informative annex on durability), the column header “Indicative strength class” has been revised to read “Indicative minimum strength class,” aligning the durability recommendations with national choices of minimum concrete classes required to achieve the intended design working life.

The image is a schematic from Eurocode 2 illustrating the internal force and deformation patterns in a reinforced-concrete beam section when a simplified, rectangular stress block is used to model the concrete compression zone. It consists of three coordinated parts:

1. Cross-section geometry (left)  
   • A vertical rectangle represents the beam cross-section (width into the page not shown).  
   • The top portion of height x is hatched and labelled “A₂”; this is the equivalent area over which a uniform compressive stress is assumed to act.  
   • A dotted horizontal line at depth x from the top marks the neutral axis.  
   • The overall effective depth of the section down to the tension reinforcement is indicated by d.  
   • Two small filled circles at the bottom, connected by a dashed line, denote the tensile reinforcement area Aₛ.  
   • Arrows beside A₂ and Aₛ point from the labels to the compression block and to the reinforcement, respectively.

2. Simplified rectangular stress distribution (centre/right)  
   • Immediately to the right of the cross-section, a narrow vertical rectangle of height x and unit width λ is drawn.  
   • The label “λ” on its top edge indicates the coefficient by which the actual concrete compressive stress fcd is multiplied to form the equivalent block (so that the block has an area λ·x representing the resultant compressive force per unit width).  
   • This rectangular block represents the ultra-simplified stress diagram: the concrete in the compression zone is assumed to carry a constant stress equal to λ·fcd over its entire depth x.

3. Actual linear strain profile (far right)  
   • Beside the stress block is a triangular shape depicting how concrete strain actually varies linearly through the section.  
   • Its neutral-axis hinge is at the level where strain is zero (the same horizontal position as the neutral axis in the cross-section).  
   • The triangle slopes upward from zero strain at the neutral axis to a maximum compressive strain εcu3 at the extreme top fiber.  
   • It slopes downward from zero to a tensile strain εs at the bottom fiber (where the reinforcement is located).  
   • The vertical dimension of this strain diagram is also x, tying it back to the depth of the compression zone.  

Together, these three views convey:  
– how a reinforced-concrete section is idealized by collapsing the actual, linear concrete stress–strain relationship into a rectangular block of height x and uniform intensity;  
– how the position of the neutral axis x and the effective depth d define the lever arm for internal bending forces;  
– and how the actual strain distribution drives the values of εcu3 (ultimate concrete strain) and εs (reinforcement strain) that permit equilibrium between the compressive block A₂·fcd·λ and the tensile force in the steel Aₛ·σₛ.

The illustration consists of two parts side by side, united under the heading “Figure 3.6: Stress-strain relationship for confined concrete.” On the left is a sketch of a concrete cylinder in three-dimensional view, intended to show the state of stress under confinement. On its top face a single large downward arrow is labelled σ₁ = f_ck,c, indicating the axial compressive stress applied to the specimen. Around the curved side surface two smaller horizontal arrows are drawn, one on each side, both labelled σ₂ (equal to σ₃). These signify the uniform lateral confining pressure provided, for example, by closely spaced ties or links in a column. In effect the diagram represents a triaxial compression test in which the axial load equals the confined concrete’s characteristic strength f_ck,c and the radial pressures (σ₂, σ₃) are the confining stresses.

On the right is a two-dimensional stress–strain graph. The vertical axis is marked σ_c (compressive stress) and the horizontal axis ε_c (compressive strain), both treated as positive in compression. Two stress–strain curves are overlaid:

  •  A dashed curve of higher peak, representing the behavior of concrete under confinement. Its apex reaches σ₁ = f_ck,c at a strain labelled ε_c2,c, followed by a plateau or gentle drop extending to an ultimate compressive strain ε_cu2.  
  •  A thinner solid (or dotted) curve beneath it, representing unconfined concrete, reaching a lower peak stress f_ck at a smaller strain ε_c2 and terminating at its own ultimate strain ε_cu2,c.  

A call-out “A” points to a location on the unconfined curve roughly at mid-height, emphasizing the contrast in curvature and stiffness between unconfined and confined response in the pre-peak range.

Key features of the right-hand plot:

  – The initial slopes of both curves coincide, reflecting the same elastic modulus up to low strains.  
  – The confined curve departs above the unconfined one beyond about 0.2 ε_c2, showing sustained increase in stress with further strain.  
  – Peak compressive stress and corresponding strain are higher under confinement (f_ck,c at ε_c2,c) than for plain concrete (f_ck at ε_c2).  
  – Post-peak ductility is markedly improved for confined concrete, with a softer stress decay and larger ε_cu2 limit.  

Taken together, the two sketches convey the principle that lateral confinement elevates both strength and deformation capacity of concrete. In design terms (as set out in clause 3.1.9 of Eurocode 2) this justifies using modified stress–strain parameters—higher peak stress f_ck,c and larger critical strains—in the analysis of tied or jacketed members.

The diagram presents both the “idealised” and the “design” stress-strain relationships for reinforcing steel under tension (and by symmetry, compression) as used in Eurocode 2.  It is labelled as Figure 3.8 and appears in the “Materials” section (3.2 Reinforcing steel).  The key features of the illustration are as follows:

1.  Axes and Units  
    – Vertical axis (σ): stress in the steel (MPa).  
    – Horizontal axis (ε): axial strain in the steel (dimensionless).  

2.  Idealised Curve (“A”)  
    – Begins at origin with a steep elastic branch of slope E_s (modulus of elasticity).  
    – Reaches the characteristic yield strength f_yk at strain ε = f_yk / E_s.  
    – Exhibits a rising “strain‐hardening” branch from f_yk up to k·f_yk at higher strain.  Here k is defined by the ratio of characteristic tensile strength to characteristic yield:  
         k = (f_t / f_y)_k  
    – After reaching k·f_yk the curve flattens into an ultimate plateau at constant stress k·f_yk.  

3.  Design Curve (“B”)  
    – Starts with the same elastic branch up to the design yield stress f_yd, where:  
         f_yd = f_yk / γ_s  
      γ_s is the partial safety factor for reinforcing steel.  
    – Beyond f_yd the design curve either:  
      • Continues as a horizontal plateau at f_yd up to the ultimate design strain ε_ud, or  
      • Rises linearly (less steeply than the idealised branch) to reach k·f_yk / γ_s at strain ε_ud.  
    – The design ultimate strain ε_ud is typically taken as 0.9·ε_uk (where ε_uk is the characteristic maximum‐load strain of the steel).  

4.  Annotations and Callouts  
    – Point “A” marks the idealised strain‐hardening region between f_yk and k·f_yk.  
    – Point “B” shows the design branch rising from f_yd to k·f_yk / γ_s.  
    – Dashed lines represent the idealised envelope; solid lines represent the simplified design envelope.  
    – Vertical dashed lines locate key strains ε = f_yk / E_s, ε = ε_ud and ε = ε_uk.  
    – Horizontal dashed lines locate stresses f_yk and k·f_yk (idealised), and their reduced design values f_yd and k·f_yk / γ_s (design).  

5.  Context within Eurocode 2  
    – Used in Section 3.2 to justify the simplified stress‐strain relationships for cross‐section design.  
    – Supports the selection of characteristic material parameters (f_yk, f_tk, ε_uk) and partial factors (γ_s) listed elsewhere in the code.  
    – Informs detailing rules that require bars to reach sufficient ductility and strength before yielding.  

6.  Related Note on Annex E (Durability)  
    – In Table E.1N (which classifies environmental exposure and recommends concrete strength), the caption should read “Indicative minimum strength class” instead of “Indicative strength class.”  

Overall, Figure 3.8 provides a clear, comparative view of how reinforcing steel is idealised in theoretical analyses versus how it is safely represented in design calculations, accounting for safety factors and guaranteed ductility limits.

The image is a black-and-white line drawing labeled “Figure 3.9: Stress-strain diagram for typical prestressing steel (absolute values are shown for tensile stress and strain)”.  It consists of a two-axis plot:

• Vertical axis (ordinate) is labeled σ (stress)  
• Horizontal axis (abscissa) is labeled ε (strain)  

Along the vertical axis two reference stress levels are indicated by dashed lines:  
  – The lower dashed line corresponds to the 0,1 % proof stress, marked “fₚ₀,₁ₖ”.  At the left margin of the horizontal axis the location of the 0,1 % strain is also shown as a short vertical tick.  
  – A higher dashed line represents the characteristic tensile (ultimate) strength, marked “fₚₖ”.

The actual stress–strain response of the prestressing steel is plotted as a thick solid curve that begins at the origin and proceeds as follows:  
 1. An initial steep, nearly linear rise from (0,0) up to the 0,1 % proof stress at the 0,1 % strain mark.  
 2. A relatively flat plateau in which stress remains close to fₚ₀,₁ₖ while strain increases beyond 0,1 %.  
 3. A gently rising branch beyond the yield plateau, bending upward from fₚ₀,₁ₖ toward fₚₖ.  This branch terminates at the point where the solid curve reaches the fₚₖ level.  
 4. From fₚₖ the curve continues almost horizontally—indicating limited additional stress gain—out to a strain labeled εᵤₖ (the strain at maximum load), after which the steel would fracture.  

A thin dashed straight line is drawn from the origin, passing through the 0,1 % proof point and extending up to the ultimate strain.  This represents the elastic tangent extrapolated beyond yield, for comparison with the actual inelastic behavior.

Underneath the plot, the caption clearly identifies the figure number and describes its purpose: to show—on absolute scales—the typical tensile stress-strain relationship of high-strength prestressing steel used in concrete structures.

The illustration is a two-curve stress-strain diagram, reproduced from Eurocode 2, Figure 3.10, showing both the idealised (characteristic) and the design (factored) relationships for prestressing steel under tensile loading. The horizontal axis is total tensile strain ε, increasing from left to right. The vertical axis is stress σ, increasing upward. Both axes are unlabelled numerically but are divided into regions by dashed lines that mark key stress and strain values.

At the far right of the diagram, a vertical dashed line denotes εuk, the ultimate tensile strain at maximum load. A second vertical dashed line, located left of εuk, identifies εud, the design ductility strain limit (often taken as 0.9 εuk). To the left still lies the elastic-limit strain corresponding to the design stress fpd/ Ep, where fpd is the design stress for prestressing steel and Ep its modulus of elasticity.

Horizontally on the stress axis, three reference stresses are marked by dashed horizontal lines. The topmost is fpk, the characteristic tensile strength (ultimate strength) of the prestressing steel. Beneath that is fp0,1k, the characteristic 0.1 % proof stress. A third dashed line at fp0,1k / γS represents the design proof stress after application of the partial factor γS for steel.

Two stress-strain curves are shown. Curve A (drawn as a lighter, upward-sloping dashed line) is the idealised diagram: it starts at the origin, rises steeply through the elastic region, slightly levels off near fp0,1k, then continues upward with reduced slope to reach fpk at εuk. This embodies the full characteristic behavior including strain hardening.

Curve B (drawn as a solid, flattened polygonal line) is the design diagram: it follows an initial elastic slope to the point (ε = fp0,1k / Ep, σ = fp0,1k / γS), then continues with a reduced slope up to the limit strain εud, ending horizontally at the design ultimate stress fpk / γS for ε ≥ εud. Beyond εud the diagram is capped horizontally, meaning that further strain does not increase the design stress.

The two curves are labeled with the letters “A” and “B” near their mid-sections: “A” for the idealised (characteristic) curve and “B” for the design (factored) curve. The caption below the graph reads: “Figure 3.10: Idealised and design stress-strain diagrams for prestressing steel (absolute values are shown for tensile stress and strain).”

In the context of durability provisions (Table E.1N in Annex E of the same standard), any reference to “Indicative strength class” is to be replaced by “Indicative minimum strength class” to clarify that the table provides baseline concrete classes for environmental exposure conditions, not merely suggestive values. This distinction ensures that reinforcement and cover requirements derived from those concrete classes meet the minimum criteria for service life and corrosion protection.

The table you are looking at is “Table 4.1: Exposure classes related to environmental conditions in accordance with EN 206-1.”  It is one of the durability‐related tables in Eurocode 2, intended to assist the designer in choosing minimum concrete quality and cover requirements so that reinforcement and embedded metals are adequately protected over the intended service life.  Below is a structured description of its contents and organization:

1.  Table purpose  
 – Classify the various environmental exposures that may act upon concrete elements (moisture cycles, chlorides, freeze–thaw, aggressive chemicals, abrasion, etc.)  
 – Link each exposure class to a three-letter code (e.g. XC2, XD3, XF4, XA1, etc.)  
 – Provide both a short “Description of the environment” (textual definition of the exposure) and “Informative examples where exposure classes may occur” (real‐world situations)

2.  Overall layout  
 • Column 1: Exposure class code  
 • Column 2: Description of the environment (qualitative conditions)  
 • Column 3: Informative examples (typical structures or locations)

3.  Major groups of exposure and their codes  
 A. “X0” (no risk)  
  – Definition: All exposures except freeze/thaw, abrasion or chemical attack for unreinforced concrete; “very dry” for reinforced  
  – Examples: Interior concrete with very low humidity, non‐reinforced elements in controlled environments  
 B. Corrosion induced by carbonation (XC1→XC4)  
  – XC1 “Dry or permanently wet”  
   • e.g. indoor concrete with low humidity; permanently submerged elements  
  – XC2 “Wet, rarely dry”  
   • e.g. foundations; any surface in continuous water contact  
  – XC3 “Moderate humidity”  
   • e.g. indoor spaces with moderate/high humidity; sheltered external concrete  
  – XC4 “Cyclic wet and dry”  
   • e.g. external surfaces subject to intermittently wet conditions not classed as XC2  
 C. Corrosion induced by chlorides (XD1→XD3)  
  – XD1 “Moderate humidity” from de-icing salts  
   • e.g. concrete exposed to airborne road salts  
  – XD2 “Wet, rarely dry”  
   • e.g. swimming-pool shells; industrial wastewater containment  
  – XD3 “Cyclic wet and dry”  
   • e.g. bridge undersides subject to salt spray; car parks, pavements in cold climates  
 D. Corrosion induced by chlorides from sea water (XS1→XS3)  
  – XS1 “Airborne salt, no direct sea-contact”  
   • e.g. coastal buildings  
  – XS2 “Permanently submerged”  
   • e.g. marine piers, submerged piling  
  – XS3 “Tidal, splash and spray zones”  
   • e.g. splash area of harbour walls, tidal piers  
 E. Freeze/thaw attack (XF1→XF4)  
  – XF1 “Moderate saturation, no de-icing agents”  
   • e.g. vertical façade exposed to rain and frost  
  – XF2 “Moderate saturation, with de-icing agents”  
   • e.g. roadside barriers, bridge parapets sprayed with salt  
  – XF3 “High saturation, no de-icing agents”  
   • e.g. horizontal surfaces exposed to rain and frost  
  – XF4 “High saturation, with de-icing or seawater”  
   • e.g. deck slabs of roads/bridges; splash zone in marine freezing climates  
 F. Chemical attack (XA1→XA3)  
  – XA1 “Slightly aggressive chemical environment” (e.g. natural soils, groundwater)  
  – XA2 “Moderately aggressive” (e.g. sewage, polluted groundwater)  
  – XA3 “Highly aggressive” (e.g. industrial chemicals, acid–sulfate soils)  
 G. Abrasion (not shown in the excerpt but normally classified XF/AB codes)

4.  How this table is used  
 – The designer first identifies the relevant exposure class for each element on the basis of service conditions.  
 – The class code feeds into subsequent clauses that specify minimum concrete cover, maximum w/c-ratio or, in Annex E (Table E.1N), the “Indicative minimum strength class” of the concrete to achieve the required durability.  
 – National Annexes may replace the “indicative” values by “mandatory minimum” parameters (strength, cover) for their territory.  

In short, Table 4.1 provides a systematic link between environmental conditions, Eurocode exposure‐class codes, and practical examples, forming the cornerstone of durability checks in reinforced and prestressed concrete design.

 This Eurocode supersedes ENV 1992-1-1, 1992-1-3, 1992-1-4, 1992-1-5, 1992-1-6 and 1992-3.

 In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.
 Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.
 For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.
 In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreement1 between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products - CPD - and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).

 The Member States of the EU and EFTA recognise that Eurocodes serve as reference documents for the following purposes :
 – as a means to prove compliance of building and civil engineering works with the essential

 The Eurocodes, as far as they concern the construction works themselves, have a direct relationship with the Interpretative Documents2 referred to in Article 12 of the CPD, although they are of a different nature from harmonised product standards3.  The National Standards implementing Eurocodes will comprise the full text of the Eurocode (including any annexes), as published by CEN, which may be preceded by a National title page and National foreword, and may be followed by a National annex.
 The National annex may only contain information on those parameters which are left open in the Eurocode for national choice, known as Nationally Determined Parameters, to be used for the design of buildings and civil engineering works to be constructed in the country concerned,
 i.e. :

 – values to be used where a symbol only is given in the Eurocode,
 – country specific data (geographical, climatic, etc.), e.g. snow map,
 – the procedure to be used where alternative procedures are given in the Eurocode.
 It may contain
 – decisions on the application of informative annexes,
 – references to non-contradictory complementary information to assist the user to apply the Eurocode.

 EN 1992-1-1 describes the principles and requirements for safety, serviceability and durability of concrete structures, together with specific provisions for buildings. It is based on the limit state concept used in conjunction with a partial factor method.
 For the design of new structures, EN 1992-1-1 is intended to be used, for direct application, together with other parts of EN 1992, Eurocodes EN 1990,1991, 1997 and 1998.
 EN 1992-1-1 also serves as a reference document for other CEN TCs concerning structural matters.
 EN 1992-1-1 is intended for use by:
 – committees drafting other standards for structural design and related product, testing and execution standards;
 – clients (e.g. for the formulation of their specific requirements on reliability levels and durability);
 – designers and constructors ;
 – relevant authorities.
 Numerical values for partial factors and other reliability parameters are recommended as basic values that provide an acceptable level of reliability. They have been selected assuming that an appropriate level of workmanship and of quality management applies. When EN 1992-1-1 is used as a base document by other CEN/TCs the same values need to be taken.
 This standard gives values with notes indicating where national choices may have to be made.  1.5.2.1 Precast structures. Precast structures are characterised by structural elements manufactured elsewhere than in the final position in the structure. In the structure, elements are connected to ensure the required structural integrity.
 1.5.2.2 Plain or lightly reinforced concrete members. Structural concrete members having no reinforcement (plain concrete) or less reinforcement than the minimum amounts defined in Section 9.
 1.5.2.3 Unbonded and external tendons. Unbonded tendons for post-tensioned members having ducts which are permanently ungrouted, and tendons external to the concrete cross-section (which may be encased in concrete after stressing, or have a protective membrane).
 1.5.2.4 Prestress. The process of prestressing consists in applying forces to the concrete structure by stressing tendons relative to the concrete member. “Prestress” is used globally to name all the permanent effects of the prestressing process, which comprise internal forces in the sections and deformations of the structure. Other means of prestressing are not considered in this standard.

 (1) Shrinkage and creep are time-dependent properties of concrete. Their effects should generally be taken into account for the verification of serviceability limit states.
 (2) The effects of shrinkage and creep should be considered at ultimate limit states only where their effects are significant, for example in the verification of ultimate limit states of stability where second order effects are of importance. In other cases these effects need not be considered for ultimate limit states, provided that ductility and rotation capacity of the elements are sufficient.
 (3) When creep is taken into account its design effects should be evaluated under the quasi- permanent combination of actions irrespective of the design situation considered i.e. persistent, transient or accidental.
 Note: In most cases the effects of creep may be evaluated under permanent loads and the mean value of prestress.

The extract you’ve provided includes “Table 4.2,” which defines the minimum concrete cover cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ required purely to satisfy bond‐related requirements (see EN 1992-1-1 clause 4.4.1.2(3)). In the broader design flow this cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ is one of the competing cover values (alongside durability cover, fire cover, etc.) that get compared and the largest is adopted (cₘᵢₙ = max {cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ; cₘᵢₙ,dur + …; 10 mm}). Below is a detailed breakdown of Table 4.2 itself:

1. Table Title and Purpose  
   – Title: “Table 4.2: Minimum cover, cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ, requirements with regard to bond.”  
   – Purpose: To prescribe the least cover needed to ensure safe development of bond forces and adequate concrete compaction around reinforcement.

2. Table Layout  
   The table has two columns:  
   • Arrangement of bars (a categorization of how the reinforcing steel is grouped)  
   • Minimum cover cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ (the numerical cover requirement expressed in terms of bar dimensions)

3. Categories of Bar Arrangement  
   a) Separated bars  
      – Definition: Individual reinforcing bars spaced apart (i.e. not touching).  
      – Prescribed cover: cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ = “diameter of bar.”  
        • If you are using a 16 mm bar, the minimum cover for bond alone would be 16 mm.  
   b) Bundled bars  
      – Definition: Two or more bars placed in direct contact or very close together, acting as a pack.  
      – Prescribed cover: cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ = equivalent diameter (φₙ).  
        • φₙ is the equivalent “bundle” diameter calculated per Clause 8.9.1 of EN 1992-1-1.  
        • In effect you treat the bundle as one larger bar of diameter φₙ when determining cover.

4. Footnote / Special Aggregate-Size Adjustment  
   – “* If the nominal maximum aggregate size is greater than 32 mm, cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ shall be increased by 5 mm.”  
     • Rationale: Larger aggregate requires slightly more cover to ensure proper compaction and full embedment of reinforcement.

5. How This Table Is Used in Design  
   – Step 1: Identify whether your reinforcement is “separated” or “bundled.”  
   – Step 2: Read off cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ in terms of bar diameter or φₙ.  
   – Step 3: Add 5 mm if using aggregate > 32 mm.  
   – Step 4: Compare this bond‐governed cover with other minimum covers (durability, fire, etc.) and adopt the largest cₘᵢₙ per the code formula.

6. Cross-References  
   – Clause 4.4.1.2(3) – introduction to cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ for bond.  
   – Clause 8.9.1 – definition and calculation of equivalent diameter φₙ for bundled bars.  
   – Clause 4.4.1.2 overall – sequence for determining final design cover cₘᵢₙ.

In summary, Table 4.2 is a compact lookup that ties the physical arrangement of bars directly to a cover requirement, ensuring bond strength and adequate compaction. Designers take the greater of this bond cover and all other cover requirements (durability, fire resistance, special exposures), plus any deviation allowances, to arrive at the cover to be detailed on drawings.

The table reproduced above, “Table 4.3N: Recommended structural classification,” is part of the procedure for selecting the durability-related minimum concrete cover, cmin,dur, in EN 1992-1-1. It provides a simple, prescriptive way to determine or adjust the “structural class” (S1…S4) needed for a desired 50 year service life, based on the exposure class of the concrete and on certain quality or detailing provisions.  The structural class in turn feeds into Tables 4.4N and 4.5N, which list the actual cover values for reinforcing and prestressing steel.

1. Table layout  
- Title: “Table 4.3N: Recommended structural classification.”  
- The top­most row of column headings identifies the exposure classes from EN 206-1 Table 4.1:  
   • X0 (no risk of corrosion or attack)  
   • XC1 (dry or permanently wet)  
   • XC2 / XC3 (wet, rarely dry / wet, rarely dry)  
   • XC4 (cyclic wetting and drying)  
   • XD1 (moderate chloride environment)  
   • XD2 / XS1 (wet, rarely dry, chlorides from de­icing salts / exposure to airborne salts)  
   • XD3 / XS2 / XS3 (cyclic wetting and drying with de-icing salts / seawater spray and wetting).

2. Rows and Entries  
The left-hand column of the table lists three “allowance” or “modifying” items:  

  A. Design Working Life of 50 years – minimum concrete strength required in each exposure to achieve the reference structural class S4.  In other words, if you choose to maintain S4 and still qualify for reducing cover, the concrete strength must meet or exceed the value shown in the cell for your exposure class.  If you cannot meet that strength, you must remain at S4 or even higher (i.e. no reduction).  

     • X0, XC1:  ≥ C30/37  
     • XC2 / XC3:  ≥ C35/45  
     • XC4, XD1, XD2 / XS1:  ≥ C40/50  
     • XD3 / XS2 / XS3:  ≥ C45/55  

   In each of these cells the instruction reads “reduce class by 1” – meaning you may step down from the baseline S4 to S3 if you satisfy the strength requirement for that exposure.  If you cannot, you stay at S4 (or potentially a higher class if your National Annex demands it).  

  B. Member cast with slab on two sides (reinforcement affected by construction): “reduce class by 1” in every exposure column.  This reflects the improved protection provided by having concrete cover on two faces.  

  C. Quality of the concrete production ensured (e.g. factory control, certified plant): again “reduce class by 1” under all exposures.  High and consistent production quality reduces the risk of local cover deficiencies or honeycombing.  

3. How to use the table  
- Start with the recommended reference class S4 (for 50 year life and the indicative strengths of Annex E).  
- For each condition (A, B, C) that applies, you may reduce the class by one grade.  For example:  
   • If your exposure is XC2 and your mix is C40/50 or better, you may drop from S4 to S3 (row A).  
   • If, additionally, that member is cast against slabs on two faces, you may drop another class (S3→S2) under row B.  
   • If factory production control is in place, you could drop yet another class (S2→S1) under row C, ending up at S1.  

- Your final structural class (never below S1, never above S4 unless specifically raised by National Annex) then determines cmin,dur via Table 4.4N (reinforcement) or 4.5N (prestressing).  

4. Context in the standard  
This table is one of the “recommended” approaches in the indicative National Annex (the designation “N” signals that fact).  A Country may adopt different modifications, but the logic remains: higher exposure demands higher structural class (and thus greater cover), while good material quality, favorable member detailing and higher concrete strength permit stepping down one or more classes to optimize cover thickness without sacrificing durability.

The input “Table 4.4N” is a matrix of minimum concrete-cover requirements, cmin,dur (in millimetres), for reinforcing‐steel durability under different exposure and structural-service-life classes. It is intended to be used in the calculation of the overall minimum cover cmin (see EN 1992-1-1 clause 4.4.1.2), where  
 cmin = max {cmin,b; cmin,dur + Δcdur,γ – Δcdur,st – Δcdur,add; 10 mm}.

1. Table Structure  
• Rows (vertical axis) list six “Structural Class” designations, S1 through S6. These classes reflect the intended design working life, concrete quality (strength, w/c ratio) and any national-annex modifications. Typical recommended structural class for a 50 year life is S4, but S1–S6 allow selection for shorter or longer life, special concrete compositions, air-entrainment, etc.  
• Columns (horizontal axis) list seven “Exposure Classes” in accordance with Table 4.1 of EN 1992-1-1:  
  – X0: negligible risk (dry, indoor)  
  – XC1: dry or permanently wet (internal)  
  – XC2 / XC3: wet, rarely dry or cyclic wet/dry (e.g. internal surfaces subject to condensation)  
  – XC4: moderate humidity (external sheltered)  
  – XD1 / XS1: de-icing salts or industrial atmosphere with low salinity or low chemical attack  
  – XD2 / XS2: frequent de-icing salts or aggressive marine/industrial atmosphere  
  – XD3 / XS3: very severe conditions (sea spray, chemical attack).

2. Numeric Content (cmin,dur in mm)  
Structural class → Exposure class columns  
S1 → X0: 10, XC1: 10, XC2/3: 10, XC4: 15, XD1/XS1: 20, XD2/XS2: 25, XD3/XS3: 30  
S2 → 10, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35  
S3 → 10, 10, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40  
S4 → 10, 15, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45  
S5 → 15, 20, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50  
S6 → 20, 25, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55

3. Observations and Usage  
– Cover increases both with more severe exposure class (moving right) and with more demanding structural class (moving down).  
– The minimum guaranteed cover is never less than 10 mm, and may reach up to 55 mm in the worst service/exposure combination (S6 / XD3-XS3).  
– Designers select the appropriate structural class (S1–S6) based on intended design life, concrete quality and environmental aggressiveness. Exposure class is chosen per site conditions. The intersection gives cmin,dur.  
– This value is then adjusted by additive safety Δcdur,γ (typically 0 mm), minus reductions for stainless steel Δcdur,st or additional protection Δcdur,add (often 0 mm) before comparison with bond requirement cmin,b and the fixed floor of 10 mm.  
– National Annexes may modify both structural-class definitions and the numerical values of cmin,dur, as well as the adjustment terms.  

In a RAG/vector-store context, key attributes to extract are:  
• Structural_Class (S1–S6)  
• Exposure_Class (X0, XC1, XC2/XC3, XC4, XD1/XS1, XD2/XS2, XD3/XS3)  
• cmin_dur (numeric, mm)  
• Notes on national-annex adjustability.

The excerpted table (designated Table 4.5N) provides recommended minimum concrete cover values cmin,dur for prestressing steel, taking account of both the structural class of the member and the environmental exposure class. These cmin,dur values form one term in the overall minimum cover expression  
  cmin = max { cmin,b ; cmin,dur + Δcdur,γ − Δcdur,st − Δcdur,add ; 10 mm }  
(see EN 1992-1-1 clause 4.4.1.2).  

1. Table Layout  
• Rows (Structural Class):  
  – S1 through S6, corresponding to increasingly stringent durability requirements (S1 being the lowest-durability class, S6 the highest).  
• Columns (Exposure Class):  
  – X0 (no risk of corrosion or attack)  
  – XC1 (dry or permanently wet interior)  
  – XC2 / XC3 (moderately humid or cyclic wet–dry interior)  
  – XC4 (external sheltered)  
  – XD1 / XS1 (external moderate humidity or inland de-icing salts; internal low chlorides)  
  – XD2 / XS2 (external moderate to high humidity with de-icing salts; internal moderate chlorides)  
  – XD3 / XS3 (external high humidity with airborne chlorides; internal high chlorides)  

2. Numerical Values (cmin,dur in mm)  
Structural Class → Exposure Class  
• S1: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40  
• S2: 10, 15, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45  
• S3: 10, 20, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50  
• S4: 10, 25, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55  
• S5: 15, 30, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60  
• S6: 20, 35, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65  

3. Interpretation and Use  
• For a given member, identify its structural class S1–S6 (related to intended design life, concrete strength, w/c ratio, and aggregate characteristics).  
• Identify the relevant exposure class (see EN 1992-1-1 Table 4.1) describing the aggressive agents likely to reach the steel (chlorides, carbonation, freeze/thaw, etc.).  
• Read off cmin,dur from the intersection of row and column.  
• Add the “additive safety element” Δcdur,γ (often 0 mm unless specified by a National Annex).  
• Subtract any reductions permitted for stainless steel Δcdur,st and/or additional protection Δcdur,add (both often 0 mm in recommended practice).  
• Compare with the minimum for bond cmin,b (from Table 4.2) and the absolute floor of 10 mm; the greatest of these three criteria is the adopted cover.  

4. Contextual Notes  
• Table 4.5N covers only prestressing steel; analogous Table 4.4N gives values for ordinary reinforcing steel.  
• National Annexes may adjust both the exposure classes’ definitions and the numerical minima.  
• The recommended default structural class is S4 for a 50-year design life and “indicative” concrete strengths (Annex E). Lower classes down to S1 may be permissible for shorter lives or less aggressive environments.  
• In practice, practitioners select a cover that satisfies durability (this table) as well as bond requirements and fire resistance, ensuring both safety of prestress transfer and long-term protection against corrosion.

The image is a two‐part schematic (labelled “Figure 5.5: Plastic rotation θs of reinforced concrete sections for continuous beams and continuous one‐way spanning slabs”) illustrating how the plastic hinge zone and the corresponding plastic rotation θs are idealized in simplified plastic analysis of continuous members (clause 5.6.2 of EN 1992-1-1).

Top diagram  
• A continuous two‐span beam (or slab) of constant overall depth h is shown in elevation by a solid horizontal line (undeformed axis).  
• Under load, the beam deflects into a smooth sagging curve (dashed line).  
• A bilinear approximation of that deflected shape over the interior support zone is indicated by two straight, inclined segments (fine dotted lines) meeting at a point of maximum curvature reversal.  
• On each side of that critical section, the length of the plastic hinge zone is idealized as 0.6 h (dimensioned above the beam). Thus the full hinge region spans 1.2 h but is split equally either side of the section where moment crosses zero in the plastic regime.  
• The angle between those two straight segments is marked θs. That is the plastic rotation that must be available at the support section for plastic redistribution (yield‐hinge formation) under the ultimate load combination.  
• To the right of the sketch, a double‐headed vertical arrow labelled h indicates the member’s depth.

Bottom diagram  
• A simply‐supported single span element is shown, the support being represented by a small triangular bearing symbol under mid-span.  
• Its sagging deflected shape under uniform load is again shown by a dashed curve.  
• Adjacent to the support, a short straight segment (fine dotted) of length 0.6 h approximates the plastic hinge zone.  
• The plastic rotation θs is the angle between the tangent to the dashed deflected curve and the original horizontal axis, measured over that hinge length.  
• The overall depth h is again indicated at the right.

How it ties into the code text  
– In simplified plastic analysis (EN 1992-1-1 § 5.6.2), the formation of plastic hinges over a length of approximately 1.2 h (0.6 h on each side of the plastic section) is assumed.  
– The required plastic rotation capacity θs is calculated from the design bending moments and material properties, ensuring that the actual plastic hinge can develop without brittle failure.  
– These idealizations allow designers to check ultimate limit states in continuous beams or one‐way slabs without full non-linear analysis, provided the steel reinforcement (classes B or C) and concrete strength fall within prescribed limits and that hinge zones remain ductile.

There are four distinct curves—two for each reinforcement class—distinguished by line style and by concrete strength class annotations near each curve:

1. Class C reinforcement:  
  - Rendered as a dashed line.  
  - Two variants are shown:  
    • “≤ C 50/60” (higher dashed curve): starts at ~18 mrad when xu/d = 0, rises sharply to a peak of approximately 32 mrad around xu/d ≈ 0.10–0.12, then falls nearly linearly to about 25 mrad at xu/d ≈ 0.30 and down to ~8 mrad by xu/d = 0.45.  
    • “C 90/105” (lower dashed curve): begins near 17 mrad at xu/d = 0, peaks around 30–31 mrad at xu/d ≈ 0.10–0.15, then declines to roughly 15 mrad by xu/d ≈ 0.35 and to about 7 mrad at xu/d = 0.45.

2. Class B reinforcement:  
  - Rendered as a solid line.  
  - Two variants are shown:  
    • “≤ C 50/60” (upper solid curve): starts at roughly 8 mrad at xu/d = 0, increases to a maximum of about 14 mrad at xu/d ≈ 0.15, then decreases approximately linearly to around 6 mrad at xu/d = 0.45.  
    • “C 90/105” (lower solid curve): starts near 7 mrad at xu/d = 0, climbs to about 13 mrad at xu/d ≈ 0.15, then tapers off to roughly 5 – 6 mrad by xu/d = 0.45.

Overall, the graph quantifies how the ultimate permissible plastic rotation capacity of a reinforced-concrete cross section varies with the position of its neutral axis (xu/d), the type of steel (Class B vs. Class C), and the concrete strength class (≤ C 50/60 vs. C 90/105). It is intended to guide designers in structural plastic analysis (EN 1992-1-1) when checking hinge rotations at ultimate limit states.

The illustration is a seven-part schematic, captioned “Figure 5.7: Examples of different buckling modes and corresponding effective lengths for isolated members.” Each subfigure (a through g) shows a slender, prismatic column of actual length l subjected to an axial compressive load (vertical downward arrow). The dashed line in each sketch traces the first‐mode buckled shape. Symbols at the ends denote support conditions: a small circle for a pinned (hinged) end, a thick black block or filled line for a fixed (built‐in) end, and the absence of a symbol for a free end. Beside each column is the corresponding effective buckling length l₀ expressed in terms of the actual length l.

a) Pinned–pinned (both ends hinged). The member deflects in a single half‐sine wave. l₀ = l  
b) Fixed–free (one end built‐in, one end free). The buckled shape is a quarter‐sine; the free end moves most. l₀ = 2 l  
c) Fixed–pinned (one end built‐in, the opposite end hinged). The dash curve is neither full nor quarter sine, reflecting intermediate restraint. l₀ ≈ 0.7 l  
d) Fixed–fixed (both ends built‐in). The first‐mode shape has two quarter‐waves meeting at mid-height. l₀ = 0.5 l  
e) Hinged–restrained by a rigid diaphragm or floor above (mode with rotation θ shown at the top support). Although one end can rotate by θ, the horizontal bracing makes the effective length equal to the clear member height. l₀ = l  
f) Partially restrained at both ends (rotations θ shown): neither fully pinned nor fully fixed, so the effective length falls between 0.5 l and l. 0.5 l < l₀ < l  
g) Support conditions that provide less restraint than fixed–free (rotation plus translation at ends), producing a buckled shape more extreme than (b). l₀ > 2 l  

Below the sketches, the caption reiterates that these are idealized “isolated members,” meaning each column is treated separately (without interaction from adjacent columns or walls) when determining its effective buckling length. In the context of Eurocode 2 (EN 1992-1-1), this figure feeds into the calculation of slenderness λ = l₀/i (Section 5.8.3.1), where i is the radius of gyration of the (uncracked) cross‐section. The various l₀/l ratios shown here are used to adjust the classical Euler buckling formulas to account for real boundary-condition effects in reinforced‐concrete members.

The graphic reproduced in “Figure 5.8 Definition of eccentricities eᵧ and e_z” is a black-and-white line drawing of a member’s cross-section (shown as an ellipse) together with its principal axes, overall dimensions and the position of the resultant axial force.  Key features of the figure are:

1. Cross-section outline  
   – Depicted as an ellipse (shaded), representing a member with constant symmetrical cross-section.  
   – The centroid of the section is at the geometric centre of the ellipse.

2. Principal axes and dimensions  
   – A vertical arrow labelled “z” at the top, and a horizontal arrow labelled “y” at the right, indicate the principal directions.  
   – The overall depth of the section in the z‐direction is denoted by “b” (shown as a vertical dimension line alongside the ellipse).  
   – The overall breadth in the y‐direction is denoted by “h” (shown as a horizontal dimension line below the ellipse).  

3. Radii of gyration  
   – Along the vertical (z) direction, two small horizontal tick marks inside the ellipse define “i_z” (distance from the centroid to the top or bottom of the ellipse).  
   – Along the horizontal (y) direction, two small vertical tick marks define “i_y” (distance from the centroid to the left or right of the ellipse).  
   – These represent the section’s radii of gyration about the corresponding axes.

4. Axial force and eccentricities  
   – A circle with a cross inside (⨂) is placed to the right of the centroid, indicating the line of action of the design axial force N_Ed.  
   – A dimension line from the section’s central vertical axis to the load symbol is labelled “eᵧ,” the eccentricity along the y‐axis.  
   – A dimension line from the section’s central horizontal axis down to the load symbol is labelled “e_z,” the eccentricity along the z‐axis.  

5. Governing criteria (shown as text above and beside the drawing)  
   – It states the conditions under which biaxial bending can be neglected:  
     “eᵧ / h_eq ≤ 0,2  or  e_z / b_eq ≤ 0,2”  
   – Definitions given in the caption/text:  
     • b, h  are the gross section width and depth  
     • b_eq = i_y ⋅ √12 ;  h_eq = i_z ⋅ √12  (effective rectangular‐section dimensions)  
     • λᵧ, λ_z  are slenderness ratios l₀ / i in each principal direction  
     • i_y, i_z  are the radii of gyration about the y and z axes  
     • e_z = M_Edy / N_Ed ;  eᵧ = M_Edz / N_Ed  (eccentricities from the respective second‐order design moments)  
     • M_Edy  is the design moment about the y-axis including second‐order effects  
     • M_Edz  is the design moment about the z-axis including second‐order effects  
     • N_Ed  is the design value of axial force in the member  

Overall, the figure conveys in schematic form the geometry of a symmetric cross-section, its principal inertial axes, how to locate and measure eccentricities of an axial load from those axes, and the limit conditions (in terms of normalized eccentricities) under which the simpler uniaxial‐bending checks may be applied instead of a full biaxial‐bending analysis.

The table is labeled “Table 5.1: Coefficients of friction μ of post-tensioned internal tendons and external unbonded tendons.” Its purpose is to provide characteristic values of the friction coefficient μ to be used when calculating prestress losses due to tendon‐duct interaction (see EN 1992-1-1, clause 5.10.4). These values enter into Expression (5.45) for friction losses ∆Pμ(x) = Pmax·[1 – exp(–(θ·μ + k)x)], where μ is the coefficient of friction between tendon and duct, θ is the accumulated angle along the tendon, and k is an allowance for unintended deviations.

  – Adjacent to each shear cut, on the side into which the beam would crack under shear, a pair of dimension bars mark off a length “lbd” measured from the section face back into the beam.  
  – This zone of length “lbd” is the anchorage‐ or development‐length zone prescribed by Eurocode 2 for defining which longitudinal bars contribute to shear resistance.

  – From each shear section cut, a dashed line is drawn back into the beam at an angle of 45°, signifying the likely path of a principal shear crack under loading.  

• Longitudinal tension reinforcement and the area Asl  
  – Within each “lbd” zone, the longitudinal tension bars are sketched as solid black lines.  
  – A downward‐pointing leader arrow from the label “Asl” indicates the total cross‐sectional area of all such bars whose length beyond the section cut is at least lbd + d.  
  – The reinforcing bars are shown extending continuously through the crack plane and well into the development‐length zone.  

• Cross‐section marker “A–A”  
  – Underneath each tension‐bar group, a box marked “A” (twice) indicates that if one were to take a transverse section at that location, it would be labelled “Section A–A.”  In practice, that section area is used to compute the reinforcement ratio ρl = Asl / (bw d).  

Interpretation in context of Expression (6.2) (VRd,c):  
– Asl is the sum of the areas of those longitudinal bars lying on the tension side that extend at least lbd + d from the shear section.  
– The beam depth d locates the tension steel cover and lever arm.  
– The 45° line illustrates that bars crossing a potential inclined shear crack are the ones counted.  
– The nominal web width bw (not shown) together with d and ρl feeds into the concrete shear resistance VRd,c = [CRd,c·(100 ρl fck)^(1/3) + k1 σcp]·bw d.

General layout  
• A horizontal flange (top hat) is shown in section – this could be a slab flange or a beam flange – sitting on a vertical web.  
• A concentrated downward load on the flange is sketched by a short, heavy downward arrow at the slab surface.  

Shear‐reinforcement bar  
• A single straight bar enters from the right, at approximately mid-web height, horizontally.  
• That bar is bent through 90° into the flange, runs along the underside of the flange for a short distance, then is bent back down or hooked.  
• From the hook it continues as an inclined leg crossing the web-flange interface at an angle α (measured from the vertical). This inclined leg represents the shear‐reinforcement element that intercepts potential diagonal shear cracks.

• “av” is shown by a horizontal double‐arrow dimension from the left face of the web to the line of action of the applied load. In shear‐span terminology av is the distance from the critical shear section to the point of load application.  
• A reduced length “0,75 av” is indicated by a shorter arrow above the flange, marking the lever arm over which the direct strut action is effective in very short spans (i.e. when av < 2 d, see EN 1992-1-1 Clause 6.2.3(8) and (6)).

- By engaging the flange and web in this bent‐leg arrangement, the bar acts both as a local tie in the flange, and as an inclined stirrup that can directly carry diagonal shear (shear cracks) in extremely short spans.  
- The use of “0,75 av” reflects a simplified reduction of the shear span for concentrated loads close to supports (see Expression (6.19)): the contribution of the load to shear resistance may be reduced when av < 2 d, and the effective shear‐span becomes 0,75 av instead of av.

- Clause 6.2.3(8): reduction of shear force by β = av/(2 d) for av between 0,5 d and 2 d, and limiting 0,75 av as an effective lever arm.  
- Clause 6.2.3(6): cot α limits for concrete struts and shear‐link inclination.  
- Clause 8.4–8.6: requirements for anchorage length of bent bars, minimum cover, hook geometry and anchorage coefficients (α1…α5) that control lbd.  

Overall, the sketch conveys a practical detailing solution for punching or diagonal shear in “short shear spans” by means of a single bent shear bar anchored into the flange, engaging the web at a controlled angle α and over a reduced span of 0,75 av.

A line‐drawing schematic entitled “Figure 6.9: Indented construction joint” shows in cross‐section the interface between an existing (old) concrete member and newly cast concrete, arranged so that load transfer by shear and bond is enhanced by a toothed or indented profile. Three distinct regions are shaded or lettered:  
• Region A (hatched diagonal lines sloping up and to the right) marks the newly cast concrete. 
• Region B (left‐and‐right parallel lines) marks the original, old concrete. 
• Region C (unshaded or lightly hatched) indicates the construction joint or neutral filler zone between old and new.  
Along the top of the joint, the new concrete (A) forms a horizontal “tooth” extending into the old (B), with a total horizontal projection denoted h₂. A dimension line above this tooth shows “h₂ ≤ 10 d,” where d is the nominal diameter of reinforcing bars crossing the joint. Likewise, beneath the joint the old concrete forms a matching tooth of depth h₁ into the new, with “h₁ ≤ 10 d.” Horizontal dimension arrows mark both h₁ and h₂ relative to a baseline through the joint.  
At the right end of the profile, a triangular‐shaped projection is shown; its sloping face makes an acute angle α with the horizontal. An arc and two radial lines emanating from the pivot at the base of the triangle define α, with text “45° ≤ α ≤ 9 ” (intended “90°”). This calls for the slope of every inclined face in the saw‐tooth profile to be no flatter than 45° and no steeper than 90° to the horizontal, ensuring adequate mechanical interlock.  
Vertical phantom lines bound the region of interest and suggest multiple repeating teeth. The saw‐tooth has flat horizontal crests at the new‐old interface, vertical “risers” at the back of each tooth, and inclined sloping faces at the front, forming a continuous zig‐zag path for shear forces.  
Overall, the figure conveys three key detailing rules for an indented construction joint in reinforced concrete:  
 1. Matching teeth must penetrate both new and old concrete by lengths not exceeding ten bar diameters (h₁, h₂ ≤ 10 d).  
 2. The inclined faces of the teeth must form angles α within 45° to 90° to ensure proper shear transfer and prevent concrete splitting.  
 3. The repeating jagged profile provides a mechanical key so that after the new concrete sets, loads crossing the joint are resisted not just by bond but also by interlock.
