The illustration, labeled “Figure 6.12: Verification model for punching shear at the ultimate limit state,” comprises two coordinated views—a cross-sectional sketch (a) above and a plan sketch (b) below—that together define the manner in which a concentrated load acting over a small loaded area is checked against the shear capacity of a slab or foundation.

1. Cross-Sectional View (a)  
  • The topmost horizontal lines represent the slab’s top surface (upper line) and its underside (lower line), separated by the slab’s total depth "h."  
  • From the underside, two vertical “column” elements rise up into the slab. The left column is shown at a horizontal distance “2d” from a control section; the right column is at a distance “c” (a more general loaded-area projection). Here “d” denotes the slab’s effective depth (distance from the top surface to the centroid of the tension reinforcement).  
  • A pair of inclined lines, each meeting the top of a column and intersecting the underside of the slab at a shallow angle θ, mark the “basic control sections.” These sloping lines illustrate the critical sections over which shear forces are evaluated; the figure indicates θ = arctan(1/2) ≈ 26.6°.  
  • A dashed vertical line bisecting the sketch hints that the slab extends into and beyond the plane of the page.  

2. Plan View (b)  
  • At the center is a small solid circle labeled “D – loaded area Aload.” This represents the footprint of the concentrated load (e.g. the column head or footing pad) bearing on the slab.  
  • Surrounding that is a lightly shaded annular region swept by a heavy dashed line at a radius equal to “2d.” This circular path is the “C – basic control perimeter u1.” It lies at a constant distance 2d from the edge of the loaded area and is where the punching shear stress is checked.  
  • Outside this, a larger dashed perimeter marked “rcont – further control perimeter” indicates the location beyond which shear reinforcement is not required once the basic check has been satisfied.  
  • The region between the loaded area and the basic control perimeter is hatched and labeled “B – basic control area Ac1.” This area is that portion of the slab which effectively transmits shear to the surrounding concrete outside the load patch.  

Key points illustrated and defined by this figure:  
  – The “basic control perimeter” is taken at a distance of 2d from the loaded area’s boundary (EN 1992-1-1, cl. 6.4.2(1)).  
  – Verification of punching shear capacity involves ensuring that the shear stress vEd = VEd/(u1·d) does not exceed the design resistance vRd,c at that perimeter.  
  – If vEd > vRd,c, shear reinforcement must be provided and extended until an outer perimeter uout,ef (shown here as rcont) is reached where vEd ≤ vRd,c.  

By combining the sectional and plan representations, the figure encapsulates the standard punching-shear check: locate the critical shear perimeter at 2d, compute design shear stresses from the known column reaction, and compare them to the concrete’s shear capacity; if necessary, detail reinforcement until the stress falls below the allowable.

The illustration is a composite figure showing:

1. A formula, rendered at top of the page, defining the “effective depth” deff for a biaxially reinforced slab in terms of the two effective depths dy and dz in orthogonal directions:
   deff = (dy + dz) / 2  
   where dy and dz are the effective depths of the reinforcement in two orthogonal directions.

2. Three plan-view sketches of typical loaded areas with their associated “basic control perimeters” u₁, each drawn at a uniform offset of two times the effective depth (2d) from the edge of the loaded area. The three cases are:

   a. Circular Loaded Area  
      – A filled‐grey circle represents, for example, a round column or circular footing load.  
      – A dashed loop drawn around the circle at a constant normal distance labeled “2d” defines u₁, the control perimeter for punching‐shear checks.  

   b. Rectangular Loaded Area  
      – A filled‐grey rectangle of width by (horizontal direction) and depth bz (vertical direction) depicts a typical rectangular column or pedestal.  
      – A dashed “rounded‐corner” rectangle surrounding it, at an outward offset of 2d in every direction, is the control perimeter u₁.  
      – Dimension arrows show the clearances 2d on each face.  

   c. T-shaped Loaded Area  
      – A filled‐grey “inverted‐T” shape stands for a T-beam or bracket bearing area.  
      – Again, a dashed outline at 2d offset—bending around all protruding legs of the T—marks the basic control perimeter u₁ for punching shear.  

3. A single caption below the three sketches reads:
   Figure 6.13: Typical basic control perimeters around loaded areas

Taken together, the formula and the three plan views illustrate how, in the punching‐shear design of slabs or footings (see EN 1992-1-1 §6.4.2), one first computes an “effective slab depth” deff from the reinforcement cover depths in the two principal directions and then traces a perimeter u₁ at a distance of 2·d (or 2·deff) around any concentrated load area (circular, rectangular or complex‐shaped). That perimeter is the locus at which punching‐shear stresses vEd are checked against the allowable shear resistance vRd,c (Expression 6.2a) and, if necessary, where shear reinforcement is detailed.

The illustration is a plan‐view sketch (labelled “Figure 6.14: Control perimeter near an opening”) showing how to lay out the basic punching‐shear control perimeter for a loaded area that lies close to a free edge or hole in a flat slab.  Key features are:

– Loaded area A: drawn as a filled‐in (black) sector inside the slab.  This could represent the face of a column, a point load region or any small concentrated load patch.  
– Effective depth d: the vertical distance from the slab’s top surface down to its centroid of (tension) reinforcement.  A dimension “2d” is marked normal to one edge of A to show that the basic control perimeter u₁ is to be set at a distance of 2d all around A.  
– Adjacent opening or edge: immediately to the left of the loaded area is a rectangular cut‐out in the slab (e.g. a window, access opening or slab edge).  Its outline is drawn in plan, and the loaded area A lies within 6 d of that opening.  
– Basic control perimeter (u₁): shown as a broken (dashed) line at 2 d from the face of A.  However, because part of that 2d–perimeter would lie inside the opening (i.e. unsupported concrete), that portion of the circle is deemed “ineffective” and is omitted.  
– Modified control perimeter: around the opening, the dashed line is replaced by tangents drawn from the corners of the loaded area A to the edges of the opening.  These tangents mark the new boundary of u₁ in regions where the 2d ring would otherwise pass through the opening.  
– Dimensional notation l₁ and l₂: above the plan view two horizontal arrows indicate two possible cases of the opening’s width relative to its distance from A:  
     • In the left sub‐sketch l₁ ≤ l₂, meaning the opening’s projection toward A is not so large that it completely overlaps the 2d band.  The modified control perimeter simply cuts off the 2d ring where it meets the opening.  
     • In the right sub‐sketch l₁ > l₂, meaning the opening is wide enough that two tangents are needed on opposite faces of A; in this case the perimeter has two straight segments on either side of the opening that are longer than in the first case.  
– Shaded strip: immediately adjacent to A and bounded by the new perimeter.  This dark shaded zone indicates the slice of slab (of width d, sloping down into the plane) at which the punching shear stress vEd is to be evaluated.  In practice one would compute the shear force carried by this band and divide by the perimeter length and depth d to check vEd against the design shear resistance vRd,c (see Eurocode 2 § 6.4.2).  
– Caption and call‐out “A”: a boxed label pointing to the loaded area identifies it as the region under concentrated action.  

Taken together, the figure demonstrates the Eurocode rule that if the basic 2 d control perimeter around a loaded area would intersect an unsupported opening or free edge, the perimeter must be “clipped” back to tangents drawn to the opening’s edges.  This ensures that shear is only checked where concrete actually exists, and that unsupported portions do not artificially widen the critical punching loop.

The illustration consists of three small plan-view sketches showing how to draw the “basic control perimeter” u₁ around a concentrated load (or support reaction) that lies close to one or two free edges of a slab or foundation.  In every case:  
– The shaded (cross-hatched) block represents the loaded area or column footprint.  
– The continuous lines at top or at left/right represent the free edges of the slab or the boundary of the soil pressure zone.  
– The dashed curve is the control perimeter u₁, traced at a constant distance of 2·d away from the loaded area, but trimmed where it would lie outside the slab.  Here d is the slab’s effective depth.  

Sketch (a) shows a rectangular load located near one edge:  
•  A distance 2·d is measured outwards from all edges of the rectangle, but where this clearance would fall outside the slab, the curve “hugs” the slab edge instead.  
•  To the left and above the rectangle you see the slab edges; the dashed line “drops down” from those edges and wraps around the two exposed sides of the load block.  

Sketch (b) is the same situation viewed symmetrically against a single support edge.  The control perimeter again remains 2·d from the loaded area, but conforms to the free boundary when it would otherwise lie beyond it.  

Sketch (c) illustrates a load at a corner of the slab:  
•  Both horizontal and vertical free edges are present.  
•  The control perimeter is again drawn at 2·d, but since two sides of the rectangle are already on the slab boundary, the u₁ curve only bulges into the interior, forming roughly a quarter-circle shape.  

Altogether, these diagrams emphasize that when a load is close to an edge or corner, the basic control perimeter for punching shear checks is still nominally at 2·d, but must be truncated by the actual slab limits.  The zone between the loaded area and this perimeter is where shear stress and potential punching failure are evaluated.

This is a schematic section through a shallow footing of variable thickness, illustrating how the critical (“control”) section for punching‐shear is located when the slab or base slab has sloping sides. Key features and annotations are as follows:

– Overall geometry  
  • At the top, a rectangular column or pedestal sits centrally on a thickened zone of the footing. That loaded area is marked “A” and is the region over which vertical pressure from the column is transmitted.  
  • Below the loaded area the footing has maximum thickness, then its underside slopes outward to a thinner edge slab. This taper produces a variable depth from the loaded zone out to the perimeter.

– Control section depth “d”  
  • On the right side a vertical dimension line labeled “d” measures the effective depth from the underside of the loaded area down to the level where the punching‐shear check is made.  
  • Even though the concrete section thickness varies outside the loaded area, the control plane is taken at a constant vertical distance “d” beneath all points of the loaded perimeter.

– Inclined projection lines and angle θ  
  • From each corner of the loaded area “A” two oblique solid lines fan outward, tracing the edges of the region of influence where shear stresses must be checked.  
  • Dashed lines close to those solids represent the usual 45° (or arctan 1) lines often used in simplified punching‐shear models. A note “θ ≥ arctan ( )” reminds the designer that the minimum inclination of these lines must not be smaller than the angle at which concrete struts are assumed (typically ≥ 45°).  

– Purpose in design  
  • This detail shows how to locate the perimeter at which shear stresses v_Ed should be compared to the design punching‐shear resistance v_Rd,c (see EN 1992-1-1, Clause 6.4.2).  
  • In a uniform‐depth slab the control section is simply horizontal at d below the loaded area. Here, because the slab thickness reduces beyond the thickened portion, the control plane remains horizontal and cuts through the thinner edge region at depth d.  

– Annotations and figure caption  
  • The top‐loaded block is explicitly labeled “A – load.”  
  • At the bottom of the drawing, the caption reads:  
    “Figure 6.16: Depth of control section in a footing with variable depth.”  

In practice, the engineer uses this graphic to ensure that, even when footing thickness tapers, the basic punching‐shear check is carried out at a constant distance d beneath the loaded footprint. The oblique projection lines help define the one‐way spread of shear stresses and confirm that the critical section lies entirely within the uniform “edge slab” outside the thickened zone.

The diagram is a vertical cross‐section through a one‐way slab with an enlarged column head, illustrating the special control perimeters used for punching‐shear verification when the head projection lₕ is less than twice the head depth hₕ (i.e. lₕ < 2·hₕ). Key features, dimensions and annotation are as follows:

• Slab and column head geometry  
  – The horizontal slab has a total effective depth d (measured from the top soffit to the neutral axis or centroid of tension reinforcement).  
  – Beneath the slab lies a column head of depth hₕ. The head projects equally on both sides of the column, with clear projection c measured from the column face to the underside of the slab bearing surface.  

• Basic loaded area (B) and basic control perimeter (A)  
  – Point B in the sketch marks the outline of the area on which the reaction or concentrated load from the column is assumed to act (this is normally the column section itself).  
  – Point A identifies the “basic control perimeter,” u₁, which in this special case coincides with the outer perimeter traced at a radial distance r_cont from the centre of the column.  

• Control‐perimeter location r_cont  
  – The sketch shows r_cont measured horizontally from the column centroid to the control section in the slab (outside the column head).  
  – According to the clause noted in the accompanying text, because lₕ < 2·hₕ, punching shear need be checked only at this single exterior perimeter. The distance r_cont is given by one of the prescribed expressions:  
      • r_cont = 2·d + lₕ + 0.5·c (for circular head), or  
      • r_cont = 2·d + 0.56·(l₂·l₁)^½ or 2·d + 0.69·l₁, whichever is smaller, in the rectangular‐head case.  

• Inclined strut representation  
  – A dashed line indicates the assumed concrete‐strut path (angle θ) that carries compression from the slab underside back down into the column head.  
  – A second dashed line with angle θ′ shows the hypothetical strut from the loaded area up through the slab. The angles illustrate the inclination of internal compression fields used in strut‐and‐tie or punching‐shear truss models.  

• Symmetry and annotation  
  – The vertical centreline denotes a symmetry plane: the geometry on left and right halves is identical.  
  – Dimension arrows and lettered call‐outs (“A” for the control perimeter; “B” for the loaded area) tie back to the standard punching‐shear procedure described in the text.  

By showing only the external control section and omitting an interior control perimeter, the figure embodies the exception in Eurocode 2 that, for slab‐heads deeper than half their projection length, the punching‐shear check need only be applied to the perimeter outside the enlarged head.

The figure is a schematic cross‐section through a flat slab that has an enlarged column head (or “drop panel”) where the projection of that head beyond the underside of the slab, lH, exceeds twice the sum of the slab’s effective depth and the head thickness (i.e. lH > 2·(d + hH)).  It is labelled “Figure 6.18: Slab with enlarged column head where lH > 2(d + hH).”

General layout  
- A horizontal slab of total depth h (not all shown) carries a regular grid of top reinforcement (small black circles) and bottom reinforcement (small red circles).  The centroid of the bottom steel defines the effective depth, d, measured from the slab’s top surface down to the level of the bottom bars.  
- Directly below the slab is a column head of constant thickness hH, wider than the column shaft.  The column width at slab level (i.e. the width of the shaft) is shown as c.  Below the column head the shaft continues (not dimensioned in this figure).

Control perimeters for punching shear  
- Two concentric “control perimeters” are defined around the column centre line, at the slab underside, to check punching shear:  
  • r_cont,int (the inner control radius) is shown as a bracket and arrow from the column centre to a dashed vertical line.  Its value follows Expression (6.37):  
     r_cont,int = 2·(d + hH) + 0.5·c  
  • r_cont,ext (the outer control radius) is the larger bracket extending to the line of red reinforcement dots on the slab underside.  It follows Expression (6.36):  
     r_cont,ext = 2·d + lH + 0.5·c  

• Along both perimeters small filled circles mark the locations at which the shear stress is checked (often three or four points equally spaced in plan).  

Strut inclination  
- A dashed diagonal line represents the theoretical concrete “strut” in a punching‐shear truss model and is inclined at an angle θ of 26.6° to the vertical, as shown.  This angle defines the direction of the principal compressive stress trajectory from the loaded area toward the perimeter.  

Two viewing boxes  
- On the right the letter “A” in a box indicates the view on the “outer” perimeter (r_cont,ext) where punching shear is usually first checked.  
- On the left the letter “B” in a box indicates the view on the “inner” perimeter (r_cont,int), closer to the column head, which may govern if the head is large enough to intercept the shear cone.  

Key dimensions and labels  
- d: the slab’s effective depth, measured from top surface to centroid of bottom bars.  
- hH: additional depth of the enlarged column head below the slab underside.  
- c: width of the column flange (i.e. the column shaft’s dimension at slab level).  
- lH: the horizontal projection of the column head beyond the column shaft on each side (not shown dimensioned but implied in r_cont,ext formula).  
- θ = 26.6°: the strut‐angle used for shear‐cone geometry.  

Context in EN 1992-1-1  
This detail illustrates how to locate the punching‐shear control perimeters when a slab incorporates an enlarged column head (“drop head”).  By extending the shear cone through the head, the inner perimeter moves out to intercept the head’s face (r_cont,int), then the usual 2d offset (plus half the column width) defines the outer perimeter (r_cont,ext).  These distances ensure the correct application of Expressions (6.36) and (6.37) for punching‐shear checks in Section 6.4 of the Eurocode.

The illustration is a schematic for sizing concrete struts in a strut‐and‐tie model when the strut carries compression only (i.e. no transverse tension).  It is labelled “6.23: Design strength of concrete struts without transverse tension.”  Key features and annotations are as follows:

1. Geometry of the strut  
   • The strut is represented as a solid rectangular block (shown in cross-section) that spans horizontally between two supporting nodes.  
   • Its depth into the page is not shown; the drawing is a 2-D cross-section through the strut.  

2. Loading on the strut  
   • Vertical compressive loads (arrows pointing downward) are applied along the top surface of the strut.  A matching set of vertical arrows (pointing upward) act on the bottom surface.  These depict the normal compressive force distributed over the strut’s width.  
   • Large horizontal arrows at each end of the strut illustrate the net compressive force along the strut axis.  The left‐hand arrow points rightward, and the right‐hand arrow points leftward, showing that the strut is in axial compression between two nodes or loading points.  

3. Region A designation  
   • A small square marked “A” is placed adjacent to the side of the strut.  This refers to “region A” in the code clause and denotes that in this region the concrete strut is subject either to (a) transverse compressive stress on its side faces or (b) no transverse stress at all.  In either case, no tensile stress acts across the sides of the strut.  

4. Design strength symbol  
   • Above the right‐hand horizontal arrow is the notation “σ_Rd,max,” indicating the design value of the maximum compressive stress the concrete strut may carry without transverse tension.  

5. Caption and context  
   • Below the diagram is the caption “6.23: Design strength of concrete struts without transverse tension.”  In Eurocode-2 this figure accompanies clause 6.5.2(1), which states that for struts in region A the maximum allowable design stress σ_Rd,max may be taken equal to f_cd (the design compressive strength of concrete).  

In summary, the drawing conveys that when a concrete strut carries only axial compression (and no side‐face tension), its design compressive stress need not be reduced for tension effects, and may be taken up to f_cd.  The double set of vertical arrows emphasizes the distributed nature of the compressive load on top and bottom surfaces, while the large horizontal arrows show the axial load path.  The region “A” call-out reminds the engineer that this benign case (transverse compression or zero transverse stress) allows full use of the concrete’s compressive capacity.

The image is a simple schematic entitled “Figure 6.24: Design strength of concrete struts with transverse tension.” At its core is a horizontal concrete block drawn in cross-section. The block is represented as a solid rectangle whose interior is hatched with closely spaced, thin horizontal lines—these lines evoke layers of reinforcement or the “web” of the strut where transverse splitting might occur.  

On each of the left and right narrow faces of the block there is a single large solid arrow, drawn in black, pointing inward toward the block’s center. These opposing arrows illustrate the compressive force being applied to the strut from both ends. Immediately adjacent to the right arrow, just outside the block’s face, the notation “σ_Rd,max” is placed, indicating the design compressive stress at which the strut reaches its ultimate capacity under transverse tension.  

Inside the block, arranged in two vertical columns, are sets of small arrows: four arrows pointing upward and four arrows pointing downward. These internal arrows symbolically represent the tensile splitting stresses that develop transversely (i.e. perpendicular to the main compression direction) due to Poisson effects or crack‐induced expansion. They make clear that, under high compressive loading, the concrete strut must also resist these transverse tensile forces.  

No dimensions, scales or numeric values appear on the drawing—its purpose is purely conceptual. The clean, black-and-white line art uses no shading beyond the interior hatching; all arrows and text are rendered in a single consistent stroke weight. The caption sits beneath the rectangle, identifying this as the standard design detail for accounting for transverse tension when determining the maximum allowable compressive stress in cracked concrete struts.  

Overall, the diagram communicates that concrete members under axial compression must be checked not only for crushing in the loading direction but also for the transverse tension that tends to split the strut apart, and that the peak allowable stress σ_Rd,max must reflect both effects.

A left-hand gutter strip shows the standard’s designation and national annex date. The body of the page is part of Clause 6.5 (Strut-and-tie models) and specifically addresses the calculation of transverse tensile forces in smeared-reinforcement compression fields (nodes and discontinuity regions).

• a) for partial discontinuity regions (b ≤ H/2), see Figure 6.25 a:  
  T = (1/4) · (b–a)/b · F  

• b) for full discontinuity regions (b > H/2), see Figure 6.25 b:

The image is a schematic representation of a concrete “compression node without ties,” as used in strut‐and‐tie modeling for regions where plane‐section assumptions break down (e.g. corbels, deep beams, concentrated loads).  Key features and annotations are as follows:

1. Geometry of the node  
   - The node is drawn as an approximately triangular solid of concrete.  
   - Its base is a horizontal bearing surface (e.g. support or loaded area), shown as a thick black line at the bottom.  
   - Three struts of concrete meet at a central apex:  
     • One vertical strut (in the middle), transmitting the total incoming compression.  
     • Two symmetrically or asymmetrically inclined struts, one sloping up and left, the other sloping up and right.

2. Compressive forces in the struts  
   - F_cd,1 denotes the vertical compressive force emerging from the base.  
   - F_cd,1 is resolved into two contributions at the base: F_cd,1l (left) and F_cd,1r (right) along the bearing surface. They sum to F_cd,1.  
   - The central vertical strut carries a compressive stress labeled σ_c0 at its mid‐height.  
   - Along the left‐inclined strut, the compressive force is labeled F_cd,2; along the right‐inclined strut, it is F_cd,3.

3. Tie forces (steel reinforcement)  
   - Although captioned “without ties,” the small round symbols at the ends of the inclined struts hint at locations where tensile forces could be taken by reinforcement in a tied node.  
   - At the toe of each strut (where it meets the assumed tie), a design tensile resistance σ_Rd,i is indicated (σ_Rd,2 on the left, σ_Rd,3 on the right, and implicitly σ_Rd,1 for the base).

4. Strut lengths and angles  
   - Below each strut is a dimension a_i:  
     • a₁ is the vertical distance from the base face to the central node apex, measured along the vertical strut.  
     • a₂ is the length of the left‐inclined strut from the node apex down to its heel.  
     • a₃ is the analogous length on the right.  
   - Implicitly, each strut makes an angle θᵢ with the vertical or horizontal, governing the ratio of compressive to tensile forces in the adjoining tie (not shown).

5. Annotation conventions  
   - Solid arrows along struts show the direction of compressive force flow toward the node or away from it.  
   - Small black‐filled circles mark the idealized “nodes” or joints where struts and (absent) ties intersect.  
   - Greek letters denote stress levels:  
     • σ_c0 at the node center (multiaxial compression stress).  
     • σ_Rd,i at each tie location (design tensile stress capacity).  
   - Subscripts in F_cd,i and σ_Rd,i index the branch (1 = vertical/base, 2 = left strut, 3 = right strut).

Taken together, this diagram encapsulates the force‐equilibrium of a three‐legged compression node: the sum of compressive thrusts (F_cd,2 + F_cd,3) must equal the incoming vertical compressive force F_cd,1, and any tensile demand (absent here) would be carried by ties sized to resist σ_Rd,i over an anchorage length. While no actual reinforcement ties are drawn (“without ties”), the notation makes clear where and how such ties would be placed if required to maintain equilibrium in tension zones of a discontinuity region.

This drawing (labelled “Fig. 6.27: Compression-tension node with reinforcement provided in one direction”) illustrates a strut-and-tie model node in reinforced concrete where one set of tensile reinforcement (“tie”) balances two compressive struts. It is shown in an oblique/perspective view to emphasize three-dimensional geometry, force paths and key dimensions.  

Overall geometry  
• Node body – a roughly trapezoidal solid representing concrete confined by compression in two directions and tension in one. Its “thickness” (dimension out of the page) is denoted u. Jagged hatching on the left faces suggests compressive stress distribution in the concrete struts.  
• Reinforcement – three parallel lines (bars) run horizontally through the middle of the node, representing the tension tie. They emerge from the right face and are anchored along a development length l_bd measured along the centre-line of the bars.  

Compression struts and forces  
• Lower compression strut (horizontal): At the bottom left face, a vertical upward-pointing arrow is marked F_cd1. Directly above that arrow is a shaded rectangular patch on the face, annotated σ_Rd,1, showing the design compressive stress in that region.  
• Upper compression strut (inclined): On the top left face, an inclined downward-pointing arrow labelled F_cd2 acts on a hatched patch annotated σ_Rd,2. The strut slopes down from the drawing’s upper left toward the tie in the mid-section.  

Tension tie and force  
• Tie force: On the right face, three horizontal arrows pointing right are labelled F_td, indicating the resultant tensile force carried by the reinforcement.  

Key dimensions and clearances  
• Tie centreline spacing: The vertical distance between the tie centreline and each compression face is broken into three equal segments: s₀ (top), s (middle) and s₀ (bottom). These illustrate the requirement for balanced clearances above and below the reinforcement.  
• Overall thickness u: Measured from the outermost compression face vertically to the opposite face, covering the two s₀ segments plus the tie corridor s.  
• Compression chord lengths:  
  – a₁ is the horizontal distance from the tie centre to the end of the lower compression patch (toe of the bottom strut).  
  – a₂ is the corresponding length measured along the inclined top chord from tie centre to toe of the upper strut.  
• Development length l_bd: Measured along the tie’s centreline, extending from the face plane to the point where the steel reaches full stress transfer.  
• Minimum edge distance: A note “≥ 2 s₀” indicates that the anchorage and strut toes must lie at least twice the s₀ distance from the outer edges to ensure sufficient concrete cover and confinement.  

Annotations  
• σ_Rd,1 and σ_Rd,2 denote design values of concrete compressive stress in the two struts.  
• F_cd1 and F_cd2 are the applied or resulting compressive forces in the lower and upper struts, respectively.  
• F_td is the tensile force in the reinforcement tie.  
• All dimensions (u, s₀, s, a₁, a₂, l_bd) and forces are integral to verifying equilibrium and ensuring the node zone can develop the required stresses without crushing or splitting of the concrete nor bond failure of the steel.  

This figure encapsulates the essential parameters for designing a compression-tension node with one-direction reinforcement: geometry, force paths, clearances and anchorage requirements in a strut-and-tie model.

The graphic is a schematic “strut‐and‐tie” node (Eurocode-2 Figure 6.28), showing a concrete compression strut that fans into two sets of tension ties (reinforcing bars) in orthogonal directions. Its principal elements are:

• Concrete strut (σRd,max)  
  – Shaded triangular‐wedge shape in the middle  
  – One curved end (top left) represents the region where the strut develops from a loaded or supported boundary (e.g. a column head or bearing plate)  
  – The other end converges to an internal “node” point marked by an X—this is where the compressive stress σRd,max is checked  

• Compression force  
  – Arrow labeled Fcd acting normal to the face of the strut (pointing toward the node)  

• Tension ties (Ftd,1 and Ftd,2)  
  – Two sets of parallel bars represent reinforcement anchored into the node  
  – One set projects to the right, arrowed as Ftd,1  
  – One set projects downward, arrowed as Ftd,2  
  – Each group of bars is shown with typical reinforcing‐bar cross‐section hatching at its insertion face  

• Geometry and dimensions  
  – The two faces of the strut that meet the ties are each dimensioned “a1” (bottom face toward Ftd,2) and “a2” (sloping face toward Ftd,1)  
  – These represent the width of the compression strut bearing on each tie direction and are used when checking bearing stresses or designing reinforcement in the adjacent concrete  

• Overall interpretation  
  – This detail models a node where a compressive load is carried obliquely through concrete, then resisted by steel reinforcement in two mutually perpendicular directions  
  – It illustrates:  
    • How to identify the critical compression strut and its maximum stress region  
    • Where to resolve the compression force into tensile tie forces in the reinforcing bars  
    • The two orthogonal legs of the reinforcement that must be designed to carry Ftd,1 and Ftd,2 back to the rest of the structure  

• Key Eurocode-2 strut‐and‐tie principles shown

  – Detailing of reinforcement anchorage into a discontinuity region (the node)  

By representing the concrete strut as a shaded wedge, the diagram emphasizes the need to verify concrete capacity under multiaxial compression at the node, and by showing the two orthogonal tie runs, it underlines the requirement to provide sufficient, properly anchored reinforcement in both directions to safely transmit the tensile reactions.

The figure, captioned “6.29: Design distribution for partially loaded areas,” is a three-dimensional schematic of a rectangular concrete element (slab or footing) illustrating how a concentrated load applied over a small area at its top face is spread out into a larger resisting area farther down in the thickness.  Key features are as follows:

• Geometry of the element  
  – Outer block: a prismatic concrete member of total thickness “h.”  
  – Loaded area A₀ (denoted Ac₀): a small, centrally located, dark‐bordered rectangular patch on the top face. Its plan dimensions in one direction are labeled “b₁.”  
  – Distribution area A₁ (denoted Ac₁): a larger, shaded rectangular patch on the underside or mid-depth plane, representing the zone over which the applied load is assumed to be carried by the concrete.  

• Load‐transfer envelope  
  – From each corner of the small top patch, dashed lines (sloping outward) extend down to the corners of the larger bottom patch. These lines trace the edges of an imaginary “wedge” or truncated pyramid that defines the region of concrete mobilizing compressive resistance.  
  – A call‐out marker “A” beside the sloping face points to one of these dashed lines and is labeled “line of action,” indicating the path along which the load is assumed to disperse.  

• Dimensional annotations and design limits  
  – Vertical dimension from top loaded area down to the level of distribution area: “d₂,” with an over‐printed inequality “d₂ ≤ 3 d₁,” enforcing that the spreading depth may not exceed three times the effective depth d₁.  
  – Effective depth e.g. for bending is shown as “d₁,” measured from the top of the loaded area down to a reference plane (often the centroid of tension reinforcement).  
  – The plan enlargement of the loaded patch is denoted by “b₂” on the underside; a note beside the bottom face reads “b₂ ≤ 3 b₁,” meaning the horizontal spread in any direction is limited to three times the original loaded‐area dimension.  
  – A dimension line between the top and bottom patches is labeled “h ≥ (b₂ – b₁)/2,” reflecting the minimum element thickness needed to achieve the required spread.  

• Centers of load and reaction  
  – On both the top and bottom patches, small filled circles mark the centroid of the loaded area (top) and the centroid of the resisting distribution area (bottom).  

• Purpose in design context  
  – The illustration underpins the code’s clause on local crushing and partial‐area loading (EN 1992-1-1 §6.3.1).  It shows how, for a uniformly applied load over Ac₀, the concentrated resistance is evaluated by enlarging the area down through the slab until the load intensity falls to an acceptable value.  The inequalities b₂ ≤ 3 b₁ and d₂ ≤ 3 d₁ ensure that pyramidal spread is realistically bounded, and the thickness requirement h ≥ (b₂ – b₁)/2 guarantees sufficient concrete to develop the bearing resistance.

In sum, the drawing conveys a design model in which a small bearing patch at the surface “fans out” through the concrete to a larger reaction area, subject to simple geometric limits on how far and how much the load may spread before checking crushing capacity or shear.

The sketch is a purely schematic S–N (stress–number of cycles) diagram plotted on double–logarithmic axes to represent the “characteristic fatigue strength curve” for reinforcing (and prestressing) steel.

Axes and general layout  
• Vertical axis (ordinate): log Δσ_Rsk, i.e. the logarithm of the design fatigue stress range Δσ_Rsk.  
• Horizontal axis (abscissa): log N, i.e. the logarithm of the number of load cycles N.  
• A single continuous curve is drawn, consisting of three main portions:  
  1. An initial horizontal plateau at the highest stress-range level (region A),  
  2. A first descending portion beyond the end of that plateau,  
  3. A second, longer descending branch after a distinct “knee” in the curve.  

Key features, left to right  
1. Region A (“reinforcement at yield”)  
   – Extends from very low cycle counts up to a first transition on the order of 10²…10³ cycles (this exact N₁ is not given numerically in the sketch).  
   – Here the fatigue stress range equals (or is very close to) the yield strength of the steel; hence the curve is essentially flat (slope ≈ 0 on the log–log plot).  
   – Above this plateau the notation “b = k₁” is shown, indicating that the fatigue curve in low-cycle regime follows a power-law exponent b₁ if one were to draw beyond pure flatness.  

2. First descending branch  
   – Begins where the plateau ends, but still at relatively low N.  
   – On the log–log plot it falls off with an approximate slope of –1 (the diagram annotates this locally as “1” beside the inclined line), meaning Δσ · N = constant in that intermediate regime.  
   – This drop continues until the curve reaches a secondary plateau.  

3. Secondary plateau (intermediate endurance level) and “knee” at N*  
   – The sketch shows a short horizontal segment at a lower stress range than region A.  
   – Immediately to its right is a vertical dashed line labelled “N*,” marking the characteristic transition cycle count between “high-cycle” and “very-high-cycle” fatigue behavior.  

4. Second descending branch  
   – For N > N*, the curve again slopes downward in log–log space, annotated with “b = k₂.”  
   – The slope magnitude is again close to 1 on the log–log plot (indicating a power-law exponent b₂), but the coefficient (k₂) is smaller than the coefficient k₁ of the first branch, so this branch lies below and declines more gradually.  

5. Asymptotic behavior  
   – Although not explicitly drawn beyond the second straight line, one infers that at extremely large N (beyond the far right of the sketch) the curve would approach an “endurance limit” or run-out life level. In practice, for some steels there is a fatigue limit below which unlimited life is assumed.  

Annotations and interpretation  
– “b = k₁” marks the exponent (slope) governing the first descending branch once the low-cycle plateau ends.  
– “b = k₂” marks the exponent for the final high-cycle branch beyond N*.  
– The boxed letter “A” on the initial plateau flags the region where the stress range corresponds to yield of the reinforcement.  
– All axes and labels are in logarithmic form; straight lines on this plot correspond to power-law relationships Δσ ∝ N⁻ᵇ.  

In summary, Figure 6.30 is a highly idealized, piecewise-linear approximation of the S–N curve for reinforcing or prestressing steel, showing:  low-cycle plateau at or near yield,  two descending power-law branches with exponents b₁ and b₂,  and a transition or “knee” at N* delineating the first and second high-cycle regimes.

The table reproduced below is taken from EN 1992-1-1 (the European Standard for the design of concrete structures) and appears in the fatigue‐related provisions of Clause 6.8. It gives the key parameters for the so-called S–N curves (stress–number of cycles curves) that are used to assess whether reinforcing steel and associated devices have adequate resistance to fatigue under repeated loading.  

Table 6.3N: Parameters for S–N curves for reinforcing steel  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Type of reinforcement           │ N*       │ Stress exponent   │ Δσ_Rsk (MPa)  
                                │          │ k₁      │ k₂       │ at N* cycles  
────────────────────────────────┼──────────┼─────────┼──────────┼────────────  
Straight and bent bars¹        │ 10⁶      │ 5       │ 9        │ 162.5      
Welded bars and wire fabrics   │ 10⁷      │ 3       │ 5        │ 58.5       
Splicing devices               │ 10⁷      │ 3       │ 5        │ 35.0       
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  

1.   N*  (reference number of cycles)  
     – This is the number of load cycles at which the characteristic stress range Δσ_Rsk is defined.  
     – Straight and bent bars use N* = 1 000 000 cycles; welded bars, wire fabrics and splicing devices use N* = 10 000 000 cycles.  

2.   Stress exponents k₁, k₂  
     – The Wöhler (S–N) curve is often expressed in the form Δσ_Rk∙N^k₂ = constant, or via separate exponents for different stress regimes.  
     – k₁ is the exponent governing the high‐cycle fatigue region; k₂ governs the lower‐cycle region.  
     – For straight and bent bars: k₁ = 5, k₂ = 9; for welded bars and wire fabrics or splicing devices: k₁ = 3, k₂ = 5.  

3.   Δσ_Rsk (characteristic stress range at N*)  
     – This is the nominal stress‐range amplitude (in MPa) below which the relevant reinforcement is assumed to survive at least N* cycles without fatigue failure (probability basis defined in EN 1992).  
     – 162.5 MPa for straight and bent bars; 58.5 MPa for welded bars and wire fabrics; 35 MPa for splicing devices.  

4.   Footnote on bent bars  
     – Bent bars (i.e. bars with hooks or bends) exhibit reduced fatigue capacity compared with straight bars. In encouraging consistency with test data, a reduction factor ζ may be applied to Δσ_Rsk:  
         ζ = 0.35 + 0.026 D/φ  
       where D is the mandrel (bend) diameter and φ is the bar diameter.  

How the table is used in design:  
– In Clause 6.8 the standard requires that fatigue damage be computed (e.g. via the Palmgren–Miner rule) and that the stress ranges imposed under characteristic load cycles do not exceed the S–N curve parameters given here.  
– For each reinforcement category, the design stress‐range under frequent or equivalent loading (∆σ_S,equ) multiplied by the appropriate partial factor must lie below Δσ_Rsk at the reference cycles N*.  
– If multiple cycle amplitudes occur, their damage fractions n_i/N(∆σ_i) are summed; the total must be < 1.  

In short, Table 6.3N provides the designer with the fatigue endurance limits and curve exponents needed to assess whether reinforcing steel details (straight bars, welded fabric, splices) will safely withstand the specified number of load cycles without fatigue‐induced cracking or failure.

The table reproduced below (Table 6.4N in EN 1992-1-1) gives the reference parameters for the S-N curves of prestressing steel. These parameters are used in the fatigue verification of prestressed members (see Clauses 6.8.5 and 6.8.7), in particular in the expression  
 n(Δσ) = k₁ · (N*)ᵏ²   
where N* is the reference number of cycles, k₁ and k₂ are material exponents, and Δσᵣₛₖ is the corresponding stress range at N* cycles.  

1. Columns and their significance  
 • “S-N curve of prestressing steel used for”  
  – Identifies the type of application or tendon arrangement: pre-tensioning versus post-tensioning, and within post-tensioning sub-categories (single strand, straight/curved tendons in plastic ducts, curved in steel ducts, splicing devices).  
 • “N*”  
  – The reference number of load cycles (in millions) at which the characteristic stress range Δσᵣₛₖ is specified. All entries here use N* = 10⁶ cycles.  
 • “stress exponent” k₁, k₂  
  – Two empirical exponents defining the slope and intercept of the S-N curve on log–log axes. They appear in the fatigue damage law: damage ∝ (Δσ)ᵏ².  
 • “Δσᵣₛₖ (MPa) at N* cycles”  
  – The stress range (in MPa) that the steel can sustain for N* cycles without fatigue failure, as read from the S-N curve.  

2. Row-by-row breakdown  

Pre-tensioning  
 • N* = 10⁶ cycles  
 • k₁ = 5, k₂ = 9  
 • Δσᵣₛₖ = 185 MPa  
 – Typical straight pre-tensioned wires or strands bonded directly to the concrete.  

Post-tensioning  
 a) single strands in plastic ducts  
  – N* = 10⁶, k₁ = 5, k₂ = 9, Δσᵣₛₖ = 185 MPa  
  – Grouted or unbonded single strands encased in polymer sheaths; behaviour close to pre-tensioned steel.  

 b) straight or curved tendons in plastic ducts  
  – N* = 10⁶, k₁ = 5, k₂ = 10, Δσᵣₛₖ = 150 MPa  
  – Multiple-wire tendons (e.g. 7-wire strand) either straight or deviated, in non-metallic ducts. Higher k₂ reflects a steeper S-N slope and lower endurance at high cycle counts.  

 c) curved tendons in steel ducts  
  – N* = 10⁶, k₁ = 5, k₂ = 7, Δσᵣₛₖ = 120 MPa  
  – Externally post-tensioned tendons or deviated tendons within steel sheaths. Steel duct friction and deviations reduce endurance.  

 d) splicing devices  
  – N* = 10⁶, k₁ = 5, k₂ = 5, Δσᵣₛₖ = 80 MPa  
  – Fitted couplers or mechanical connectors between prestressing bars/strands. Lowest endurance rating owing to stress concentrations at joints.  

3. How to use the table in design  
 – In fatigue checks, calculate the applied stress range Δσₛ under the frequent or damage-equivalent load combination.  
 – Use k₂ and k₁ from the appropriate row to determine the allowable cycle count or check Δσₛ against Δσᵣₛₖ, applying partial safety factors γ_fat as per Clause 6.8.5.  
 – For variable-amplitude loading, use Min­er’s rule: ∑ nᵢ / Nᵣ(Δσᵢ) < 1.  

4. Notes and national choices  
 – The recommended values above may be replaced by national annex values if agreed.  
 – All parameters assume standard strand/wire grades (e.g. f_pk = 1860 MPa) and should be adjusted if different steels or environmental conditions apply.

The information is presented in Table 7.1N under the heading “Recommended values of wₘₐₓ (mm)”.  Its purpose is to give, for various environmental exposure classes, the maximum allowable crack width wₘₐₓ in millimetres under serviceability load combinations for two broad types of members:  
  • Reinforced concrete members (and prestressed members with permanently unbonded tendons) checked under the quasi-permanent load combination.  
  • Prestressed members with bonded tendons checked under the frequent load combination.  

Structure of the table:  
– Three operating columns:  
  1. “Exposure Class” (lists the concrete exposure categories defined in EN 1992-1-1)  
  2. “Reinforced members and prestressed members with unbonded tendons – Quasi-permanent load combination” (gives wₘₐₓ for this category)  
  3. “Prestressed members with bonded tendons – Frequent load combination” (gives wₘₐₓ for this category)  

– Three data rows, one for each group of exposure classes:  
  Row 1 (mild exposure):  
    • Exposure classes X0 and XC1  
    • wₘₐₓ = 0,4 mm¹ under quasi-permanent loading in reinforced/unbonded members  
    • wₘₐₓ = 0,2 mm under frequent loading in bonded-tendon members  

  Row 2 (moderate exposure – carbonation or chloride not from sea-water):  
    • Exposure classes XC2, XC3 and XC4  
    • wₘₐₓ = 0,3 mm under quasi-permanent loading in reinforced/unbonded members  
    • wₘₐₓ = 0,2 mm² under frequent loading in bonded-tendon members  

  Row 3 (severe exposure – cyclic wetting/drying or de-icing salts or marine splash):  
    • Exposure classes XD1, XD2, XS1, XS2 and XS3  
    • wₘₐₓ is not explicitly listed for quasi-permanent loading in reinforced/unbonded members (the table cell is left blank)  
    • For bonded-tendon prestressed members the requirement is stated simply as “Decompression,” meaning that no tensile cracking is permitted – all tendon zones must remain in compression.  

Footnotes:  
  1 Applies to the X0/XC1 classifications.  
  2 Applies to the XC2–XC4 classifications.  

How to read:  
– If you are designing a reinforced beam or slab in an environment rated XC3, you would limit the crack width under the quasi-permanent combination to 0,3 mm.  
– If you are designing a post-tensioned member in a marine-splash zone (XS2) with bonded tendons, you must ensure that the tendon always remains in compression (no cracking permitted), rather than aiming for a numerical crack-width limit.

Each of the three subfigures (a, b and c) shows on the left a schematic section of the member with its principal dimensions and overlaid hatched region indicating that part of the section which is deemed effective in tension when cracks form.  On the right of each sub-figure is the corresponding idealized strain (ε) distribution through the section depth, from maximum tensile strain ε1 at the level of reinforcement to zero strain ε2 at the section’s compression edge.

The effective tension zone begins at a distance hc,ef below the tensile face (bottom) of the beam and extends upward to the level of the neutral axis or crack tip (the dotted line at depth d marks the centroid of the tensile reinforcement).  
   - Reinforcement: several steel bars (solid circles) lie in the hatched region B, which represents A c,eff for bending cracks.  
   - Notation:  
     • h = total section depth  
     • d = effective depth (distance from extreme compression fiber to centroid of tension bars)  
     • x = neutral-axis depth measured from compression face

   - Strain diagram: a right-triangle with base ε1 (at the bottom steel level) tapering linearly to ε2 = 0 at the top.

2. Subfigure b) Slab  
   - Cross-section: similar to the beam but with symmetrical top and bottom reinforcement.  Hatched areas B appear both above and below the central neutral axis; only the lower region contributes to crack control under downward loading.  The slab thickness is h, reinforcement centroid at depth d, and effective tension depth hc,ef is measured upward from the slab soffit.  
   - Reinforcement: numerous bars in the hatched area B.  
   - Strain diagram: identical linear distribution from ε1 at the bottom to ε2 = 0 at the top.

3. Subfigure c) Member in Pure Tension

Table Identifier  
• Table 7.2N “Maximum bar diameters φ*s for crack control”  

Purpose and Context  
This table provides recommended upper limits on the diameter of reinforcing bars (φ*) in millimetres, to ensure that crack widths in reinforced concrete remain within acceptable serviceability bounds. It is used when designing members where crack control is required. The three columns of maximum bar size correspond to three limiting crack widths (wₖ): 0.4 mm, 0.3 mm, and 0.2 mm. The table applies under the quasi-permanent combination of loads for reinforced members and under the frequent combination for prestressed members, as per EN 1992-1-1 recommendations.  

Structure and Contents  
The table has four columns and eight data rows.  

Columns  
1. Steel stress [MPa]  
   – Characteristic tensile stress in the reinforcement at serviceability limit state, in megapascals.  
   – Values: 160, 200, 240, 280, 320, 360, 400, 450.  

2. Maximum bar size [mm] for wₖ = 0.4 mm  
   – Upper bound on bar diameter (φ*) if the calculated crack width wₖ is limited to 0.4 mm.  

3. Maximum bar size [mm] for wₖ = 0.3 mm  
   – Corresponding diameter limit if wₖ must not exceed 0.3 mm.  

4. Maximum bar size [mm] for wₖ = 0.2 mm  
   – Diameter limit for more stringent crack control (wₖ ≤ 0.2 mm).

Units and Notation  
• All sizes φ* are in millimetres (mm).

Footnote  
1. These maxima assume typical crack‐width control conditions (cover, reinforcement distribution, service load combinations). National Annexes may modify values.  

Usage Notes  
• Select the reinforcement bar diameter not to exceed the value in the column matching the anticipated service stress level and required crack-width limitation.  
• For prestressed members, use the “frequent” load combination. For ordinary reinforcement, use the “quasi-permanent” combination.  
• If the required maximum crack width lies between 0.2 mm and 0.3 mm, interpolate between the two columns.  
• A dash (–) indicates that crack control to that width is not practicable at that stress level.

The excerpted table (“Table 7.3N”) appears in the context of crack-width control for reinforced or prestressed concrete members (clause 7.3.3.2 of EN 1992-1-1). It provides recommended upper bounds on the center-to-center spacing of longitudinal steel bars so that, under the quasi-permanent or frequent serviceability load combination, the maximum crack width does not exceed prescribed limits (wk = 0.4 mm, 0.3 mm or 0.2 mm). When designing a member, one first determines the stress in the tension reinforcement under the relevant serviceability combination (σs [MPa]). Based on that stress and the acceptable crack-width limit (wk), the table yields the maximum permissible spacing between bars.

Table structure and content  
• Column 1 “Steel stress [MPa]” lists representative levels of reinforcement stress at cracking sections: 160, 200, 240, 280, 320 and 360 MPa.  
• Columns 2–4 give, for three crack-width targets (wk = 0.4 mm, 0.3 mm, 0.2 mm), the corresponding maximum bar spacing in millimetres. A dash (“–”) indicates that, at the given steel stress, a 0.2 mm crack width cannot be attained by practical bar spacing (i.e. the required spacing would be unrealistically small).  

Data summary  
 Steel stress σs [MPa]  | wk = 0.4 mm | wk = 0.3 mm | wk = 0.2 mm  
 ————————————|——————|——————|——————  
 160              | 300 mm    | 300 mm    | 200 mm  
 200              | 300 mm    | 250 mm    | 150 mm  
 240              | 250 mm    | 200 mm    | 100 mm  
 280              | 200 mm    | 150 mm    |  50 mm  
 320              | 150 mm    | 100 mm    |     –  
 360              | 100 mm    |  50 mm    |     –  

How to use in design  
1. Compute the expected reinforcement stress σs under the quasi-permanent load combination (including prestress losses, long-term effects, etc.).  
2. Decide on the maximum allowable crack width wk for the exposure and functional requirements of the structure (see Table 7.1N in the Standard).  
3. Locate in column 1 the steel stress level closest to σs (or interpolate between rows for intermediate values).  
4. Read off the maximum bar spacing from the column matching wk. Ensure actual bar spacing does not exceed this value.  

Notes and limitations  
– The values assume normal‐ductility ribbed bars in good bond conditions, cover and confinement as per EN 1992.  
– For combined two‐way reinforcement (e.g. slabs), check both directions; use the shorter permissible spacing.  
– Where prestressing tendons provide crack control, the same table may be applied by substituting the net tensile stress in the non‐prestressed reinforcement after accounting for bond.  
– If σs exceeds 320 MPa and a 0.2 mm crack width is required, special measures (e.g. closer spacings, smaller bars, added skin reinforcement or epoxy‐coated bars) must be adopted.

The table shown is “Table 7.4N: Basic ratios of span / effective depth for reinforced-concrete members without axial compression.”  It is intended for use in simplified deflection checks (see Clause 7.4.2 of EN 1992-1-1) and gives recommended limits on the span-to-effective-depth ratio, l / d, for common beam and slab systems.  In simplified form, once the ratio of actual steel stress under Serviceability Limit State (σs) to 310 MPa has been accounted for, the deflection requirement l / d ≤ K·(310/σs) (Expression 7.16) is satisfied if the unmodified ratio l / d does not exceed the values in the table.

Columns and headings  
•  “Structural system”  
 –  Lists five typical support and loading configurations:  
  1.  Simply supported beam (or one- or two-way simply supported slab)  
  2.  Mid-span of a continuous beam or one-way continuous slab or two-way slab continuous over the longer direction  
  3.  Exterior span of beam or slab (cantilevering one- or two-way slab over a support)  
  4.  Flat slab (slab on columns without beams), based on the longer span  
  5.  Cantilever  

•  “K”  
 –  A dimensionless coefficient by which the basic ratio l / d (for σs = 310 MPa) is multiplied.  Its purpose is to account for restraint conditions and load distribution inherent to each system.  
   
•  “Concrete highly stressed (ρ = 1.5 %)”  
 –  The basic l/d limit assuming a relatively high reinforcement ratio (ρ = As/(b·d) ≈ 1.5 %), which produces higher cracking moments and reduced effective stiffness.  

•  “Concrete lightly stressed (ρ = 0.5 %)”  
 –  The basic l/d limit assuming a lower reinforcement ratio (ρ ≈ 0.5 %), which cracks earlier and deflects more under the same load.  

Table entries  
1.  Simply supported beam or one- or two-way spanning slab  
 K = 1.0  
 •  ρ = 1.5 % → l/d ≤ 14  
 •  ρ = 0.5 % → l/d ≤ 20  

2.  Mid-span of continuous member (span beyond first support)  
 K = 1.3  
 •  ρ = 1.5 % → l/d ≤ 18  
 •  ρ = 0.5 % → l/d ≤ 26  

3.  Exterior span (over-hanging or free end between supports)  
 K = 1.5  
 •  ρ = 1.5 % → l/d ≤ 20  
 •  ρ = 0.5 % → l/d ≤ 30  

4.  Flat slab on columns without beams (control based on longer span)  
 K = 1.2  
 •  ρ = 1.5 % → l/d ≤ 17  
 •  ρ = 0.5 % → l/d ≤ 24  

5.  Cantilever  
 K = 0.4  
 •  ρ = 1.5 % → l/d ≤ 6  
 •  ρ = 0.5 % → l/d ≤ 8  

How to use the table  
 ­• Determine the structural configuration and corresponding row.  
 ­• Decide whether your tension reinforcement ratio ρ is “high” (≈ 1.5 %) or “low” (≈ 0.5 %).  
 ­• Read off the limiting l/d from the relevant column.  
 ­• If your element’s actual mid-span steel stress σs differs from 310 MPa, adjust the limit by multiplying K by (310 / σs).  Thus the permissible l/d becomes  
      l/d ≤ K · (310/σs)  

Applicability and notes  
 – These values are intended as conservative, easy-to-apply checks for normal building and bridge beams and slabs.  
 – For structural systems not listed, or where more accuracy is needed (long-span slabs carrying sensitive partitions, unusual load patterns, deeply cambered members, etc.), full deflection calculations under quasi-permanent load (Clause 7.4.3) or refined stiffness models should be used.  
 – The table assumes uncracked sections up to the Serviceability Limit State, and accounts statistically for cracking, tension stiffening and redistribution in continuous spans.  
 – For lightweight-aggregate concrete or for members with imposed deformations, additional corrections (see Clause 11 and Clause 7.4.1) may apply.

This record captures the content and intent of “Table 8.1N: Minimum mandrel diameter to avoid damage to reinforcement.”  It appears in a clause dealing with the detailing of ribbed bars (Section 8.3 of the Standard) and defines the recommended minimum bending radii (mandrel diameters) for straight bars or wires when forming bends, hooks or loops, so as to avoid bar fracture or cracking of the surrounding concrete.

1. Context and Purpose
 • Applies to bending of de-raked or ribbed reinforcement (rebars or wire) used in drawn-up forms, U-hooks, 90° or 180° hooks, closed loops, stirrup legs, etc.  
 • Ensures that the bending process (and subsequent stresses at the bend) does not damage the bar or the concrete cover.  
 • References Figure 8.1 for typical anchorage shapes (bent-down bars, standard hooks, U-shaped loops).

2. Table Structure
 • Two columns:
   – “Bar diameter” (nominal diameter φ of the bar or wire)  
   – “Minimum mandrel diameter for bends, hooks and loops (see Figure 8.1)”  
 • No separate units column; all diameters expressed in multiples of the bar diameter (φ).

3. Content (Two Diameter Ranges)
 Row 1:  
  – Bar diameter φ < 16 mm  
  – Minimum mandrel diameter = 4 × φ  
 Row 2:  
  – Bar diameter φ > 16 mm  
  – Minimum mandrel diameter = 7 × φ  

4. Implicit Rules and Notes
 • If a bar is exactly 16 mm, the specifiers should interpret whether it falls in the first or second category; conservative practice would use 7φ if in doubt.  
 • The rule covers all standard hooked ends and loops used for tension anchorage; it does not apply to mechanical end fittings or proprietary anchorages (which are covered elsewhere).  
 • The table assumes ordinary ribbed reinforcement in normal-weight concrete; supplementary rules for lightweight aggregate concrete are in Section 11.  
 • These bending radii are “mandrel diameters,” meaning the physical diameter of the bending form around which the bar is bent, measured on its outside face.

5. How It’s Used in Design and Detailing
 • When preparing shop drawings or specifying bar schedules, designers select an appropriate mandrel (steel tube or form block) whose diameter meets or exceeds the value given by the table.  
 • Fabricators use this to set up bending machines or jigs: e.g. a 12 mm bar requires a 48 mm mandrel (4×12), while a 20 mm bar requires a 140 mm mandrel (7×20).  
 • Checking reinforcement execution on site: inspectors confirm that bend radii match at least the table’s minimum.  
 • Prevents local weakening of bars and ensures the required development or anchorage length is not compromised by a tight bend.

6. Rationale
 • Smaller bars (<16 mm) can tolerate tighter bends (4φ) without yielding or fracturing.  
 • Larger bars (>16 mm) require broader curves (7φ) because their cross-sectional area and rib pattern make them less ductile in bending.  

By extracting “Bar diameter” and the corresponding “Mandrel diameter multiplier,” this table provides a clear rule-of-thumb for detailing standard bends and hooks, supporting consistent reinforcement fabrication and reliable bond performance in reinforced-concrete members.

Below the four sketches, the figure is captioned “Figure 8.2: Description of bond conditions.” The intent is to classify situations where the standard bond coefficient η₁ = 1,0 may be used (cases a and b) versus those requiring a reduction to η₁ = 0,7 (cases c and d), depending on bar inclination, element thickness, and concrete compactability around the bar.

The illustration, labeled “Figure 8.3: Values of c_d for beams and slabs,” consists of two schematic cross‐sectional diagrams side by side, each showing how to determine the effective concrete cover distance c_d when calculating reinforcement anchorage in beams and slabs. Both diagrams depict a right‐angle corner of a structural member (either a beam or a slab) outlined by dashed lines representing the formwork or mold surfaces. Two reinforcement bars are shown in plan view as solid circles positioned close to the inner corner.

1) Diagram (a) Straight bars  
– The corner of the mold or section is shown by two perpendicular dashed lines, one vertical and one horizontal.  
– Two solid dots (representing straight reinforcing bars of equal diameter) lie inside the corner, separated from each other by a horizontal distance labeled “a.”  
– A vertical dimension line from the bottom mold face up to the center of the lower bar is marked “c,” indicating the actual clear cover from the bottom surface to the bar center.  
– A horizontal dimension line from the left mold face to the center of the left bar is labeled “c₁,” indicating the clear cover measured perpendicular to that face.  
– Directly between the two bars, a small horizontal arrow spanning half their spacing is labeled “a / 2.”  
– Beneath the figure, the formula is stated:  
 c_d = min(a / 2, c₁, c)  
  meaning that the effective cover distance c_d used in anchorage calculations is the smallest of one‐half the bar spacing, the lateral cover to the mold face, and the vertical cover to the bottom face.

2) Diagram (b) Bent or hooked bars  
– The same corner geometry and two-bar arrangement are shown, but with the implication that the bars are terminated in a bend or hook inside the section. The bars themselves are again rendered as two solid dots at identical locations.  
– The horizontal cover to the left mold face remains labeled “c₁.” The vertical cover “c” to the bottom face is shown but is crossed out or omitted from the c_d formula.  
– A horizontal arrow between the dot symbols again indicates “a,” and a second arrow indicates “a / 2.”  
– Below this diagram the modified formula reads:  
 c_d = min(a / 2, c₁)  
  showing that for hooked or bent bars only the lateral cover and half‐spacing control the effective cover dimension, not the vertical cover.

Together, these two simple but precise sketches make it clear that when checking anchorage or lap lengths in beams and slabs, the value of c_d – which influences the anchorage coefficient α₂ – is determined by whichever of the specified distances is smallest, with the vertical cover to the bottom face dropped entirely for hooked bars.

The table (referred to in the text as Table 8.2) lists five dimensionless coefficients, α₁ through α₅, which modify the basic anchorage length of a straight bar (lᵦ,rqd) to give the actual design anchorage length (lᵦd).  Each coefficient accounts for a different influence on bond strength and is applied multiplicatively:

1.  α₁ — Effect of bar geometry (“form of the bars”):  
    •  For straight bars or bars in compression: α₁ = 1,0  
    •  For hooked or otherwise bent bars in tension:  
       –  If concrete cover c₍d₎ > 3·φ  then α₁ = 0,7  
       –  Otherwise α₁ = 1,0  
    (φ = bar diameter)

2.  α₂ — Effect of concrete cover:  
    •  In compression: α₂ = 1,0  
    •  In tension (straight or bent bars):  
       α₂ = 1 – 0,15·(c₍d₎ – φ)/φ, but not less than 0,7 and not more than 1,0  
    (c₍d₎ is the minimum cover to the bar)

3.  α₃ — Effect of confinement by transverse reinforcement not welded directly to the bar:  
    •  In compression: α₃ = 1,0  
    •  In tension:  
       α₃ = 1 – K·λ, constrained 0,7 ≤ α₃ ≤ 1,0, where  
       –  K is a coefficient from Figure 8.4 (≈ 0,12 … 0,2),  
       –  λ = (ΣAₛₜ – ΣAₛₜ,min)/Aₛ, the ratio of actual transverse‐hoop area to the minimum required (ΣAₛₜ,min = 0,25·Aₛ for beams, zero for slabs).

4.  α₄ — Effect of one or more welded transverse bars (φₜ > 0,6·φ) bearing on the concrete:  
    •  In both tension and compression: α₄ = 0,7

5.  α₅ — Effect of external pressure acting transverse to the anchorage length:  
    •  Applies only in tension (no compression value listed)  
    •  α₅ = 1 – 0,04·p, constrained 0,7 ≤ α₅ ≤ 1,0, where p is the mean transverse pressure [MPa] at ULS.

The design anchorage length is then  
     lᵦd = α₁·α₂·α₃·α₄·α₅·lᵦ,rqd  
subject also to a minimum anchorage length:  
     lᵦd ≥ lᵦ,min  (where lᵦ,min = max{0,3·lᵦ,rqd; 10·φ; 100 mm} in tension, and 0,6·lᵦ,rqd in compression).

Additionally the product (α₂·α₃·α₅) must not fall below 0,7.  This table thus provides a systematic way to lengthen or shorten the straight‐bar anchorage in response to bar shape, cover, confinement, welded anchors and external pressure.

The figure “Welded transverse bar as anchoring device” is a schematic, line-diagram detail showing how a small bar, welded transversely to a larger reinforcement bar, can supplement bond anchorage in concrete.  Key features of the drawing are:

– A long, horizontal line represents the main reinforcing bar (of diameter φₗ) embedded in concrete.  It lies parallel to the underside of the structure, at a nominal concrete cover distance c below the unloaded face.  
– Welded onto the top side of the main bar is a short transverse bar of diameter φₜ.  This transverse bar bears directly on the surrounding concrete and provides mechanical anchorage through bearing friction and compressive confinement.  
– The weld is highlighted by a triangular symbol at the junction of the two bars, with an arrow labeled F_wd pointing to it.  F_wd denotes the design shear capacity of the welded joint, which must be at least as large as the force developing in the main bar at ultimate load.  
– From beneath the main bar, vertical arrows labeled σ_cm point upward against the underside of the bar.  These arrows represent the mean compressive stress in the concrete perpendicular to the plane of the two bars.  In design formulas, σ_cm appears in the parameter y = 0.015 + 0.14 e^(–0.18 x), which accounts for the influence of normal pressure on bond strength.  
– To the right of the weld detail, a vertical dimension line marks the concrete cover “c,” measured from the outer concrete face to the centerline of the main bar.  This cover controls the geometry factor x = 2 (c/φₜ) + 1 in the expression for y, and it also figures into the minimum required anchorage length.  
– The inset caption reinforces that this arrangement—welding a transverse bar of diameter φₜ onto the main bar—serves as a discrete anchoring device, combining bond stress (from the ribbed bar) with bearing against the transverse bar and shear capacity of the weld.

Context from Eurocode-type rules (e.g. Expression 8.9) shows that for small diameter transverse bars (φₜ ≤ 12 mm) the anchorage capacity F_btd may be taken as the design shear strength of the weld F_wd, limited by a concrete crushing criterion:  
 F_btd = F_wd ≤ 16 A_s f_cd (φₜ/φₗ).  

Here A_s is the cross-section of the main bar, f_cd is the design compressive strength of concrete, and φₗ and φₜ are the nominal bar diameters.  The welded transverse bar drives bearing stress into the cover zone, confines the concrete locally and thereby helps achieve the required anchorage length l_bd without resorting to excessively long straight embedment lengths or expensive mechanical couplers.

 6.3 Torsion
 (1)P Where the static equilibrium of a structure depends on the torsional resistance of elements of the structure, a full torsional design covering both ultimate and serviceability limit states shall be made.

The illustration is a schematic, black-and-white line drawing showing how two lapped reinforcement bars should be arranged in adjacent layers to satisfy minimum spacing and staggered-lap requirements (as required by Eurocode 2, Clause 8.7.3 and Figure 8.7).  It consists of three horizontal bars drawn in side-elevation, each carrying a tensile force Fs (indicated by an arrow at the free end of each bar, pointing left).

 •   Top bar: runs continuously from left to right. Its right-hand end carries the force arrow “Fs.”  
 •   Middle bar (lapped bar): shorter than the top bar, its right-hand end butts up beneath the lap zone of the top bar; it too carries “Fs” at its free end.  
 •   Bottom bar: like the top bar, runs the full width and carries Fs at its end.

Between the top and bottom bars the middle bar is offset vertically, creating two distinct lap zones rather than aligning all three bars in one plane. A vertical, double-headed dimension arrow labeled “a” marks the clear distance between the underside of the top bar’s lap and the top side of the bottom bar’s lap layer.  This clear spacing “a” must meet the code’s requirement (no less than 2 φ or 20 mm, and to avoid increases in lap length must not exceed 4 φ or 50 mm).

A horizontal, double-headed arrow between the end of the middle bar’s lap and the adjacent lap of the longer bars is labeled “≥ 0,3 l₀.”  This indicates that the longitudinal distance between the centres (or ends) of two adjacent lap zones must be at least 0.3 times the calculated basic lap length l₀, ensuring that the stress transfer regions do not overlap and that cracking or spalling is minimized.

Below the drawing is the caption “Figure 8.7: Adjacent laps,” matching the text in the code.  The figure as a whole demonstrates:

  •  Bars in tension may be lapped 100 percent in one layer only if they comply with the spacing rules.  
  •  When bars are in multiple layers (as here), only 50 percent of the reinforcement can be lapped in any one section.  
  •  Clearances both longitudinally (≥ 0.3 l₀) and transversely/vertically (a ≥ 2 φ or 20 mm; ≤ 4 φ or 50 mm) are mandatory to ensure force transmission and prevent concrete spalling or large cracks.

This simple line diagram—no shading or color—serves as a practical visualization of how to stagger lapped bars, comply with minimum spacing, and achieve robust structural performance in reinforced concrete members.

The input table (Table 8.3) provides the design engineer with tabulated values of the coefficient α6, which enters directly into the calculation of the required lap length (l₀) for reinforcement bars in tension. This coefficient modifies the basic development length to account for the overall density of lapped bars in a given section.

1. Table Structure  
• Title: “Values of the coefficient α6”  
• Column headers:  
  – “Percentage of lapped bars relative to the total cross-section area”  
  – Four discrete percentage categories:  
     • < 25%  
     • 33%  
     • 50%  
     • > 50%  
• Single data row: under each percentage category is the corresponding α6 value.  
• Footnote: “Intermediate values may be determined by interpolation.”

2. Data Content  
• When less than 25% of the total reinforcement area is lapped, α6 = 1.0.  
• At exactly 33% lapped area, α6 = 1.15.  
• At 50% lapped area, α6 = 1.4.  
• When more than 50% of the cross-sectional reinforcement is lapped, α6 reaches the upper bound of 1.5.

3. Context and Use in Lap Length Calculation  
• In Eurocode-style design rules (see Expression 8.10), the design lap length l₀ is given by  
     l₀ = α1 · α2 · α3 · α5 · α6 · l₍b,rqd₎ ≥ l₀,min  
  where α6 is the tabulated coefficient reflecting the reinforcement congestion in the lap zone.  
• The variable l₀,min has its own lower bound (see Expression 8.11) based on 0.3α6 l₍b,rqd₎, 15φ (fifteen times bar diameter), and 200 mm.  
• α6 may alternatively be computed by the expression α6 = (ρ₁/25)^0.5, where ρ₁ is the percentage of total reinforcement area lapped within 0.65 l₀ from the lap centre (Figure 8.8). However, whichever method is used, α6 is constrained between a minimum of 1.0 and a maximum of 1.5. The present table provides direct values for common banded percentages, avoiding more complex calculation.  
• For intermediate reinforcement densities (for example 40%), the designer may linearly interpolate between the tabulated values (e.g. interpolate between α6 = 1.15 at 33% and α6 = 1.4 at 50%).

4. Design Implications  
• Lower α6 (close to 1.0) applies when laps are relatively sparse (< 25%), meaning the basic development length need not be increased for congestion.  
• As the proportion of lapped bars grows, α6 increases—reflecting reduced bond performance due to bar proximity, potential conflict with concrete cover and transverse ties, and higher local stress concentration.  
• Once congested laps exceed 50% of the area, the full magnification factor of 1.5 is applied, ensuring a robust safety margin in high-density reinforcement zones.

By capturing these discrete α6 values in a vector store, a retrieval-augmented generation system can quickly pull the correct magnification factor for lap length checks, interpolate when needed, and integrate it into the overall lap-length computation alongside the other α-coefficients.

The image is a two‐part schematic (labelled “Figure 8.9: Transverse reinforcement for lapped splices”) showing the required layout of transverse bars when splicing two longitudinal reinforcement bars over a lap length l₀. Part (a) illustrates the case of bars in tension; part (b) shows bars in compression. Key dimensions, forces and reinforcement quantities are all annotated.

1. Common elements in both (a) and (b):
   - Two straight longitudinal bars overlap over a central lap length denoted l₀.
   - On either side of the central zone, arrows labelled Fₛ indicate the direction of the tensile or compressive force in each bar.
   - The total area of transverse reinforcement required to confine the splice is split equally on each side of the lap: each group is labelled ΣAₛₜ/2.
   - A maximum clear spacing of 150 mm is shown between adjacent transverse bars (arrowed “≤ 150 mm”).

2. Part (a) – bars in tension:
   - The two longitudinal bars pull outward (arrows Fₛ point away from the lap center).
   - The lap length l₀ is divided into three equal segments of length l₀/3. These subdivisions are marked directly under the overlap.
   - The transverse reinforcement (ΣAₛₜ/2) is placed within the outer third zones of the lap—i.e. extending for l₀/3 from each end of the lap length toward the center.
   - Within those outer thirds, individual vertical strokes represent individual transverse bars, spaced at no more than 150 mm.
   - There is no additional notation about bar diameter clearance because for tension splices one bar of transverse reinforcement at each end inherently provides confinement.

3. Part (b) – bars in compression:
   - Here the arrows Fₛ on each longitudinal bar point toward the lap center, indicating compressive forces.
   - The lap length l₀ is again split into three equal l₀/3 zones.
   - Transverse reinforcement (ΣAₛₜ/2) is again located in the two outer thirds, but in this compression case an extra dimensional control is required: each group of transverse bars must lie no farther than 4 φ from the corresponding end of the lap (where φ is the bar diameter). This is shown by a double‐ended arrow labelled “4 φ” at each end of the lap.
   - As before, the bars are spaced at ≤ 150 mm and the total transverse‐steel area is divided equally on each side.
   - The vertical strokes again represent the individual transverse links or hoops that wrap or tie through the longitudinal bars.

Taken together, this figure conveys the European Design Code provisions for lapping reinforcement: under tensile lap splices (8.7.5.1 – 8.7.2 and Figure 8.9a) the transverse links can simply be located within the outer thirds of the overlap, while for compression splices (Figure 8.9b) at least one link must be positioned not more than 4 φ from each lap end. The equal split of ΣAₛₜ/2 on either side ensures the required confining pressure is applied symmetrically.
