The input image (labelled Figure 8.10) is divided into two schematic diagrams, one above the other, illustrating two distinct methods of lapping welded‐mesh reinforcement fabrics in concrete beams: (a) intermeshed fabric and (b) layered fabric. Both sketches are viewed in longitudinal section, showing only the main longitudinal bars and the small transverse wires (shown as solid red circles) that are welded at regular spacing.

1. Common Elements  
- A horizontal pair of rectangular bars (drawn as long, narrow white rectangles with black outlines) represent two consecutive lengths of the main longitudinal reinforcement.  
- An arrow labelled “Fs” (force in tension) points leftwards from the free end of the top bar, indicating the direction of the tensile force that is being transferred through the lap.  
- Beneath and slightly behind these longitudinal bars, a row of evenly spaced red dots represents the transverse wires welded to the mesh. These dots bracket the overlapping region.  
- A dimension line beneath the bars is marked “l₀,” denoting the required lap length measured from the point where the two bars begin to overlap to the end of the overlapped region.

2. (a) Intermeshed Fabric (Longitudinal Sections)  
- In this top diagram, the two main longitudinal bars are interwoven: one bar is slipped through the transverse‐wire openings of the other. The overlap zone thus shows the bars alternating in front of and behind one another, so that each bar’s transverse wires interlock.  
- The red circles in the overlap region are arranged in two staggered rows (one for each bar), but many appear at nearly the same horizontal locations, underscoring how the wires of one mesh pass between the wires of the other.  
- The overlap length l₀ extends from the point where intermeshing begins (indicated by the right‐most transverse‐wire dot aligning with the front bar) to the end of the back bar at right.  
- This interlocking arrangement ensures mechanical engagement and is especially recommended where fatigue loads occur.

3. (b) Layered Fabric (Longitudinal Sections)  
- In the lower diagram, the two main bars simply lie one above the other in two distinct layers, without weaving. The top bar is displaced slightly rearwards, and the bottom bar slightly forwards, creating a clear step at each end of the overlap.  
- The transverse wires (red dots) of each layer appear in their respective planes: the top bar’s wires lie above the bottom bar’s, with no interpenetration. Their horizontal spacing is identical to that in (a), but the two rows are vertically separated.  
- The lap length l₀ again runs from the leading edge of the bottom bar to the trailing edge of the top bar.  
- This simpler layering method is typically used where calculated ultimate‐limit‐state stresses do not exceed 80 % of the reinforcement’s design strength, or additional measures (such as increased effective depth or higher steel stresses for crack control) are taken when close to lap ends.

Overall, Figure 8.10 clearly contrasts the intermeshed versus layered lap arrangements for welded mesh fabrics, with the required lap length l₀ and the layout of transverse wires highlighted in each case.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the information contained in the supplied table (Table 8.4), suitable for indexing in a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store. Wherever possible, the description makes explicit the relationships, units, and intended application context.

1. Table identity  
   • Table number: 8.4  
   • Table title: “Required lap lengths for secondary wires of fabrics”  
   • Context note: All secondary reinforcement bars in a fabric may be lapped at the same location. The values listed are minimum lap lengths l₀ for secondary wires; when two secondary wires are lapped, they must extend so as to overlap two main wires.

2. Column definitions  
   A. “Diameter of secondary wires (mm)”  
      – Indicates the nominal bar or wire diameter categories, in millimeters.  
      – Uses the symbol φ (phi) to denote diameter.  
      – Divided into three non-overlapping ranges:  
         • φ ≤ 6 mm  
         • 6 < φ ≤ 8.5 mm  
         • 8.5 < φ ≤ 12 mm  

   B. “Lap lengths”  
      – Specifies the minimum required overlap length l₀, in millimeters.  
      – Also stipulates a minimum count of “wire pitches” contained within the lap zone. A wire pitch is the center-to-center spacing between adjacent wires in the fabric.  
      – Presented as a compound requirement: “≥ [length] mm; at least [N] wire pitches.”

3. Row-by-row content  
   1. Row for φ ≤ 6 mm:  
      – Minimum lap length l₀ = 150 mm  
      – Must include at least 1 wire pitch inside the overlapped region  
   2. Row for 6 < φ ≤ 8.5 mm:  
      – Minimum lap length l₀ = 250 mm  
      – Must include at least 2 wire pitches inside the overlapped region  
   3. Row for 8.5 < φ ≤ 12 mm:  
      – Minimum lap length l₀ = 350 mm  
      – Must include at least 2 wire pitches inside the overlapped region  

4. Purpose and application  
   • Ensures adequate transfer of stress between overlapped (lapped) secondary wires in welded fabric reinforcement.  
   • Allows designers and engineers to pick the correct lap length based on secondary bar diameter.  
   • Guarantees that a sufficient number of wire spacings (pitches) falls within the lap, which enhances mechanical interlock and bond performance.

5. Key takeaways for retrieval or prompt design  
   • When querying for “lap length for secondary wire,” match the diameter condition φ against the three ranges to retrieve the required l₀ and pitch count.  
   • The lap length always increases with the diameter range, reflecting the need for greater bond area on larger bars.  
   • The pitch-count requirement is a secondary check to ensure that overlap zones contain a minimum discrete count of wires, not just a continuous length.

By capturing the table’s structure (two columns, three categorical rows), its units, symbol conventions, and the compound condition (length plus pitch count), this description provides a clear, self-contained reference for any downstream retrieval or reasoning task about lapping secondary reinforcement wires in fabric mats.

Text annotations common to both sketches  
• At the top of each U, the callout “ΣAsv ≥ 0.5 As₁” appears twice, indicating that the sum of the area of vertical (perpendicular to the tension face) transverse reinforcement Asv must be at least half the cross‐sectional area of one anchored bar.  
• Along the sides of each U, a callout for ΣAsh with a value—either “≥ 0.25 As₁” or “≥ 0.5 As₁”—indicates the minimum sum of the area of horizontal (parallel to the tension face) transverse reinforcement Ash.  

Left‐hand sketch (n₁ = 1, n₂ = 2)  
• Only one U‐shaped bend is shown (one layer of bent bars). Because n₁ = number of layers = 1, a single layer of transverse hooks suffices.  
• Two anchored bars (n₂ = 2) are placed at the inside of the bend, shown as two hollow circles on the curved toe of the U. Two continuing bars are shown as solid circles below the anchored bars.  
• The bottom annotation reads “ΣAsh ≥ 0.25 As₁,” reflecting equation (8.12) for the parallel direction when only one layer is present.  

Right‐hand sketch (n₁ = 2, n₂ = 2)  
• Two nested U‐shaped bends indicate n₁ = 2 layers of bent anchorage. Thus more transverse reinforcement is provided in the parallel direction.  
• Again, two hollow circles mark the two anchored bars, and two solid circles mark the continuing bars.  
• The bottom annotation here reads “ΣAsh ≥ 0.5 As₁,” showing the increased requirement when two layers are used rather than one.  

Caption and notation  
• The figure’s caption reiterates that this detail applies where no transverse compression is present (necessitating confining links or mechanical anchorage for large‐diameter bars).  
• The sketch includes the notations:  
 – As₁: cross‐sectional area of one anchored bar  
 – n₁: number of layers of U‐shaped anchorage hooks  
 – n₂: number of bars anchored in each layer  
 – ΣAsv: total area of links in the direction perpendicular to the tension face (Asv ≥ 0.25 As₁·n₂ per layer)  
 – ΣAsh: total area of links in the direction parallel to the tension face  

Overall, the drawing illustrates two possible arrangements of additional transverse reinforcement—one with a single layer of hooks and one with two layers—clearly tying back to the equations in the adjacent text (clauses 6–8 of Section 8.11) governing Ash and Asv for large‐diameter bar anchorage without transverse compression.

sections: 8  Additional rules for large diameter bars

content:
(1) For bars with a diameter larger than φlarge the following rules supplement those given in 8.4 and 8.7.
 Note: The value of φlarge for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended value is 32 mm.
 (2) When such large diameter bars are used, crack control may be achieved either by using surface reinforcement (see 9.2.4) or by calculation (see 7.3.4).
 (3) Splitting forces are higher and dowel action is greater with the use of large diameter bars. Such bars should be anchored with mechanical devices. As an alternative they may be anchored as straight bars, but links should be provided as confining reinforcement.
 (4) Generally large diameter bars should not be lapped. Exceptions include sections with a minimum dimension 1,0 m or where the stress is not greater than 80% of the design ultimate strength.
 (5) Transverse reinforcement, additional to that for shear, should be provided in the anchorage zones where transverse compression is not present.
 (6) For straight anchorage lengths (see Figure 8.11 for the notation used) the additional reinforcement referred to in (5) above should not be less than the following:
 in the direction parallel to the tension face:
 Ash = 0,25 As n1
 (8.12)
 in the direction perpendicular to the tension face:
 Asv = 0,25 As n2
 (8.13)
 where:
 As is the cross sectional area of an anchored bar,
 n1 is the number of layers with bars anchored at the same point in the member
 n2 is the number of bars anchored in each layer.
 (7) The additional transverse reinforcement should be uniformly distributed in the anchorage zone and the spacing of bars should not exceed 5 times the diameter of the longitudinal reinforcement.
 (8) For surface reinforcement, 9.2.4 applies, but the area of surface reinforcement should not be less than 0,01 Act,ext in the direction perpendicular to large diameter bars, and 0,02 Act,ext parallel to those bars.

(1) Unless otherwise stated, the rules for individual bars also apply for bundles of bars. In a bundle, all the bars should be of the same characteristics (type and grade). Bars of different sizes may be bundled provided that the ratio of diameters does not exceed 1,7.
 (2) In design, the bundle is replaced by a notional bar having the same sectional area and the same centre of gravity as the bundle. The equivalent diameter, φn of this notional bar is such that:
 φn = φ √nb ≤ 55 mm
 (8.14)
 where
 nb is the number of bars in the bundle, which is limited to:
 for vertical bars in compression and for bars in a lapped joint,
 nb ≤ 3 for all other cases.
 (3) For a bundle, the rules given in 8.2 for spacing of bars apply. The equivalent diameter, φn, should be used but the clear distance between bundles should be measured from the actual external contour of the bundle of bars. The concrete cover should be measured from the actual external contour of the bundles and should not be less than φn.
 (4) Where two touching bars are positioned one above the other, and where the bond conditions are good, such bars need not be treated as a bundle.

The image is a crisp reproduction of a page from the Norwegian National Annex to EN 1992-1-1:2004 (Concrete Design – Eurocode 2), showing sections 8.9 and the beginning of 8.10.  The layout is portrait, black text on white ground, with a narrow left-hand margin containing running footer information (“© of Freedom AS / S109191 / 2025-07-21 11:14 / NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014+NA:2024”).

1. Header  
   - At the very top, centered:  
     • “NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014+NA:2024”  
     • Directly beneath in slightly smaller type: “EN 1992-1-1:2004 (E)”

2. Section 8.9 – Bundled bars  
   • 8.9.1 General  
     (1) States that unless otherwise noted, all individual-bar rules apply to bundles; each bundle must consist of bars of identical type and grade, and diameter ratios within a bundle may not exceed 1.2.  
     (2) Defines a bundle’s “equivalent diameter” φₙ via φₙ = φ · √n_b ≤ 55 mm, where φ is single-bar diameter and n_b the number of bars. Limits n_b ≤ 4 for vertical bars in compression or in a lap; n_b ≤ 3 for all other cases.  
     (3) Refers to spacing rules of clause 8.2, stipulating that clear distances between bundles (measured between external contours) and concrete cover should be at least φₙ.  
     (4) Permits two touching bars, one above the other, to avoid classification as a bundle if placement conditions are good.

   • 8.9.2 Anchorage of bundles of bars  
     (1) For tensioned bundles, curtailment (cutting back) may occur over supports. Bundles with φₙ < 32 mm can be curtailed near supports without staggering; if φₙ ≥ 32 mm, bars must be staggered longitudinally (see Figure 8.12).  
     (2) If individual bars are anchored with staggered lengths > 1.3 l_b,rqd (where l_b,rqd is based on each bar’s diameter), the single-bar diameter may be used in l_bd calculations; otherwise use the bundle’s φₙ.  
     (3) For compression anchorages, staggering is unnecessary. For φₙ ≥ 32 mm bundles, at least four ≥ 12 mm-diameter links (ties) must be provided at each end of the bundle, plus an extra link just beyond the truncated bar end.

3. Figure 8.12 – Anchoring of widely staggered bars in a bundle  
   • A simple, black-line schematic showing three parallel horizontal bars.  
   • From the left support: the first bar is cut off after a length ≥ l_b, the middle bar extends farther, and the third bar even farther, creating a staggered “stepped” profile. Above the bars two arrows mark the horizontal dimensions “≥ l_b” and “≥ 1,3 l_b.”  
   • A beam is subjected to a tensile force F_s indicated by a right-pointing arrow on the rightmost bar.  
   • A vertical cutting plane A–A is drawn near the bar ends; beneath is the cross-section symbol (“A–A”) showing a cluster of three circular bar sections in triangular formation.

4. Section 8.10 – Prestressing tendons (beginning)  
   • 8.10.1 Arrangement of prestressing tendons and ducts  
     (1) P (prescriptive text) requires duct/tendon spacing to allow proper concrete placement and compaction and to achieve full bond.  
     (1) (duplicate numbering) specifies minimum clear horizontal and vertical spacing per Figure 8.14; alternative layouts are allowed only where tests demonstrate satisfactory ultimate behavior concerning:  
       – concrete compression at the anchorage  
       – concrete spalling  
       – tendon anchorage  
       – concrete placement between tendons.  
       Durability and corrosion risk at element ends must also be considered.  
     (2) Prohibits bundling of tendons in anchorage zones unless concrete placement and bond performance are proven satisfactory.

Overall, the page combines normative text, a simple bar-staggering detail, and the transition into prestressing-tendon arrangement rules, all laid out in Eurocode style with clear numbering and a single illustrative figure.

The image is a schematic, labelled “Figure 8.13: Lap joint in tension including a fourth bar,” showing both a longitudinal elevation and a cross‐section through a tension splice of prestressing bars.  In the elevation view at top:

• Three primary bars (collectively labelled “1”) are drawn as solid parallel lines extending from left to right.  An arrow at the right end marks the applied tensile force Fs pulling toward the right.  
• A fourth bar (“4”), the lapping bar, approaches from the right and overlaps the main bundle in the splice zone.  Its end is staggered part‐way along the length of the primary bars rather than aligned with them.  
• One of the main bars is individually indicated as “3” (shown dashed in the overlap region) to highlight how each bar in the original bundle is successively offset in longitudinal position relative to the lapping bar.  
• The total lap length is subdivided into four equal segments, each of length 1.3 l₀ (where l₀ is the basic development length for a single bar).  These four “1.3 l₀” intervals are marked along the bottom of the elevation, illustrating that the lapping bar is inserted at least 1.3 l₀ away from each adjacent main‐bar end.  

Below and to the right, a circular cross‐section depicts the arrangement of bars in the splice region:

• Three bars of the original tension bundle (again labelled “1”) are grouped roughly in a triangular pattern within the concrete section.  
• The fourth, lapping bar (“2”) is shown as an additional circle placed just outside one corner of the triangle.  Its position is slightly offset so that no more than four bars occupy any given cross‐section, in accordance with code requirements.  
• The circle enclosing all four bars represents the equivalent bundle diameter φₙ used for design checks.  

Key details conveyed by the figure:  
- Bundles of three prestressing bars with an equivalent diameter ≥ 32 mm must have individual bars staggered over a lap joint by at least 1.3 l₀ (see text clause 8.9.1(3)).  
- Bar No. 4 functions as the “lapping” bar and is inserted between the main bars in a stepped fashion to avoid excessive congestion or reduced bond capacity.  
- Dimensions and staggering ensure that at no section do more than four bars overlap, and that each bar achieves its full development length free of interference.  

Together, the elevation and section views make clear how to arrange and space a tension splice of a three‐bar bundle plus a fourth lapping bar so as to satisfy anchorage, bond, and constructibility requirements without exceeding maximum bundle diameters or bar counts in any cross‐section.

The illustration is a plan-view schematic (Figure 8.14) showing four pre-tensioned tendon ducts—represented as solid red circles—arranged in a simple rectangular grid. Surrounding each circle are dimension lines with arrowheads indicating the required “clear” centre-to-centre and edge-to-formwork spacings. The key variables are:

• φ (phi): the diameter of an individual pre-tensioned tendon or duct.  
• dg: the maximum nominal size of aggregate in the concrete mix.

1. Edge Clearance (tendon to formwork or concrete face)  
   At the top of the drawing, a single dimension line runs vertically from the top-most duct to the boundary line (representing the underside of the formwork or outer concrete face). This is labelled “φ,” indicating that the minimum clear cover from the tendon centre to the edge of the casting surface must be at least one tendon diameter.

2. Vertical Spacing Between Tendons  
   On the left side of the graphic, a vertical pair of tendons is joined by a double-headed arrow. Alongside it are two annotations: “≥ dg” and “≥ 2φ.” This means the minimum clear vertical distance between the centrelines of two adjacent ducts must be at least the larger of (a) the maximum aggregate size dg, or (b) twice the tendon diameter (2φ).

3. Horizontal Spacing Between Tendons  
   Along the bottom of the drawing, two bottom-row tendons are linked by a horizontal double-headed arrow. Next to this arrow are three criteria, stacked one above the other:
      – “≥ dg + 5”  
      – “≥ 2φ”  
      – “≥ 20”  
   In other words, the clear horizontal spacing between tendon centres must simultaneously satisfy:  
      a) at least dg plus 5 mm,  
      b) at least twice the tendon diameter, and  
      c) at least 20 mm.  
   The inclusion of “+ 5” on dg allows a small extra gap beyond the largest aggregate particle, and the fixed 20 mm ensures a minimum even if φ or dg are small.

4. Overall Layout  
   By showing four tendons in a tight rectangular pattern, the figure conveys how these minimum spacing rules apply in both orthogonal directions for any array of ducts. The red circles have no fill pattern beyond their solid color, emphasizing that they stand for the cross-section of each tendon or duct. The arrows use a standard engineering-drawing style (thin lines, open arrowheads) and each critical dimension is annotated with “≥” to denote “not less than.”

Caption (beneath the graphic):  
“Where φ is the diameter of pre-tensioned tendon and dg is the maximum size of aggregate. Figure 8.14: Minimum clear spacing between pre-tensioned tendons.”

Context from clause 8.10.1 (Arrangement of prestressing tendons and ducts):  
• These spacing rules ensure adequate concrete placement, compaction, bond development around each tendon, and prevent aggregate entrapment between ducts.  
• Bundling of tendons in anchorage zones is discouraged unless special formwork and compaction tests demonstrate satisfactory performance.

 8.10 Prestressing tendons
 8.10.1 Arrangement of prestressing tendons and ducts
 (1)P The spacing of ducts or of pre-tensioned tendons shall be such as to ensure that placing and compacting of the concrete can be carried out satisfactorily and that sufficient bond can be attained between the concrete and the tendons.
 (1) The minimum clear horizontal and vertical spacing of individual pre-tensioned tendons should be in accordance with that shown in Figure 8.14. Other layouts may be used provided that test results show satisfactory ultimate behaviour with respect to:
 - the concrete in compression at the anchorage
 - the spalling of concrete
 - the anchorage of pre-tensioned tendons
 - the placing of the concrete between the tendons.
 Consideration should also be given to durability and the danger of corrosion of the tendon at the end of elements.
 (2) Bundling of tendons should not occur in the anchorage zones, unless placing and compacting of the concrete can be carried out satisfactorily and sufficient bond can be attained between the concrete and the tendons.

The image is a two-dimensional schematic, drawn in plan view, that illustrates the minimum clear spacing requirements between circular post-tensioning ducts. It consists of four red discs (each representing the cross-section of a duct) arranged in two groupings—one on the left side of the drawing and one on the right—together with dimension lines and call-outs indicating the required clearances in both vertical and horizontal directions. At the very bottom of the illustration is the caption “Minimum clear spacing between ducts,” and just below that is a note clarifying that “φ is the diameter of post-tension duct and d_g is the maximum aggregate size.”

Left-hand grouping (vertical stack):
 • Two red circles are stacked vertically. A vertical dimension line to their left carries two labels: “≥ φ” and, below it, “≥ 40 mm.” This indicates that the clear vertical spacing between the centers (or edges) of the ducts must be at least the duct diameter φ, and in any event not less than 40 mm.

Right-hand grouping (vertical stack):
 • Similarly, two red circles are stacked vertically on the right side. A vertical dimension line to their right shows “≥ d_g,” then “≥ φ,” then “≥ 40 mm.” This combination of labels specifies that the clear spacing between these ducts must be no less than the maximum aggregate size (d_g), the duct diameter φ, and a minimum absolute clearance of 40 mm.

Top-level (horizontal pair):
 • Two red circles appear at the upper center of the drawing, representing two ducts aligned roughly horizontally. A horizontal dimension line between them is annotated with three conditions: “≥ d_g + 5,” then “≥ φ,” and finally “≥ 50 mm.” This means that the minimum clear horizontal spacing between ducts must satisfy all three criteria—at least the maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm, at least one duct diameter φ, and at least an absolute 50 mm gap.

Graphic and annotation style:
 • All ducts are shown as solid filled circles in a consistent dark-red color.  
 • Dimension lines terminate in arrowheads pointing at the circle edges or center-to-center, depending on the intended measurement.  
 • Call-out text is rendered in a clean sans-serif font and is positioned adjacent to each dimension line.  
 • No numerical duct diameters or aggregate sizes are given; the diagram uses symbolic variables φ and d_g.  

Contextual relevance:
This clear-spacing diagram supports the requirements outlined in clauses 8.10.1 (“Ducts for post-tensioned tendons”) of the code text. It visually enforces the rule that ducts shall not be bundled (except in special vertical pairs), and that both concrete placement and grouting operations demand adequate spacing to prevent duct damage, ensure proper concrete compaction, and stop grout migration between ducts. By specifying these three parallel clearance criteria (aggregate size, duct diameter, and fixed millimeter minimum), the diagram ensures comprehensive compliance under varying material and geometric conditions.

The illustration is headed “Figure 8.16: Transfer of prestress in pretensioned elements; length parameters” and consists of two adjacent sub-figures—on the left, a longitudinal section through a rectangular concrete member with embedded prestressing tendon(s), and on the right, a plot of tendon stress versus distance along the member.

1. Left-hand sub-figure (member section and stress spread):
   • A horizontal concrete member is shown in profile, its overall depth (h) and effective depth to the centroid of the prestressing tendon zone (d) dimensioned by vertical arrows.  
   • Near the bottom face of the member three parallel lines represent the prestressing tendon or strand(s) running longitudinally.  
   • From the tendon location a pair of dashed lines fan out upward in a triangular or bell-shaped envelope to the top face of the member: these define the “dispersion length” ldisp over which the concentrated tendon force is assumed to spread out into a linearly varying stress distribution across the section.  
   • Measured from the start of the bonded region, a horizontal arrow marks the “transmission length” lpt, which is the distance needed for the prestress force to be fully developed in the concrete under ultimate bond stress conditions. Beyond lpt the dashed envelope reaches its maximum breadth under the top fiber.  
   • A further dashed vertical line at the far right indicates the end of the dispersion region. A call-out “A” at this line notes that, beyond the dispersion length, the concrete stress distribution in the section can be taken as linear (i.e. a straight-line variation from compression at the top fiber to tension relief at the tendon level).  

2. Right-hand sub-figure (tendon stress build-up):
   • Horizontal axis represents distance measured from the tendon release point; two vertical dashed lines mark distances lpt and lbpd (anchorage length).  
   • Vertical axis represents tendon stress σ. Two horizontal dashed lines correspond to an intermediate stress σpi (stress just after initial bond transfer) and the full design prestress σpd (ultimate stress fully applied).  
   • Between the origin and lpt the stress rises linearly from zero to the intermediate value σpi, reflecting constant bond transfer over the transmission length.  
   • Between lpt and lbpd the stress further increases from σpi up to the full prestress σpd at the end of the anchorage length.  
   • Beyond lbpd the tendon stress remains constant at σpd.  

Below the left sub-figure is the label:  
“A – Linear stress distribution in member cross-section.”  

Together, these two diagrams visually summarize:  
– the geometric relation between tendon location, member depth and the two key lengths, lpt (transmission length) and ldisp (dispersion length), required for transfer of prestress into concrete, and  
– the corresponding development of tendon force from release to full prestress over lpt and lbpd in pretensioned elements.

(1)P The ducts for post-tensioned tendons shall be located and constructed so that:
 - the concrete can be safely placed without damaging the ducts;
 - the concrete can resist the forces from the ducts in the curved parts during and after stressing;

The figure is a schematic line‐chart of how tendon stress develops along the anchorage length of a pre‐tensioned concrete member.  It uses a two‐axis plot:

•  Vertical axis (labelled “A”) represents tendon stress (σ),  
•  Horizontal axis (labelled “B”) represents distance from the end of the member (i.e. from the anchorage device).

Two curves are shown:  
 1.  A dashed straight line, marked “(1)”, representing the stress profile at the moment the tendons are released (transfer of prestress).  
 2.  A solid line, marked “(2)”, representing the stress profile at the ultimate limit state (i.e. under design load including shear effects).

Key stress levels on the vertical axis are identified by horizontal reference lines:  
 - σ_p∞  (sigma-p-infinity): the long-term tendon stress after all prestress losses have occurred.  
 - σ_pi   (sigma-p-i): the initial tendon stress at the instant of release / transfer.  
 - σ_pd   (sigma-p-d): the design tendon stress corresponding to the ultimate limit‐state force (to be used when checking anchorage zone capacity).

Along the horizontal axis three characteristic lengths are annotated by bracketed double‐arrows:  
 - l_pt1: the “basic transmission length” for the release‐stress profile (distance from the plate to the point where σ reaches σ_p i). This is the length over which bond develops the initial prestress at transfer.  
 - l_pt2: the upper‐bound design transmission length for ultimate limit state. It is the distance from the end over which the tendon stress ramps up from σ_p∞ to σ_pd.  
 - l_bp d: the total required anchorage length at ultimate limit state. It extends from the anchor plate to the point where the tendon stress first reaches the design level σ_pd, and then includes a final plateau region (constant‐stress) to ensure full development of bond.  

Curve details:  
•  At release, the dashed line starts at zero stress at the plate, increases linearly with distance, and reaches σ_pi exactly at x = l_pt1, then the dashed curve ends.  
•  At ULS (solid line), the stress also begins at zero at the plate, increases linearly at the same slope up to σ_p∞ at x = l_pt1, then continues at a lower slope from σ_p∞ at x = l_pt1 to σ_pd at x = l_pt2, and beyond that (from l_pt2 to l_bp d) the line flattens, showing constant σ_pd.  

A legend in the top right corner reiterates:  
  A – Tendon stress  
  B – Distance from end  

Below the chart is the caption:  
  “Figure 8.17: Stresses in the anchorage zone of pre-tensioned members:  
    (1) at release of tendons, (2) at ultimate limit state.”

Contextually, this diagram illustrates the concepts used in the calculation of anchorage lengths as per Eurocode provisions (see clauses 8.10.2.2, 9.2.1.3, etc.).  In particular it underpins the formula for total anchorage length  
  lbpd = lpt2 + α2·φ·(σpd – σp∞)/fbpd  
and shows why two different transmission zones (up to σp∞ then to σpd) must be considered when checking bond and anchorage in cracked sections.

sections: 10.2.3  Anchorage of tensile force for the ultimate limit state

content:
The image is a two‐part line drawing, labeled “Figure 8.18: Dispersion of prestress,” showing how prestressing force “P” spreads out into the concrete from an anchorage device. Both parts share a central longitudinal axis (dash-dotted line) that represents the centerline of the tendon location.

1. Top diagram (longitudinal view)  
   • A rectangular outline represents a prestressed concrete member in longitudinal section.  
   • Along the centerline runs the tendon location, indicated by a short dash-dot-dash line. On either side of that, two parallel dashed lines show the original tendon’s envelope before dispersion.  
   • At a vertical reference plane (shown by a dotted vertical line), the two innermost dashed lines begin to fan outward. From that plane, two straight solid lines diverge symmetrically above and below the axis.  
   • The angle between each solid line and the horizontal axis is labeled “β.” These two lines form a V-shape indicating the spread of prestress through the concrete at a half-angle of β.  
   • Above the top solid line and below the bottom solid line are small curved arrows pointing from the axis toward each solid line, each arrowed arc marked “β,” emphasizing that the spread angle on either side of the axis is β.  

2. Bottom diagram (section A, enlarged detail)  
   • Directly below the top view is a second, larger rectangular block, representing a cross-section taken at the plane marked by the vertical dash-dot reference line above. To its left, an arrow labeled “P” shows the prestressing force entering the anchorage from outside.  
   • From the point where “P” enters, three straight solid lines radiate into the block: one along the original tendon axis (dash-dotted) and two others diverging downward and upward at angle β to the axis. Each of these divergence lines is arrow-tipped, indicating the direction of stress flow.  
   • These three lines illustrate how the concentration of force fans out into the surrounding concrete. Two curved arrows at the entry point also mark the angles between the central axis and the diverging lines, each labeled “β.”  
   • A bracket at the lower edge of the block highlights the projected spread width at that face.  
   • A callout box labeled “A” sits to the right of the block, tying this enlarged detail back to the cut line “A” shown in the top diagram.  

Overall, the figure communicates that, for design simplification, the prestressing force may be assumed to disperse in concrete in a conical or prism-shaped pattern with a total included angle of 2 β (i.e. ± β to the tendon axis), where β can be taken as arctan (2/3). This visual serves to guide the design of anchorage zones by defining how far and in what angular spread the concentrated prestress force is assumed to “spread” into the surrounding concrete.

sections: 10.2.3  Anchorage of tensile force for the ultimate limit state

content:
(1) The anchorage of tendons should be checked in sections where the concrete tensile stress exceeds fctk,0,05. The tendon force should be calculated for a cracked section, including the effect of shear according to 6.2.3 (6); see also 9.2.1.3. Where the concrete tensile stress is less than fctk,0,05, no anchorage check is necessary.
 (2) The bond strength for anchorage in the ultimate limit state is:
 fbpd = ηp2 η1 fctd
 (8.20)
 where:
 ηp2 is a coefficient that takes into account the type of tendon and the bond situation at anchorage
 ηp2 = 1,4 for indented wires or
 ηp2 = 1,2 for 7-wire strands
 η1 is as defined in 8.10.2.2 (1)
 Note : Values of ηp2 for types of tendons other than those given above may be used subject to a European Technical Approval.
 (3) Due to increasing brittleness with higher concrete strength, fctk,0,05 should here be limited to the value for C60/75, unless it can be verified that the average bond strength increases above this limit.
 (4) The total anchorage length for anchoring a tendon with stress σpd is:
 lbpd = lpt2 + α2φ(σpd - σpm∞)/fbpd
 (8.21)
 where
 lpt2 is the upper design value of transmission length, see 8.10.2.2 (3) α2 as defined in 8.10.2.2 (2) σpd is the tendon stress corresponding to the force described in (1) σpm∞ is the prestress after all losses
 α2 as defined in 8.10.2.2 (2)
 (5) Tendon stresses in the anchorage zone are illustrated in Figure 8.17.

 (6) In case of combined ordinary and pre-tensioned reinforcement, the anchorage capacities of each may be summed.
 (1) The design of anchorage zones should be in accordance with the application rules given in this clause and those in 6.5.3.
 (2) When considering the effects of the prestress as a concentrated force on the anchorage zone, the design value of the prestressing tendons should be in accordance with 2.4.2.2 (3) and the lower characteristic tensile strength of the concrete should be used.
 (3) The bearing stress behind anchorage plates should be checked in accordance with the relevant European Technical Approval.
 (4) Tensile forces due to concentrated forces should be assessed by a strut and tie model, or other appropriate representation (see 6.5). Reinforcement should be detailed assuming that it acts at its design strength. If the stress in this reinforcement is limited to 300 MPa no check of crackwidths is necessary.
 (5) As a simplification the prestressing force may be assumed to disperse at an angle of spread 2β (see Figure 8.18), starting at the end of the anchorage device, where β may be assumed to be arc tan 2/3.

content:
(1)P The anchorage devices used for post-tensioned tendons shall be in accordance with those specified for the prestressing system, and the anchorage lengths in the case of pre-tensioned tendons shall be such as to enable the full design strength of the tendons to be developed, taking account of any repeated, rapidly changing action effects.
 (2)P Where couplers are used they shall be in accordance with those specified for the prestressing system and shall be so placed - taking account of the interference caused by these devices - that they do not affect the bearing capacity of the member and that any temporary anchorage which may be needed during construction can be introduced in a satisfactory manner.
 (3) Calculations for local effects in the concrete and for the transverse reinforcement should be made in accordance with 6.5 and 8.10.3.
 (4) In general, couplers should be located away from intermediate supports.
 (5) The placing of couplers on 50% or more of the tendons at one cross-section should be avoided unless it can be shown that a higher percentage will not cause more risk to the safety of the structure.

The image is a black-and-white schematic cross-section of a reinforced-concrete flanged beam (a “T-beam”), annotated to show how the tension reinforcement is to be placed within the effective flange width.  At the top, a wide horizontal slab-like flange is drawn; below it a narrower vertical web projects downward.  Key notations and dimensions are indicated by arrows and labels:

• “beff1” and “beff2” mark the portions of the flange on each side of the central web that are effective in resisting bending in tension.  The total effective flange width, “beff,” spans from the outside edge of beff1 across the web width “bw” to the outside edge of beff2, as shown by two vertical dashed lines.  
• “bw” denotes the thickness of the vertical web.  
• “hf” indicates the flange thickness, measured from the top surface of the web up to the top surface of the flange.  

Along the underside of the flange, directly above the web and extending into the two effective flange zones, a row of small circles is shown; these are labeled “As” and represent the cross-sectional area of longitudinal tension reinforcement (steel bars) that must be distributed across the effective flange width.  The circles are uniformly spaced and lie close to the flange-web junction, illustrating the recommended position of the main tensile reinforcement in a flanged cross-section.  

Inside the lower part of the web, two larger circles appear near the bottom edge; these represent prestressing tendons or bottom longitudinal bars located within external ducts or unbonded sheaths.  These are shown to remind the designer that, while the main As bars occupy the flange, the prestressing elements occupy the web and must be accounted for separately.  

A horizontal line across the top of the web denotes the soffit of the flange, and narrow horizontal strokes along the flange’s underside emphasize the concrete cover to the As bars.  All elements are drawn with straight, crisp lines and standard arrowheads to indicate dimensions.  This figure is captioned “Placing of tension reinforcement in flanged cross-section,” and serves to illustrate how to position and quantify the As bars in accordance with code provisions for T-beams: only the web width plus the effective flange projections (beff1, beff2) are considered when calculating the required area of tensile steel, and the bars must be arranged near the junction to control cracking and ensure ductile flexural behavior.

The drawing is a two‐part schematic (one large view on the left, one enlarged detail on the right) illustrating how longitudinal reinforcement is curtailed and anchored in a prestressed concrete beam, taking account of inclined cracks and the capacity of reinforcement within anchorage lengths.  

Overall Arrangement  
• A simply supported beam is shown in longitudinal section. Two small solid triangles—one near each end—mark the support locations. The beam’s top and bottom faces are represented by parallel horizontal lines.  

Left‐Hand Main View  
• Envelope of MEd/z + NEd: The central region of the beam (spanning between the two supports) is filled with closely spaced diagonal hatching. This hatched area represents the envelope of bending moment divided by lever arm plus any axial force (MEd/z + NEd), i.e. the internal force that the longitudinal steel must resist.  
• Curved tendon profile: A bold, smooth curve traces from one support up toward midspan and down again to the far support, representing the path of the prestressing tendon.  
• Acting tensile force Fs (label B): At a point on the ascending curve near midspan, an arrow marked “B” points tangentially to the tendon profile; this denotes the tensile force developed by the change in curvature of the tendon (∆Ftd).  
• Resisting tensile force FRs (label C): A second line, clinging to the hatching but lying inside the envelope, is drawn more shallowly. An arrow marked “C” on this inner line indicates the resisting tensile force provided by the longitudinal reinforcement.  
• Beginning of curtailment (al): Close to each support, the tendon curve leaves the hatched zone at a horizontal distance aₗ from the support triangle. This aₗ corresponds to the “shift rule” distance used to account for inclined crack effects (al = d in many cases).  
• Anchorage length lbd: Between the point where the reinforcement is no longer required for moment resistance and the support, several double‐headed dimension lines labelled lbd indicate the required development (anchorage) length of the straight bars or tendon’s bonded zone. These appear both above and below the tendon curve near each support.  

Right‐Hand Enlarged Detail  
• Support region focus: This inset magnifies the right‐hand support area to show in greater clarity how the envelope, tendon profile, acting and resisting force lines, and anchorage lengths interact over a short span.  
• Envelope, tendon and reinforcement lines are repeated with the same labeling conventions (A for envelope, B for Fs arrow, C for FRs arrow).  
• Multiple lbd dimension arrows mark the minimum bond length that straight or bent‐up bars must occupy in the concrete to develop their full characteristic yield without slipping.  

Caption (beneath drawing)  
Figure 9.2: Illustration of the curtailment of longitudinal reinforcement, taking into account the effect of inclined cracks and the resistance of reinforcement within anchorage lengths.  

Key points conveyed by the illustration:  
1. The internal force envelope (MEd/z + NEd) defines where reinforcement is needed—the hatched zone.  
2. The additional tensile force induced by changes in tendon curvature (∆Ftd, shown as Fs) must be resisted by steel (FRs).  
3. Reinforcement may be progressively reduced (curtailed) from the zone of maximum moment toward supports, beginning at a distance aₗ from each support.  
4. Even where no moment resistance is required, a development length lbd of steel must remain embedded to anchor the bars or tendons and mobilize full capacity.  

This figure complements the textual rules on the detailing of reinforcement anchorage (see clauses on curtailment of longitudinal bars at supports and intermediate sections, and on accounting for inclined cracks and anchorage lengths lbd).

This image is a two-part schematic (labelled a) and b)) from EN 1992-1-1 (Eurocode 2), figure 9.3, illustrating “Anchorage of bottom reinforcement at end supports.” Both diagrams show how the bottom (tensile) longitudinal bars in a beam must be embedded (“anchored”) into the support for safe transfer of the tensile force. Key elements, dimensions and labels are described below.

1. Diagram a) “Direct support: Beam supported by wall or column”  
  • The beam is represented in longitudinal section as two horizontal lines (top and bottom faces) spanning left to right. Beneath the top line is the neutral‐axis or tendon, above the lower line is the bottom reinforcement bar.  
  • At the right end, the beam bears directly onto a vertical element (wall or column), drawn as a thick vertical line.  
  • A horizontal dimension arrow, labelled “l_bd,” extends from the face of the support back into the beam’s length, indicating the required development length of the bottom bars into the span.  
  • The bottom reinforcement is shown terminating at the plane of the support; its anchorage depends on sufficient bond length “l_bd” within the beam itself.  
  • Underneath, the caption reads: “support: Beam supported by wall or column.”

2. Diagram b) “Indirect support: Beam supported by corbel or deep embedment”  
  • The beam’s longitudinal section again appears as two horizontal lines; the bottom bar is the lower line.  
  • Surrounding and supporting the beam end is a shaded, hatched rectangular block of concrete (this may represent a corbel, pile cap, thickened wall, or other permanently cast support element). This block extends above and below the beam.  
  • The width of this support block is indicated by a horizontal double-ended arrow labelled “b.”  
  • A dimension arrow labelled “l_bd” is drawn at the top of the block, measuring from the face of the support block back into the beam region. This shows that, in an indirect support, the development length can run through the supporting concrete as well, often improving anchorage.  
  • The bottom reinforcement is shown continuing into the shaded block for the full length “l_bd.”  
  • Below the graphic is the caption: “b) Indirect support: Beam supported by …” (truncated in the image, but understood as “beam supported by corbel or thickened support”).

General context (from Eurocode 2, clause 9.2.1.4):  
– l_bd is the basic anchorage length required to develop the full tensile capacity of the bar. It depends on bar diameter, concrete strength, yield strength of the steel, bond conditions and presence of transverse reinforcement (see clause 8.4.4).  
– For direct support, the anchorage must be achieved entirely within the beam span.  
– For indirect support (e.g. corbel, supporting wall or pile cap), the development length may extend through the supporting element, provided the concrete there is sound and properly confined.  
– The section width “b” of the supporting member is important for checking transverse pressure and adequate confinement of the anchored bars.  

These two simple line‐drawings help designers visualize how to detail bottom bars at the ends of simply supported beams—either resting directly on a wall/column or built into a supporting mass—so that the tensile forces are safely transferred without slipping or bond failure.

The image is a schematic, monochrome line drawing titled “Figure 9.4: Anchorage at intermediate supports” and is divided into two side-by-side sub-figures labeled a) and b). Both diagrams show a horizontal member (beam or slab) in cross-section, with its top face represented by a thick continuous line, and its tension reinforcement (steel bars) running near the bottom face, also indicated by parallel lines.

Sub-figure a) Bent-up bar anchorage  
• The top of the drawing shows the concrete member’s top face; below it is the bottom face.  
• A single reinforcement bar is drawn near the bottom, bending upward over the support zone. The vertical leg of the hook extends into the compression zone.  
• On the left of the hook, a horizontal arrow labeled “l ≥ 10 φ” spans the clear distance from the support line to the point where the reinforcement is straight, indicating that the straight length before the bend must be at least ten times the bar diameter φ.  
• On the right of the hook, a horizontal arrow labeled “l ≥ dₘ” measures from the face of the support to the start of the bend’s curvature, denoting that this development length must be at least equal to the mandrel diameter dₘ used to form the hook.  

Sub-figure b) Straight-bar and lap-splice anchorage  
• Again, the concrete top and bottom faces are shown as thick lines. Two parallel reinforcement bars lie near the bottom face, one above the other, indicating a lap splice.  
• Above the pair of overlapping bars, a double-headed arrow labeled “lᵇᵈ” marks the required lap length (the basic anchorage length lbd) over which the bars must overlap inside the concrete to develop full tensile capacity.  
• To the right of the splice, a single bar continues straight past the support face. A horizontal arrow beneath it carries the label “l ≥ 10 φ,” signifying that when hooks are not used, the bar must extend straight for at least ten times its diameter φ beyond the support face to ensure adequate anchorage.  
• The support face itself is represented by a vertical line or slight break in the concrete line, indicating the intermediate support location.  

Overall, the figure illustrates two alternative detailing methods for anchoring bottom (tension) reinforcement at intermediate supports in accordance with European detailing rules: a bent-up hook with mandrel dimensions (a), and a straight-bar lap splice plus straight extension (b). Dimension arrows, inequality notations and symbol labels (φ for bar diameter, dₘ for mandrel diameter, lbd for basic development length) clearly communicate the minimum length requirements needed to satisfy anchorage provisions.

The image is a black-and-white schematic cross-section of a rectangular reinforced-concrete beam illustrating “Examples of shear reinforcement” (labelled as Figure 9.5). It shows both the outer links (full stirrups) and two alternative forms of inner links, with labels A and B identifying them.

Overall layout  
- The beam’s cross-section is represented by two parallel horizontal lines (top and bottom faces) joined at either end by vertical lines (web faces), forming a simple rectangle.  
- Inside the rectangle, several filled circles denote the longitudinal tension bars (rebars) running along the beam’s length. These circles are arranged with two near each face and one or two centrally, reflecting a typical multi-bar tension reinforcement layout.

Label B: Outer link (full stirrup)  
- A continuous rectangular loop of reinforcement (the “outer link”) follows the full perimeter of the concrete section just inside the faces.  
- This closed stirrup encloses all the longitudinal bars, providing full confinement of the web and holding the tension and compression zones together.  
- The stirrup is drawn as a single rectangular line positioned slightly inset from the beam faces, with its corners sharply angled.  
- Small gaps or joints (not explicitly detailed) at the ends of the stirrup legs are assumed to be properly anchored or hooked as per detailing rules.

Label A: Inner link alternatives  
- Inside that outer stirrup, two U-shaped “inner link” options are shown, each marked A and pointing to one of the two alternative shapes:  
  1. A narrow U-link whose legs each embrace the two outermost longitudinal bars and turn back under the bottom faces, leaving the central bars outside its leg loop.  
  2. A wider U-link whose legs extend upward on each side, enclosing a larger group of bars, and then tie back to form a closed “U” that does not return all the way to the top face.  
- Both inner links are drawn with rounded “U” bends at their ends and with hooked or anchored leg ends at the bottom to resist slipping.  
- These inner links do not surround the outer web face, but instead only surround the central cluster of bars and provide shear resistance directly where inclined cracks are most likely to form.

Key details and context  
- The diagram exemplifies the two basic ways to provide shear reinforcement in a beam web under Eurocode 2: full perimeter stirrups (B) and supplementary or “inner” links (A) which may be used when shear demands allow fewer wraps around the section.  
- According to clause 9.2.2 of EN 1992-1-1, links should be closed, anchored by laps or hooks, and inclined between 45° and 90° to the beam’s axis. In this figure, both types of link are drawn at 90°.  
- The outer link B provides the minimum shear link ratio ρw,min and maximum leg spacing (smax) defined in expressions (9.4)–(9.8). The inner links A illustrate alternatives where part of the required shear reinforcement is concentrated around the tensile bars.  
- The black dots (longitudinal bars) and their spacing imply a typical beam section that must control both flexural cracks and shear cracks, with the inner links helping intercept inclined cracks within the web.

By comparing the two inner-link shapes (A) against the full stirrup (B), the figure makes clear how designers can choose between enclosing the entire section or only the critical interior region—so long as anchorage, spacing, and link area requirements are satisfied.

The drawing is a black-and-white schematic composed of three side-by-side subfigures (labeled a1, a2 and a3) under the caption “Figure 9.6: Examples of shapes for torsion links.” Each subfigure shows how closed‐loop links (stirrups bent 90°) may be formed around a reinforced-concrete cross-section to resist torsion. Longitudinal reinforcement bars are indicated by solid black circles. The torsion links themselves are shown as heavier continuous lines, with hooked or bent ends at right angles to form a closed enclosure around the main bars.  

Subfigure a1:  
• A simple rectangular beam cross-section is drawn as a thin outline rectangle.  
• Four black-filled circles (the longitudinal bars) are arranged two near the top flange and two near the bottom flange, close to each corner but offset slightly inward.  
• A single closed‐loop link surrounds these bars: its legs run parallel to the beam faces and turn through 90° at each corner, with short hooked ends wrapping back along the outer face. This loop fully encloses all four main bars.  

Subfigure a2:  
• Again a rectangle outlines the beam cross-section; four circles mark the longitudinal bars in the same positions as a1.  
• Two small square outlines are drawn inside the rectangle, representing either interior columns, concentrated load zones or anchorage nodes. One square is at upper left inside the link, the other at lower right.  
• A dashed double‐headed arrow between the two squares is labeled “or,” indicating an alternative placement for the internal hook legs.  
• The closed‐loop link is similar to a1—bent at the corners with 90° hooks—but also has additional link legs extending toward one of the square nodes to provide anchorage around an internal boundary or load point.  

Subfigure a3:  
• Depicts a beam‐and‐slab intersection in longitudinal section: a thin horizontal slab flange sits atop a vertical web beneath. The slab is represented by two parallel lines at the top, with several small black circles along each line marking the slab’s main reinforcement.  
• Directly below, a rectangular beam web contains four black circles at its bottom face (the longitudinal bars in tension).  
• A U-shaped link is formed around those bottom bars, then extends upward into the slab flange as two vertical legs that hook around the top reinforcement. The result is a continuous closed link crossing the beam-slab interface.  

Overall, these three sketches illustrate recommended closed torsion-link geometries—each forming a fully anchored, 90°‐bent loop around the longitudinal bars, with additional legs or embedded hooks where necessary to tie into interior nodes or adjoining slab reinforcement.

The image is a plan-view line drawing, taken from “Figure 9.7: Placing of supporting reinforcement in the intersection zone of two beams (plan view).” It shows two rectangular-section concrete beams crossing at right angles. The horizontal member, labeled “A,” is the supporting beam with overall depth h₁; the vertical member, labeled “B,” is the supported beam with depth h₂ (with the condition h₁ ≥ h₂ noted). Both beams share a common intersection “block” shaded in light gray.

Key graphic elements:
- Centerlines of both beams are shown as perpendicular dashed lines.
- The shaded intersection zone is a rectangle whose long axis aligns with beam A (horizontal).
- Reinforcement bars appear as parallel solid lines just inside the perimeter of each beam’s outline: two on the top face and two on the bottom face of beam A, similarly two bars at either side of beam B.
- Four dimension arrows, each paired with a limit expression, mark the maximum recommended extent of the supporting bars into the intersection:
   • Along beam A’s axis (horizontal), from the centerline out to the shaded region edge: ≤ h₁/2  
   • Perpendicular to A (into beam B): ≤ h₁/3  
   • Along beam B’s axis (vertical), from its centerline down into the shaded zone: ≤ h₂/2  
   • Perpendicular to B (into beam A): ≤ h₂/3  

These fractions of the member depths define the “supporting reinforcement zone” within which bars carried by one member must extend into the intersecting member to ensure proper anchorage and load transfer. The notation “h₁ ≥ h₂” next to label B clarifies that the supporting beam (A) is the deeper section.

At the bottom of the drawing is the figure caption:  
“9.7: Placing of supporting reinforcement in the intersection zone of two beams (plan view).”

Overall, the sketch graphically enforces the Eurocode-style detailing rule that any reinforcement intended to tie one beam into another must intrude into the intersection for a distance proportional to each beam’s depth—no more than one-third of its own depth across the junction, and no more than one-half of its depth measured along its span. This ensures that reinforcing bars are sufficiently anchored in the crossing beam without unnecessarily congesting the joint.

The drawing is a simplified, schematic cross-section through the free (unsupported) edge of a reinforced-concrete slab.  Its principal features are as follows:

1.   Slab Geometry  
     – The slab has total thickness “h,” shown by a vertical dimension line on the left.  
     – The right-hand face of the slab is free and unsupported (i.e. a hanging or cantilevered edge).  

2.   Reinforcement Layout  
     – Two longitudinal reinforcement bars are shown, running parallel to the slab faces and located near the top surface (i.e. within the tensile zone at an unsupported edge).  
     – The upper bar (in the view) is straight and extends back into the concrete slab for a clear embedment length.  
     – The lower bar is given a 180° hook (a U-shaped bend) immediately adjacent to the free edge; its end turns back parallel to itself and lies against the upper face of the slab.  

3.   Anchorage Requirements  
     – A horizontal dimension beneath the bars reads “≥ 2 h.”  This indicates that, whether by straight embedment or by hook, each bar must be anchored at least two times the slab thickness back from the unsupported edge.  In Eurocode-2 terms, this meets or exceeds the minimum development length for edge reinforcement.  
     – The straight bar thus relies solely on bond over a length ≥ 2h.  The hooked bar provides mechanical anchorage via its bend, which may permit a somewhat shorter straight embedment but must still satisfy the code’s hook-length rules.  

4.   Cover and Positioning  
     – Although not dimensioned in the sketch, the bars are shown close to the slab’s top face, leaving concrete cover above them (typically in accordance with fire- and durability-driven cover requirements).  
     – The vertical separation between the two bars is small, reflecting that only the minimal edge-reinforcement needed to control cracking and to resist possible uplift or rotation at the free edge is being provided.  

5.   Code Context (EN 1992-1-1, Section 9.3.1.6 and Figure 9.8)  
     – Clause 9.3.1.5–6 of Eurocode 2 states that at any free, unsupported edge a slab “should normally contain longitudinal and transverse reinforcement, generally arranged as shown in Figure 9.8.”  
     – The horizontal embedment length (or a properly bent hook) must be sufficient to develop the bar’s characteristic yield strength—here illustrated by “≥ 2 h.”  
     – The example shows that the normal main reinforcement of the slab may serve double duty as edge reinforcement, provided it complies with the anchorage-length and cover provisions of Section 8.4.  

In sum, this figure conveys a minimal edge-reinforcement detail for a slab: two parallel bars near the top flange, each anchored back into the slab by at least twice its thickness, one by straight bond length and one by a 180° hook, to satisfy the Eurocode requirement that free edges be reinforced against tensile stresses and to control crack widths.

The image is a two-part schematic (Figure 9.9) illustrating how to determine the “effective width” be of a flat slab at locations where it bears on columns.  Both sub-figures are simple plan-view sketches: a heavy continuous line represents the slab surface; a filled gray rectangle represents a column; dashed lines and dimension arrows define the parameters that go into the formula for be.  Each sub-figure carries a label (“a” or “b”), a short formula for be, plus notes on what the geometric symbols mean.   

1. Sub-figure (a) – Edge column  
 • The gray column sits immediately adjacent to one slab edge (the left hand side of the drawing).  
 • A dashed vertical line on the right of the column marks the far boundary of the “effective width.”  
 • Above the column a double-headed arrow labeled Cz spans the full width of the column.  Cz is the column width measured in the direction parallel to the slab edge.  
 • To the left of the column a dash-dot line marks the slab edge; from that slab edge a downward-pointing arrow labeled y measures the clear distance to the inside face of the column.  
 • At the slab surface line, just left of the column, a small arrow labeled A indicates the reference line or axis along which the slab is “effective.”  
 • Underneath the sketch is the formula:  
     be = Cz + y  
   and a note: “y can be > cy. Note: y is the distance from the edge of the slab to the inside face of the column.”  
 • In other words, when a column lies on an exterior slab edge, the effective width is the column width plus the overhang (y) back to the free slab edge.  

2. Sub-figure (b) – Corner column  
 • The gray rectangle represents a column located at the corner of the slab, touching two free edges (bottom and right edges of the drawing).  
 • Two dashed lines—one vertical to the right of the column, one horizontal below it—mark the extents of the effective width zone.  
 • A double-headed arrow labeled Cz again spans the width of the column, here oriented horizontally at the top of the sketch.  
 • Two arrows labeled z measure the distances from each free slab edge to the inside face of the column: one horizontal (pointing left from the right edge) and one vertical (pointing up from the bottom edge).  
 • The reference line A is again indicated on the slab surface line next to the column.  
 • Below this sketch the formula reads:  
     be = Cz + z  
   together with a note clarifying that z is the distance from the free slab edges to the column face (and that z may exceed the value of cy in earlier clauses).  
 • Thus, at a corner, the effective width is the column width plus the distance from each adjacent free edge back to the column.  

Overall, the figure provides a clear, dimensioned plan-view method for determining how far a slab panel on either an edge or a corner will “act” (i.e. be effective) in resisting bending or transmitting loads into the column.  It establishes Cz as the basic column dimension and adds either a single overhang y (edge case) or the corresponding overhang z (corner case) to form the total effective width be.

The drawing is a simplified schematic, from the Eurocode, showing how punching-shear reinforcement (“links”) is laid out around a loaded area (for instance a column or concentrated load) in a flat slab or beam–slab junction.  It combines a longitudinal section view through the slab plus a fragment of plan-view perimeters, all annotated with control-perimeter limits and spacing rules.  

1. Overall geometry  
   • A horizontal slab of effective depth d is shown spanning between beams (one beam is drawn at left, projecting more than 0.3·d beneath the slab).  At right the slab is continuous beyond the illustration.  
   • A loaded area (often a column or pad bearing) is implied at the left–center of the slab, beneath the intersection of the beam and slab.  Its plan footprint is not fully drawn, but the first and outer control perimeters are indicated in plan by two broken (dashed) rectangles.  

2. Control perimeters (plan)  
   • “A” marks the outer control perimeter at a distance ≤ k·d from the loaded area.  This outer perimeter encloses the region within which shear reinforcement must be provided.  
   • “B” marks the first (inner) control perimeter at distance kd from the loaded area.  Between the loaded area and perimeter “B,” punching shear reinforcement is not required.  Beyond “B” and up to “A,” shear links must be placed.  

3. Spacing and dimensions  
   • In the longitudinal (section) view—parallel to the beam axis—the link legs (short vertical strokes representing the legs of closed links or stirrups) are shown spaced at equal intervals not exceeding 0.75·d.  A dimension line beneath the link symbols reads “≤ 0,75 d.”  
   • The slab thickness (effective depth) is labelled “d” at the lower left of the slab section.  
   • The beam projecting below is dimensioned as “> 0,3 d” from slab underside to beam underside, ensuring adequate anchorage length and anchorage in compression zone.  
   • A dashed diagonal line cutting through the slab in section view illustrates that the control-perimeter “A” lies at or beyond that line, for clarity of where punching shear capacity changes.  

4. Notation and callouts  
   • Underneath the plan fragment, a legend reads:  
     – “A – outer control perimeter requiring shear reinforcement”  
     – “B – first control perimeter not requiring shear reinforcement”  
   • At the bottom the figure is captioned “Figure 9.10: Punching shear reinforcement.”  

5. Interpretation in design  
   • The image enforces two key Eurocode rules:  
     1. Shear links (closed stirrups around the loaded area) must be provided between the inner and outer perimeters.  
     2. Maximum spacing of those links, measured along the slab, must not exceed 0.75·d, assuring sufficient shear capacity to resist punching shear.

   • To the right of the cap the dash-dot silhouette of the cap’s side is shown, and a curved arrow between vertical and dashed inclined edges is labelled “45°,” confirming the angle of spread for the compression zone.

      b.  A taller vertical strip, centred on the vertical dashed axis, spanning nearly the full diameter in the y-direction but limited in the x-direction.  
      c.  A narrower central square (or nearly square) region, also centred, indicating the overlap of the two orthogonal strips (i.e. where bars in both directions coincide).

The image is a two-part schematic entitled “Figure 9.13: Model for tensile force with regard to inclined cracks.” It illustrates the way in which an eccentric column load produces a tensile force in the reinforcement of a footing (or beam) and how that force must be anchored, taking account of possible inclined crack paths.

Top diagram (longitudinal section through footing or beam):  
• A horizontal concrete element of overall depth h (measured to top of the beam or slab) and effective depth d (to the centroid of the bottom tension reinforcement) is shown spanning left-to-right.  
• On the far right, the beam/footing continues beyond the section of interest; on the left the element is cut at two vertical faces, labeled A (leftmost cut) and B (cut immediately under the column). The distance AB defines the “anchorage zone.”  
• At the top of the section under the column, a vertical arrow labeled NEd indicates the applied axial (eccentric) load. This arrow is offset horizontally from the centroid of the footing cross-section by an eccentricity e.  
• The compressive resultant in the concrete is shown as a force Fc acting at the underside of the top flange (or the top of the slab) at section B. The line of action of Fc lies at a perpendicular distance zi (the internal lever arm) below the centroid of the tension reinforcement.  
• The external lever arm ze is shown between the vertical line of NEd and the line of action of Fc. This establishes equilibrium of moments.  
• From the point of Fc at section B, a family of potential inclined crack planes is sketched by several dashed lines fanning downward and leftward toward the tension reinforcement. One representative crack path is shown terminating at a point on the bottom reinforcement at or before face A. Along that crack path, the tensile force Fs is mobilized in the bar.  
• On the bottom face of the beam, a straight heavy line represents the tension reinforcement, and Fs,max denotes the maximum tensile force reaching section B.  
• Between face A and the point where the rebar continues outside the cracked zone, a dimension x is shown; that is the minimum embedment length within which Fs must be anchored. In addition, lb marks the development length available for anchorage measured from face A back toward the bar’s free end.  

Bottom diagram (plan or elevation inset illustrating ground pressure):  
• At left, a narrow vertical stripe pattern denotes a column or pile top. A downward arrow labeled R represents the concentrated ground reaction beneath that column.  
• To the right, a triangular wedge of gradually expanding width represents how that reaction pressure spreads at a roughly 45° angle into the base material (footing or soil), illustrating how compressive stress fans out below the loaded area.  

Key variables called out in the figure:  
– NEd: design axial load (with eccentricity e) applied through the column onto the beam/footing.  
– e: horizontal distance between the line of action of NEd and the centroidal axis of the footing section.  
– b: clear width of the section under consideration (between faces A and B).  
– ze: external moment arm from NEd to Fc in the concrete.  
– Fc: resultant compressive force in the concrete above the centroid of tension steel.  
– zi: internal lever arm from Fc to the centroid of the bottom tension reinforcement.  
– h: total depth of the member.  
– d: effective depth to the tension steel.  
– Fs: tensile force developed in the bottom bar as a result of the eccentric loading and inclined cracking.  
– Fs,max: peak tensile force at face B.  
– x: minimum required anchorage length from the section face into the uncracked zone.  
– lb: available development length of the bar.  

Overall, this figure serves to illustrate the strut‐and‐tie or cracked‐plane approach to anchorage design in footings and beams under eccentric loads. It emphasizes that, because cracks incline through the concrete, the tensile reinforcement must be developed over a certain length x (and at least the standard development length lb) to safely transfer Fs back into the concrete without pullout.

The three sub-figures (a, b and c) present an elevation view, a plan view, and a sectional detail of the same footing and reinforcement arrangement.

1. General arrangement (figure a, elevation):  
   – A square or rectangular footing of overall width b and thickness h sits directly on a rock substrate.  
   – A column or concentrated loaded area of width c (centered on the footing) carries a vertical design axial force NEd, shown by three downward arrows.  
   – The depth of rock affected by splitting (H) is indicated beneath the footing, extending laterally from the loaded area edges to the full width of the footing.  
   – Horizontal splitting reinforcement bars are depicted as a series of parallel lines within the lower half of the footing, spanning almost the full width b. These bars are intended to resist radial tensile stresses (splitting) in the concrete and rock.  
   – The footnote “footing with h ≥ H” emphasizes that the concrete depth (h) must at least match the critical splitting depth in the rock (H).

2. Plan view (figure b, section view from above):  
   – A top-down cut through the footing shows the square outline of the footing (dimension b × b).  
   – The central loaded area or column base (size c × c) is indicated by a smaller square.  
   – Corner reinforcement bars—four in total—are marked just inside the outer perimeter of the footing. These represent the top ends of the horizontal splitting reinforcement grid.  

3. Section through the rock and footing (figure c):  
   – A vertical slice through the centerline details how the splitting bars extend longitudinally and are anchored at least to the depth H below the loaded area.  
   – The section clarifies that the rock contact surface transfers compressive load but is susceptible to tensile splitting forces away from the directly loaded region; the reinforcement prevents these forces from opening cracks.  
   – All bars are shown as continuous straight runs or hooked/anchored ends, adhering to the anchorage length requirements (lbd) referenced in EN 1992-1-1, Section 8.  

Overall, the illustration emphasizes:

– The dimensioning of the reinforcement zone so that h ≥ H, ensuring that splitting reinforcement lies within the critical depth of the rock.

The table “9.6N: Recommended minimum longitudinal reinforcement area in cast-in-place piles” provides, for three ranges of pile cross-sectional area (Ac), the corresponding minimum area of longitudinal reinforcement (As,bpmin) that must be distributed around the periphery of the pile. It is intended to ensure sufficient steel to control cracking, provide ductility, and allow proper concrete flow around the cage during casting of bored piles (see section 9.8.1 on bored-pile reinforcement).

1. Columns and Headings  
   • Pile cross-section: Ac (m²)  
   • Minimum area of longitudinal reinforcement: As,bpmin  

2. Ranges of Ac and Associated As,bpmin  
   a) Ac ≤ 0.50 m²  
      – As,bpmin ≥ 0.005 · Ac  
        • This means 0.5 % of the concrete area.  
        • E.g. for Ac = 0.40 m² ⇒ As,bpmin ≥ 0.005×0.40 = 0.002 m² (20 cm²).  

   b) 0.50 m² < Ac ≤ 1.00 m²  
      – As,bpmin ≥ 25 cm²  
        • A fixed minimum irrespective of the exact Ac, reflecting practical bar sizing.  
        • Ensures at least six bars of diameter ≥ 16 mm, with clear spacing ≤ 200 mm along the periphery.  

   c) Ac > 1.00 m²  
      – As,bpmin ≥ 0.0025 · Ac  
        • Equivalent to 0.25 % of the concrete area for larger piles.  
        • E.g. for Ac = 1.20 m² ⇒ As,bpmin ≥ 0.0025×1.20 = 0.003 m² (30 cm²).  

3. Units and Conventions  
   – Ac is expressed in square metres (m²).  
   – As,bpmin may be calculated in m² or converted to cm² for detailing.  
   – The multiplication factors (0.005 and 0.0025) denote percentages of concrete area (0.5 % and 0.25 %).  
   – The fixed 25 cm² in the middle band corresponds to the practical lower limit for bar schedules in medium-sized piles.

4. Contextual Notes from 9.8.1 (Bored Piles)  
   – Pile diameters up to a threshold h1 (recommended 600 mm) use this table to size longitudinal steel.  
   – Longitudinal bars must be at least 16 mm in diameter, with a minimum of six bars evenly spaced.  
   – Clear distance between adjacent bars around the perimeter must not exceed 200 mm to facilitate concrete placement.  
   – Transverse ties or spirals must comply with EN 1536 and be spaced to prevent bar buckling and maintain cage geometry during concreting.

5. How to Use the Table in Design  
   1. Calculate or measure Ac of the chosen pile cross-section.  
   2. Identify which of the three ranges Ac falls into.  
   3. Compute As,bpmin using the listed percentage or take the fixed value if in the middle range.  
   4. Verify that the resulting steel area can be provided with practical bar diameters and spacing rules.  
   5. Ensure transverse reinforcement (ties or spirals) and cover requirements are also met per EN 1536 and clause 9.8.1.
