The image is a schematic plan (or “horizontal slice”) through a multi-storey framed structure showing how horizontal ties should be arranged at each floor or roof level for accidental-action resistance. Key features are as follows:

1. General Layout  
- Three slab levels are shown one above the other (top, middle and bottom). Each level is indicated by a pair of heavy dashed lines, representing the continuous steel “tie” reinforcement running through the slab.  
- At each level there are three column locations, depicted by solid‐line squares. These squares represent edge or interior columns (or walls) through which the ties pass or to which they are anchored.  
- To the left of the three‐column stack is a vertical dashed-line alignment, indicating a second tie direction at right angles to the first.

2. Peripheral Tie (Label A)  
- Around the outer columns, the dashed lines run in a closed loop, linking the three columns on that plan “strip.” This loop is the peripheral tie, which must be effectively continuous around the edge of the structure’s plan at every floor/roof level.  
- Label “A” in the drawing identifies this peripheral tie. It shows that the perimeter bars pass through or around each edge column, forming a continuous frame.

3. Internal Tie (Label B)  
- Within the same strip, an internal tie runs between interior columns. On the middle level the internal tie is shown with a pair of opposing arrows: these indicate that the tie must resist tensile forces in that span direction on either side of an interior beam or column.  
- Label “B” points to one of these internal runs. It shows the tie steel grouped along the beam line through the interior column.  
- The arrows imply a continuous bar or bundle of bars spanning from one peripheral tie to the other, anchoring into them at the ends.

4. Two-Direction Tying  
- The vertical dashed line to the left illustrates the second orthogonal tie direction. In a real building, ties are usually provided in two perpendicular directions in plan, at every slab or roof level.  
- These two sets of ties (horizontal and vertical in plan) form a net that holds the slab and columns together if an accidental column loss or extreme load case occurs.

5. Key Design Principles (as reinforced by the surrounding text)  
- Ties must be “effectively continuous” throughout their length, without relying solely on lap splices in narrow joints (mechanical anchorage is recommended there).  
- Internal ties can either be distributed evenly through the slab or grouped at beams and walls—here they are shown as grouped along beam lines.  
- In walls or slabs, internal ties should lie close (within about 0.5 m) to the slab top or bottom faces.  
- Each internal tie line must be capable of resisting a specified tensile force (commonly about 20 kN/m), with the minimum per beam line given by the formula Ftie = ((l₁ + l₂)/2)·q₃ ≤ q₄.  
- Finally, all internal ties must connect back to the peripheral tie so that force transfer is assured in the accidental design situation.

In summary, Figure 9.15 depicts a three-storey building strip in plan, with continuous peripheral ties (A) around the column perimeter and internal ties (B) grouped along beam lines. Two orthogonal tie directions ensure the slab/column network remains tied together and able to redistribute loads in case of accidental loss of any single column or wall.

This figure is a two-part, schematic cross‐sectional detail illustrating how vertical reinforcement is arranged in a precast wall element that bears directly over the joint between two precast floor slabs. The purpose of the reinforcement—two steel rods of diameter φ—is to ensure adequate capacity for eccentricities and load concentrations at the wall base, as discussed in clauses 10.9.2(1)–(2) of the standard.

Left‐hand sketch (assembled section)  
• Wall element: Shown as a U-shaped profile in section, with the overall “thickness” dimension labeled h (measured between the inner faces of the vertical walls). A dashed line above indicates the top of the wall.  
• Reinforcement bars: Two vertical steel bars (indicated by solid circles in cross‐section at the bottom corners of the U) lie inside the wall thickness, one adjacent to each inner face. These have diameter φ and are intended to resist bending or tensile forces if the applied axial load per unit length exceeds 0.5 h·fcd (see text).  
• Connection to floor slabs: Immediately beneath the wall, two horizontal precast floor slabs butt together along their longitudinal edges at the centerline. The wall straddles this joint, transmitting the vertical load into both slabs and the support below. A single, central support element (such as a column or bearing pad) is shown directly under the joint.  
• Key dimensions: “h” is the wall thickness, and the bar diameter is noted as φ. The spacing of these corner bars will normally be equal to the wall thickness (i.e. they align with the two faces), but detailed anchorage into the slabs is shown in the right‐hand detail.

Right-hand sketch (enlarged bar detail)  
• Two vertical bars protruding downward through the interface of two floor slabs. They are shown as long, straight lines, each terminating in a dot at the base of the top slab to indicate embedding or anchorage.  
• Floor slabs: Represented by two parallel horizontal lines above and two below, denoting the top and bottom faces of each slab. The gap between the middle pair of lines is the joint between slabs.  
• Reinforcement spacing s: A horizontal arrowed dimension “s” measures center-to-center spacing between the two bars. Per clause 10.9.2(2), s must not exceed the lesser of 200 mm or the wall thickness h when vertical load per unit length is up to 0.6 h·fcd.  
• Dotted boundary: Encloses the region of interest, highlighting that this is an enlarged detail of the bars and their anchorage into the slabs.

Caption  
“Figure 10.1: Example of reinforcement in a wall over a connection between two floor slabs.”

Overall, the drawing emphasizes:  
- A precast wall element directly bearing on the joint of two precast floor units  
- The use of at least two vertical bars of diameter φ ≥ 6 mm, located at the wall edges  
- A maximum bar spacing s ≤ min(h, 200 mm) when loads are ≤ 0.6 h·fcd  
- The necessity to anchor these bars into each slab to ensure load transfer and handle any eccentric vertical loads without overstressing the concrete at the wall base.

The provided illustration, labeled “Figure 10.2: Examples of connections for shear transfer,” is split into two schematic cross-sectional views (a) and (b), each rendered in simple line art with a single magenta-coloured connector element. These sketches show how shear forces can be transferred across the joints between adjacent precast floor or wall units.  

1. View (a) – Concreted or Grouted Connections  
  • Two precast concrete elements are shown one above the other, separated by a thin horizontal gap.  
  • From the underside of the top element (or the top of the bottom element) projects a vertical steel connector shaped like a headed stud or bulb-anchor. In magenta, its stem rises into the gap and terminates in a larger, inverted-mushroom head that sits flush beneath the upper slab.  
  • The void around the stem and head would be filled with grout or cast concrete (not explicitly hatched here) so that once hardened, the head is locked in place and the stud is embedded rigidly in both units.  
  • Shear transfer is achieved by bond and bearing of the head against the cast-in grout, tying the two slabs together for vertical load and in-plane shear.  
  • This arrangement corresponds to section 10.9.3(4) and (8) of the design code, where connections may rely on grout to develop composite action once the fill has cured.  

2. View (b) – Welded or Bolted Connections  
  • Two adjacent concrete elements meet at a vertical joint; here the slabs are horizontally oriented and abut each other along their edges.  
  • A steel pin (depicted as a solid magenta circle) straddles the joint. On each side of that pin are steel cleats or plates, shown in thick black lines, which lie against the face of each concrete unit at an angle.  
  • These plates converge toward the central pin, and their ends would be welded or bolted to it—this sketch “shows one type of welded connection as an example.”  
  • The plates themselves would be embedded or dowelled into the concrete edge zones, transferring shear across the gap by bearing and weld-metal continuity.  
  • This style of mechanical connection is referenced in section 10.9.3(4) as an alternative to grouted joints and can be designed for larger shear demands by selecting plate size, weld length, and bolt diameter.  

Overall, the two sketches exemplify different strategies for developing diaphragm action and in-plane shear continuity in precast floor or wall systems. The grouted-in headed stud in (a) relies on bond strength and local bearing, while the welded-plate arrangement in (b) uses mechanical fastening and direct shear in steel connectors. Both are consistent with the code’s requirement to provide adequate shear transfer (10.9.3(4)–(5)) and to detail connections in line with the structural model (10.9.3(6)–(7)).

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
The table in question—identified as “Table 10.1: Maximum spacing of transverse ribs, sT, for the analysis of floor ribs and block as solid slabs”—sets out simple, rule-of-thumb limits for the transverse rib spacing needed when a precast rib-and-block floor is treated computationally as a monolithic slab.  It is typically applied under clause 10.9.3(11) of the code, which allows precast units without a full cast-in-place topping to be analyzed as a solid plate provided continuous transverse reinforcement is introduced at or through the longitudinal ribs at a spacing not exceeding the values given.

Key elements of the table:

 1. Definitions and symbols  
    a. sT = spacing of transverse ribs or transverse reinforcement, measured perpendicular to the longitudinal ribs.  
    b. sL = spacing of longitudinal ribs (or the center-to-center distance between longitudinal ribs).  
    c. lE = length (span) of the longitudinal ribs.  
    d. h = overall thickness of the ribbed floor unit (from soffit to top of ribbed section).  

 2. Principal distinction – ratio of rib-spacing to span:  
    • Column 1 (sL ≤ lE/8): applies when the longitudinal ribs are relatively closely spaced—no more than one-eighth of their span apart. This scenario implies that the slab action in the transverse direction is already favored by the dense longitudinal pattern.  
    • Column 2 (sL > lE/8): applies when longitudinal ribs are more widely spaced—more than one-eighth of their span. In this case, additional transverse ties are required to ensure slab-action behavior.  

 3. Rows by “Type of imposed loading”  
    a. Residential, snow:  
       – If sL ≤ lE/8: transverse reinforcement is not required (the floor can be treated as solid without additional transverse ribs).  
       – If sL > lE/8: provide transverse ribs or ties at a maximum spacing of 12 × h.  

    b. Other (e.g. office, assembly, industrial or unusually heavy imposed loads):  
       – If sL ≤ lE/8: transverse ribs or ties at a maximum spacing of 10 × h.  
       – If sL > lE/8: transverse ribs or ties at a maximum spacing of 8 × h.  

How this fits into the broader design context:  
  • Clause 10.9.3(11) allows an otherwise open-rib precast slab to be treated as an equivalent solid slab for simple support and load distribution checks, but only if the designer ensures adequate transverse reinforcement per Table 10.1.  
  • The table’s values integrate with other requirements—such as minimum diameters, anchorage lengths and anchorage details—so that shear transfer, bending, and diaphragm action assumptions remain valid.  
  • If imposed loads change category (for instance, from residential to “other”), or if the longitudinal rib spacing exceeds lE/8, designers must tighten the transverse reinforcement spacing accordingly.  

By following these tabulated maxima, the structural model used in analysis remains consistent with reality, ensuring that diaphragm action, lateral load distribution and shear transfer between precast units are adequately catered for without overly conservative or unconservative assumptions.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
(1) In wall elements installed over floor slabs, reinforcement should normally be provided for possible eccentricities and concentrations of the vertical load at the end of the wall. For floor elements see 10.9.1 (2).
 (2) No specific reinforcement is required provided the vertical load per unit length is ≤ 0,5h.fcd, where h is the wall thickness, see Figure 10.1. The load may be increased to 0,6h.fcd with reinforcement according to Figure 10.1, having diameter φ ≥ 6 mm and spacing s not greater than the lesser of h and 200 mm. For higher loads, reinforcement should be designed according to (1). A separate check should be made for the lower wall.
 10.9.3 Floor systems
 (1)P The detailing of floor systems shall be consistent with assumptions in analysis and design. Relevant product standards shall be considered.
 (2)P Where transverse load distribution between adjacent units has been taken into account, appropriate shear connection shall be provided.
 (3)P The effects of possible restraints of precast units shall be considered, even if simple supports have been assumed in design.
 (4) Shear transfer in connections may be achieved in different ways. Three main types of connections shown in Figure 10.2.
 (5) Transverse distribution of loads should be based on analysis or tests, taking into account possible load variations between precast elements. The resulting shear force between floor units should be considered in the design of connections and adjacent parts of elements (e.g. outside ribs or webs).
 For floors with uniformly distributed load, and in the absence of a more accurate analysis, this shear force per unit length may be taken as:
 vEd = qEd⋅be/3
 (10.4)
 where:
 qEd
 _
 is the design value of variable load (kN/m2)
 be is the width of the element
 (6) Where precast floors are assumed to act as diaphragms to transfer horizontal loads to bracing units, the following should be considered:

vEd = qEd⋅be/3. (10.4). where:. qEd. _. is the design value of variable load (kN/m2). be is the width of the element. (6) Where precast floors are assumed to act as diaphragms to transfer horizontal loads to bracing units, the following should be considered:.
 - the diaphragm should form part of a realistic structural model, taking into account the deformation compatibility with bracing units,
 the effects of horizontal deformations should be taken into account for all parts of the structure involved in the transfer of horizontal loads,
 -
 - the diaphragm should be reinforced for the tensile forces assumed in the structural model,
 - stress concentrations at openings and connections should be taken into account in the detailing of reinforcement.
 (7) Transverse reinforcement for shear transfer across connections in the diaphragm may be concentrated along supports, forming ties consistent with the structural model. This reinforcement may be placed in the topping, if it exists.
 (8) Precast units with a topping of at least 40 mm may be designed as composite members, if shear in the interface is verified according to 6.2.5. The precast unit should be checked at all stages of construction, before and after composite action has become effective.
 (9) Transverse reinforcement for bending and other action effects may lie entirely within the topping. The detailing should be consistent with the structural model, e.g. if two-way spanning is assumed.
 (10) Webs or ribs in isolated slab units (i.e. units which are not connected for shear transfer) should be provided with shear reinforcement as for beams.
 (11) Floors with precast ribs and blocks without topping may be analysed as solid slabs, if the insitu transverse ribs are provided with continuous reinforcement through the precast longitudinal ribs and at a spacing sT according to Table 10.1.
 (12) In diaphragm action between precast slab elements with concreted or grouted connections, the average longitudinal shear stress vRdi should be limited to 0,1 MPa for very smooth surfaces, and to 0,15 MPa for smooth and rough surfaces. See 6.2.5 for definition of surfaces.
 10.9.4 Connections and supports for precast elements

(1)P Materials used for connections shall be:
 - stable and durable for the design working life of the structure
 - chemically and physically compatible
 - protected against adverse chemical and physical influences
 fire resistant to match the fire resistance of the structure.
 (2)P Supporting pads shall have strength and deformation properties in accordance with the design assumptions.
 (3)P Metal fastenings for claddings, other than in environmental classes X0 and XC1 (Table 4.1) and not protected against the environment, shall be of corrosion resistant material. If inspection is possible, coated material may also be used.
 (4)P Before undertaking welding, annealing or cold forming the suitability of the material shall be verified.

(1)P Connections shall be able to resist action effects consistent with design assumptions, to accommodate the necessary deformations and ensure robust behaviour of the structure.
 (2)P Premature splitting or spalling of concrete at the ends of elements shall be prevented, taking into account
 relative movements between elements
 - deviations
 - assembly requirements
 - ease of execution
 - ease of inspection
 (3) Verification of resistance and stiffness of connections may be based on analysis, possibly assisted by testing (for design assisted by testing, see EN 1990, Annex D). Imperfections should be taken into account. Design values based on tests should allow for unfavourable deviations from testing conditions.

content:
The illustration consists of two side‐by‐side cross‐section sketches (labelled “a)” and “b)”) that visualize how transverse tensile stresses develop in compression‐loaded connections under two different loading or support conditions. Both sketches show two concrete elements (represented as thick, vertical rectangular blocks) pressed together through an intermediate “padding” layer. Superimposed on each are sets of arrows and dotted streamlines that trace the internal flow of compressive and tensile stresses across the interface. Underneath, a caption reads: “Figure 10.3: Transverse tensile stresses at compression connections.”

1. Sketch a) “Concentrated bearing”  
- Geometry: Two identical concrete blocks separated by a thin, rectangular bedding element (colored purple/magenta).  
- Compressive stress flow: Vertical, evenly spaced dotted lines run down through the top block, converge slightly as they pass through the purple pad, then re-diverge within the lower block—indicating local concentration of pressure at the pad.  
- Transverse tensile stresses: A series of horizontal solid arrows point outward from the pad edges into the adjacent concrete, largest immediately at the interface and tapering off away from the pad. Paired arrows on each side of the padding show tension “pulling” laterally, implying that local compression gives rise to perpendicular tensile stress in the plane of the interface.  
- The field of arrows is densest closest to the pad corners, emphasizing that the maximum tensile demand is concentrated around the pad’s contact perimeter.

2. Sketch b) “Expansion of soft padding”  
- Geometry: Similar pair of concrete blocks with a much thicker, black-colored pad (representing a soft or swelling bedding material).  
- Compressive stress flow: Vertical dotted lines remain parallel and uniformly spaced from top to bottom, indicating that the pad spreads the compressive load more evenly across the interface (no local “funneling”).  
- Transverse tensile stresses: Horizontal solid arrows on either side of the pad point inward toward the pad, signifying that as the soft material expands under compression, it exerts lateral pressure on the concrete faces—inducing tensile stresses that pull the adjacent concrete toward the interface. The arrows are largest near the pad mid‐depth, showing that maximum tension occurs where expansion is greatest.  
- The absence of arrow tapering suggests an almost uniform tensile distribution along the contacting surfaces.

Overall Annotation  
- Both views illustrate that compressive connections can generate significant transverse tension in the plane of adjacent concrete elements.  
- In case (a), tensile stresses stem from localized bearing; reinforcement should be placed as shown in Eurocode clause 6.5 to resist the peaked tension around the pad edges.  
- In case (b), tensile stresses are driven by pad swelling; Eurocode clause 10.5 guides calculation of required reinforcement area (As = 0.25 (t/h)·FEd/fyd), and reinforcement should lie close to the interface surfaces to control crack widths during hardening.  
- The diagrams underscore the need to consider both bearing geometry and bedding‐material behavior when designing dry or grouted compression joints.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
(1) Shear forces may be ignored in compression connections if they are less than 10% of the compressive force.
 (2) For connections with bedding materials like mortar, concrete or polymers, relative movement between the connected surfaces should be prevented during hardening of the material.
 (3) Connections without bedding material (dry connections) should only be used where an appropriate quality of workmanship can be achieved. The average bearing stress between plane surfaces should not exceed 0,3 fcd. Dry connections including curved (convex) surfaces should be designed with due consideration of the geometry.
 (4) Transverse tensile stresses in adjacent elements should be considered. They may be due to concentrated compression according to Figure 10.3a, or to the expansion of soft padding according to Figure 10.3b. Reinforcement in case a) may be designed and located according to 6.5. Reinforcement in case b) should be placed close to the surfaces of the adjacent elements.
 (5) In the absence of more accurate models, reinforcement in case b) may be calculated in accordance with Expression (10.5):
 As = 0,25 (t / h) FEd / fyd
 (10.5)
 where:
 As is the reinforcement area in each surface
 t is the thickness of padding
 is the dimension of padding in direction of reinforcement
 FEd is the compressive force in connection.
 (6) The maximum capacity of compression connections can be determined according to 6.7, or can be based on analysis, possibly assisted by testing (for design assisted testing, see EN 1990).
 10.9.4.4 Connections transmitting shear forces
 (1) For shear transfer in interfaces between two concretes, e.g. a precast element and in situ concrete, see 6.2.5.

(1)P Reinforcement shall be continuous across the connection and anchored in the adjacent elements.
 (2) Continuity may be obtained by, for example
 - lapping of bars
 - grouting of reinforcement into holes
 - overlapping reinforcement loops
 - welding of bars or steel plates
 - prestressing
 - mechanical devices (threaded or filled sleeves)
 - swaged connectors (compressed sleeves)

content:
The image is a black-and-white schematic, labelled “Figure 10.4: Indicative models for reinforcement in half joints.”  It is divided into two adjacent diagrams (left and right), each depicting an L-shaped concrete connection (a beam-to-column “half joint”) overlaid with simplified strut-and-tie networks.  Between them is a small pivot-arrow graphic, suggesting that the two views are alternative or combinable models of internal force flow.  Key graphic elements include:

Overall geometry  
• An L-shaped outline in each diagram represents the concrete cross-section of a beam meeting a column.  The upper member is horizontal, the vertical member drops down at its right end, and a short bottom flange extends to the right.  
• At each corner and along each member are small solid circles (nodes) marking key locations where struts or ties intersect or terminate.  

Forces and members  
• Solid straight lines with filled triangular arrowheads denote compressive “struts.”  These appear as:  
  – Vertical struts rising from a lower node on the bottom flange up to a node at the beam-column junction.  
  – Horizontal struts extending from the column face toward the beam free end.  
  – Diagonal struts (in the right-hand model) slanting from the upper left node cluster down to a lower right node, illustrating a primary compression path.  

• Dashed lines with open arrowheads represent tensile “ties.”  In the left diagram, ties fan out diagonally from the upper-left corner cluster of nodes toward nodes along the bottom flange and right-hand column face.  There are also ties running horizontally and vertically between node pairs.  

• A bold, solid arrow at the inside corner points into the joint — this marks the location/direction of the applied load or the critical face requiring reinforcement.  

• In the left model, a dense cluster of short dashed arrows near the top-left corner indicates multiple possible tie orientations; this cluster is shown again more concisely in the right model.  

Model comparison/combination  
• A curved rotation arrow between the two diagrams indicates that the two strut-and-tie layouts may be used separately or blended to satisfy section 6.5 design requirements.  
• The right diagram simplifies the left’s more complex fan of ties into a single principal diagonal strut, plus accompanying horizontal and vertical ties, providing an alternate “backbone” of force flow.  

Caption and note  
• Beneath the drawings is the caption: “Figure 10.4: Indicative models for reinforcement in half joints.”  
• The original context (“Half joints may be designed using strut-and-tie models according to 6.5. Two alternative models and reinforcements are indicated…”) emphasizes that these sketches illustrate only the main features of the strut-and-tie concept, not detailed bar schedules or exact dimensions.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
(1) Half joints may be designed using strut-and-tie models according to 6.5. Two alternative models and reinforcements are indicated in Figure 10.4. The two models may be combined.
 Note: The figure shows only the main features of strut-and-tie models.

The drawing is a plan-view detail (Figure 10.5) showing how to arrange and dimension reinforcement at the junction of a supporting member (lower element) and a supported member (upper element). A dashed outline encloses the “control volume” around the corner intersection, while solid lines depict the concrete elements and reinforcing bars. Key features are as follows:

1. Concrete Elements  
   - Two orthogonal members meet at a right-angle corner.  
     • The upper (supported) member runs left–right.  
     • The lower (supporting) member runs bottom–top.  
   - Both elements have a uniform concrete cover, denoted c₂ on the lower element (left side) and c₃ on the upper element (right side).

2. Reinforcing Bars  
   - Primary straight bars (solid lines) run through each member. In the upper member a straight bar extends horizontally through the section; in the lower member a straight bar extends horizontally into the corner.  
   - End‐anchored bars or horizontal loops are assumed for these straight bars.  
   - Additional bent bars (dashed lines) illustrate how vertical bends are accommodated inside the corner. Each bent bar radius is called r₂ (in the supporting member) or r₃ (in the supported member). Small circle symbols mark the center of each bending radius.

3. Effective Bearing Length and Anchorage Distances  
   - The critical distance from the element face to the point where effective bearing length a₁ begins is labeled dᵢ. Two cases are given:  
     • For horizontally anchored bars (or loops), dᵢ = cᵢ + Δaᵢ.  
     • For vertically bent bars, dᵢ = cᵢ + Δaᵢ + rᵢ.  
   - In the upper member this is shown as d₂ measured from the left dashed control-volume line to the left face of the bar. A dimension-note on top reads “d₂ ≥ a₁ + Δa₃.”  
   - In the lower member, three linear dimensions are shown in series (left to right):  
     • c₂ (concrete cover on supporting member face)  
     • “> a₁ + Δa₂” (the required anchorage length inside the member)  
     • d₃ (the total distance to the right face of the bar in the supported element)  

4. Highlighted Bearing Zone  
   - A solid purple (or dark-red) rectangle superimposed on the corner illustrates the zone of effective bearing length a₁ against which the supported member reacts. It lies entirely within the two members’ intersection.

5. Reference to Code Clauses  
   - The text refers to clause 10.9.5.2(1) for permissible deviations Δa₂ or Δa₃, which account for tolerances in anchorage length.  
   - The figure exemplifies how to detail both horizontal anchorages (without additional radius) and vertical bends (with added rᵢ) so that the total dᵢ always exceeds the required a₁ plus any allowed deviation.

Overall, Figure 10.5 demonstrates in plan view the minimum anchorage distances for reinforcement crossing a corner joint. It ensures that—even with bends and permissible deviations—the bars have sufficient embedment (d₂, d₃) in the supporting and supported elements, measured from their concrete faces (c₂, c₃), to develop the design bearing length a₁. Kennedy radii r₂ and r₃ are included for the vertical bend legs, and all dimensions are clearly annotated to align with the relevant code provisions.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
(1) Reinforcement in supporting and supported members should be detailed to ensure anchorage in the respective node, allowing for deviations. An example is shown in Figure 10.5.
 The effective bearing length a1 is controlled by a distance d (see Figure 10.5) from the edge of the respective elements where:
 di = ci + ∆ai
 with horizontal loops or otherwise end anchored bars
 di = ci + ∆ai + ri with vertically bent bars
 Where
 ci is concrete cover
 ∆ai is a deviation (see 10.9.5.2 (1)
 ri is the bend radius
 See Figure 10.5 and 10.9.5.2 (1) for definitions of ∆a2 or ∆a3.

(1)P The proper functioning of bearings shall be ensured by reinforcement in adjacent members, limitation of bearing stress and measures to account for movement or restraint.
 (2)P For bearings which do not permit sliding or rotation without significant restraint, actions due to creep, shrinkage, temperature, misalignment, lack of plumb etc. shall be taken into account in the design of adjacent members.
 (3) The effects of (2)P may require transverse reinforcement in supporting and supported members, and/or continuity reinforcement for tying elements together. They may also influence the design of main reinforcement in such members.
 (4)P Bearings shall be designed and detailed to ensure correct positioning, taking into account production and assembling deviations.
 (5)P Possible effects of prestressing anchorages and their recesses shall be taken into account.

Below is a self-contained, detailed description of the diagram and accompanying formulae for the nominal bearing length “a” as illustrated in Figure 10.6. This write-up can be directly indexed into a RAG vector store.

1. Formula block (top of image)  
  • Main equation:  
    a = a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + √(Δa₂² + Δa₃²)  
  • Definitions immediately beneath the equation:  
    – a₁: net bearing length required by the design bearing strength, not less than the minimum values in Table 10.2.  
    – F_Ed: design value of the support reaction (vertical load transferred to the bearing).  
    – b₁: net bearing width (cross-sectional width of bearing contact), see note (3).  
    – f_Rd: design bearing strength, computed per note (2).  
    – a₂: ineffective distance beyond the outer edge of the supporting member, per Figure 10.6 and Table 10.3.  
    – a₃: similar ineffective distance beyond the edge of the supported member (opposite side).

2. Contextual notes (pulled in from the accompanying text)  
  (1) Δa₂ and Δa₃ are allowances for construction and dimensional deviations:  
    – Δa₂ covers tolerances in spacing between supporting members (see Table 10.5).  
    – Δa₃ = l_n/2500, where l_n is the nominal length of the supported member.  
  (2) Design bearing strength, f_Rd, may be taken as:  
    – For dry connections: f_Rd = 0.4·f_cd.  
    – In all other cases: f_Rd = f_bed ≤ 0.85·f_cd.  
      • f_cd is the lesser of the design strengths for the supporting and supported members.  
      • f_bed is the design strength of any bedding mortar or pad.  
  (3) If a uniform pressure distribution is achieved (e.g. with mortar or neoprene pads), b₁ may be the actual bearing width. Otherwise, absent more detailed analysis, b₁ should not exceed 600 mm.

3. Lower graphics (Figure 10.6: Example of bearing with definitions)  
  A. Side-elevation sketch (left):  
    • The supported element (top) sits on a support flange (bottom). A small rectangular pad (highlighted in magenta) represents the actual bearing zone.  
    • Horizontal dimension call-outs:  
      – From the left edge of support to the start of the effective region: a₃ + Δa₃.  
      – Middle portion (effective bearing length): a₁.  
      – From the end of a₁ to the right edge of support: a₂ + Δa₂.  
      – Summation of those three spans equals the total nominal length “a”.  

  B. Plan view sketch (right):  
    • Directly above is the same magenta pad, now seen in plan.  
    • A vertical double-arrow marks the net bearing width b₁ across the pad.  
    • Surrounding outlines depict the footprint of both supported and supporting members.

4. Caption  
  “Figure 10.6: Example of bearing with definitions.”  

Together, the formula, definitional list, contextual design notes, and two orthogonal sketches (side-view and plan-view) fully define how to compute the nominal bearing length a, how to choose the design bearing strength f_Rd, and what limits to apply to the bearing width b₁. This description should serve as a complete reference for downstream retrieval or automated reasoning over bearing-design data.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
The table under consideration—“Table 10.2: Minimum value of a₁ in mm”—gives the baseline bearing length a₁ required for a simple bearing detail, expressed in millimetres, as a function of two key parameters:  
  • the type of support (line, ribbed or concentrated), and  
  • the relative bearing stress σ_Ed / f_cd acting at the interface.

1. Table layout and headings  
   – Top row (column headers):  
     • First column: “Relative bearing stress, σ_Ed / f_cd”  
     • Next three columns: the three stress‐ratio ranges “≤ 0.15”, “0.15 – 0.4” and “> 0.4.”  
   – First column (row labels): the three support categories:  
     1. “Line supports (floors, roofs)”  
     2. “Ribbed floors and purlins”  
     3. “Concentrated supports (beams)”  
   – Table body: numeric values of a₁ (in mm) for each combination of support type and stress range.

2. Numeric data summary  
   a) For light line supports (continuous bearing along a line, e.g. simple floor or roof bearing):  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.15 → a₁ = 25 mm  
     – 0.15 < σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.4 → a₁ = 30 mm  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd > 0.4 → a₁ = 40 mm  
   b) For ribbed floors and purlins (bearing distributed over discrete ribs):  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.15 → a₁ = 55 mm  
     – 0.15 < σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.4 → a₁ = 70 mm  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd > 0.4 → a₁ = 80 mm  
   c) For concentrated beam supports (line bearing concentrated at beam flanges):  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.15 → a₁ = 90 mm  
     – 0.15 < σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.4 → a₁ = 110 mm  
     – σ_Ed / f_cd > 0.4 → a₁ = 140 mm  

3. Relationship to nominal length a  
   – In Figure 10.6 the overall nominal bearing length “a” is given by  
       a = a₁ + Δa₂ + Δa₃  
     where Δa₂ accounts for tolerance on the spacing of supports (see Table 10.5) and  
           Δa₃ = l_n/2500 accounts for tolerance on the supported member length l_n.  
   – Thus the values in Table 10.2 specify the core a₁ component before adding machining or fabrication allowances.

4. Underlying assumptions on bearing strength  
   – Unless otherwise specified, design bearing strength f_Rd is taken as  
       • 0.4 f_cd for dry connections, or  
       • f_bed, limited to ≤ 0.85 f_cd for connections using bedding mortar or similar.  
     Here f_cd is the lower of the design concrete strengths of the supporting and supported members; f_bed is the bedding material design strength.

5. Notes on bearing width b₁  
   – If bearing pressure is evenly distributed via grout, neoprene pads, etc., b₁ may be taken as the actual member width.  
   – Otherwise b₁ should not exceed 600 mm unless a more refined analysis justifies a larger width.

In summary, Table 10.2 provides the minimum clear bearing length a₁ in millimetres for varying support conditions and stress levels, forming the starting point for calculating the nominal bearing length used in structural detail design.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
Here is a detailed, self-contained description of the information given in Table 10.3, suitable for inclusion in a RAG vector store. It defines the ineffective bearing length allowance ∆a₂ (in mm) from the outer edge of the supporting member, depending on (a) support material and (b) load type and intensity. Wherever “(–)” appears, a concrete padstone is required.

1. Table Title and Purpose  
   – Table 10.3: “Distance a₂ (mm) assumed ineffective from outer end of supporting member. Concrete padstone should be used in cases (–).”  
   – Defines ∆a₂, the allowance to be added to the nominal bearing length a, to cover deviations in the spacing of supporting members (see context in Clause 10.5).  

2. Governing Parameter (Columns)  
   – σ_Ed / f_cd: ratio of the applied design bearing stress (σ_Ed) to the design compressive strength of the supporting concrete member (f_cd).  
   – Three stress‐ratio ranges:  
     • ≤ 0.15  
     • 0.15 – 0.40  
     • > 0.40  

3. Support Materials and Load Types (Rows)  
   For each material, two subcategories of loading are considered:  
   – line load (uniformly distributed load across the bearing width)  
   – concentrated load (point or narrow strip load)  

   The cell entries give ∆a₂ in millimetres:

   A. Steel  
     • line load:  
       – σ_Ed / f_cd ≤ 0.15 → ∆a₂ = 0 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → ∆a₂ = 0 mm  
       – > 0.40 → ∆a₂ = 10 mm  
     • concentrated load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 5 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 10 mm  
       – > 0.40 → 15 mm  

   B. Reinforced concrete, grade ≥ C30  
     • line load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 5 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 10 mm  
       – > 0.40 → 15 mm  
     • concentrated load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 10 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 15 mm  
       – > 0.40 → 25 mm  

   C. Plain concrete or reinforced concrete < C30  
     • line load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 10 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 15 mm  
       – > 0.40 → 25 mm  
     • concentrated load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 20 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 25 mm  
       – > 0.40 → 35 mm  

   D. Brickwork  
     • line load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 10 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 15 mm  
       – > 0.40 → (–) → padstone required  
     • concentrated load:  
       – ≤ 0.15 → 20 mm  
       – 0.15 – 0.40 → 25 mm  
       – > 0.40 → (–) → padstone required  

4. Notes and Usage  
   – Wherever a dash (–) appears, the bearing stress exceeds safe limits for un-reinforced masonry in that range and a concrete padstone must be interposed.  
   – These ∆a₂ allowances compensate for misalignment or uneven spacing of supports before calculating the nominal bearing length a = a₀ + ∆a₂ + ∆a₃.  
   – ∆a₃ accounts for variations in the supported member’s length (∆a₃ = lₙ/2500).  
   – In cases where bearing pads (e.g. mortar, neoprene) guarantee uniform pressure, the full physical width may be used (clause 3 of the context excerpt). Otherwise, the design bearing width b₁ is limited to 600 mm absent more detailed analysis.

sections: 0.9 Particular rules for design and detailing

content:
Table 10.4 specifies default values for the allowance “a₃” that is to be considered ineffective beyond the outer edge of a support when calculating the nominal bearing length of a simple bearing. In many standards the overall nominal bearing length a is computed as:  
  a = actual support length + Δa₂ + Δa₃  
where Δa₃ accounts for any uncertainty or deviation at the ends of the supported member. Table 10.4 gives “a₃” in millimetres for different reinforcement detailing and two types of support—line (distributed) or concentrated (point)—in the absence of a more precise structural analysis.

1. Table Title and Purpose  
   – Title: “Distance a₃ (mm) assumed ineffective beyond outer end of support member.”  
   – Purpose: To define how far beyond a bearing support the reinforcement must be ignored (ineffective) to accommodate deviations, anchorage, cover, and bending radii.

2. Column Headings  
   – Detailing of reinforcement: Four categories describe how the reinforcement is placed or bent at the support end.  
   – Support: Two sub-columns:  
     • Line support (continuous bearing along a line)  
     • Concentrated support (bearing in a localized area or point)

3. Reinforcement Categories and Default a₃ Values  
   a) Continuous bars over support (restrained or not)  
      • Line: 0 mm  
      • Concentrated: 0 mm  
      – Rationale: Bars continuing uninterrupted across the support require no additional ineffective length.  

   b) Straight bars or horizontal loops close to the end of the member  
      • Line: 5 mm  
      • Concentrated: 15 mm, but not less than the concrete end-cover thickness  
      – Use when bars or loops terminate within a short distance of the support face.  

   c) Tendons or straight bars exposed at the end of the member  
      • Line: 5 mm  
      • Concentrated: 15 mm  
      – Applies when prestressing tendons or bars protrude beyond the support.  

   d) Vertical loop reinforcement  
      • Line: 15 mm  
      • Concentrated: “end cover + inner radius of bending”  
      – Accounts for both the protective concrete cover and the bend radius of vertical loops.

4. Notes and Conditions  
   – All values are minimum default allowances. If detailed analysis or test data justify smaller or larger allowances, those should prevail.  
   – “End cover” refers to the specified concrete cover thickness over reinforcement to the exterior face.  
   – For concentrated supports, attention must be paid to ensure that the specified minimum (e.g. 15 mm or cover + bend radius) is not undercut.

5. Integration with Bearing Length Calculations  
   – In conjunction with Δa₂ (support‐spacing deviations) and any other specified allowances, Δa₃ from this table ensures safe transfer of bearing pressure and accounts for manufacturing or positioning tolerances.  
   – If no reinforced detailing category fits exactly, conservative assignment to the next more onerous line in the table is recommended.

content:
Below is a structured, detailed description of the input table (Table 10.5) together with its role in calculating the nominal bearing length “a” of a simple bearing. This description is organized so that each element of the table can be indexed and used effectively in a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store.

1. Table Identity  
   • Table number: 10.5  
   • Title: “Allowance Δa₂ for deviations for the clear distance between the faces of the supports.”  
   • Context note: l = span length (distance between bearing supports).

2. Purpose of Δa₂  
   • Δa₂ is one component of the overall allowance added to the nominal bearing length a.  
   • It compensates for construction tolerances or deviations in the spacing of supporting members.  
   • Referenced by the formula:  
     a = (design bearing width b₁) + Δa₂ + Δa₃  
     where Δa₃ = lₙ/2500 (tolerance for the length of the supported member).

3. Table Structure  
   Column headers:  
     – “Support material”  
     – “Δa₂”

4. Row entries  
   1. Support material: Steel or precast concrete  
      • Δa₂ expression: 10 ≤ l/1200 ≤ 30 mm  
      • Interpretation:  
         – Lower bound of Δa₂ is 10 mm.  
         – Computed quantity l/1200 must be at least 10 mm and at most 30 mm.  
         – If l/1200 falls below 10 mm, use 10 mm; if it exceeds 30 mm, cap at 30 mm.  

   2. Support material: Brickwork or cast in-situ concrete  
      • Δa₂ expression: 15 ≤ l/1200 + 5 ≤ 40 mm  
      • Interpretation:  
         – Compute (l/1200 + 5 mm).  
         – Enforce a minimum Δa₂ of 15 mm and a maximum of 40 mm.  
         – If (l/1200 + 5 mm) is below 15 mm, use 15 mm; if above 40 mm, use 40 mm.

5. Units and Ranges  
   • All Δa₂ values are in millimetres (mm).  
   • The formula uses the span length l (in mm or m converted to mm).  
   • Ranges ensure consistent tolerances across different support materials.

6. Integration with Additional Context  
   • Nominal bearing length a:  
     a = b₁ + Δa₂ + Δa₃  
   • Δa₃ = lₙ/2500, where lₙ is the length of the supported member.  
   • In the absence of detailed specification, b₁ (design bearing width) may be taken as actual width or limited to 600 mm.  
   • Bearing strength fRd (not in this table) is specified elsewhere and depends on dryness or bedding materials.

7. Semantic Tags for RAG Indexing  
   • TableID: 10.5  
   • Parameter: Δa₂  
   • MaterialTypes: {“Steel”, “PrecastConcrete”, “Brickwork”, “CastInSituConcrete”}  
   • FormulaLowerBound / FormulaUpperBound  
   • Unit: mm  
   • RelatedFormula: a = b₁ + Δa₂ + Δa₃

This granular breakdown captures every element of the table—its metadata, columns, rows, numeric expressions and practical interpretation—so that each piece can be stored and retrieved precisely in a vector store for downstream reasoning or document retrieval.

(1) The nominal length a of a simple bearing as shown in Figure 10.6 may be calculated as:
 ∆a2 is an allowance for deviations for the distance between supporting members, see Table 10.5
 ∆a3 is an allowance for deviations for the length of the supported member, ∆a3 = ln/2500, ln is length of member.
 (2) In the absence of other specifications, the following values can be used for the bearing strength:
 fRd = 0,4 fcd for dry connections (see 10.9.4.3 (3) for definition)
 fRd = fbed ≤ 0,85 fcd for all other cases
 where
 fcd is the the lower of the design strengths for supported and supporting member fbed is the design strength of bedding material
 (3) If measures are taken to obtain a uniform distribution of the bearing pressure, e.g. with mortar, neoprene or similar pads, the design bearing width b1 may be taken as the actual width of the bearing. Otherwise, and in the absence of a more accurate analysis, b1 should not be greater than to 600 mm.

(1)P The nominal length shall be 20 mm greater than for non-isolated members.
 (2)P If the bearing allows movements in the support, the net bearing length shall be increased to cover possible movements.
 (3)P If a member is tied other than at the level of its bearing, the net bearing length a1 shall be increased to cover the effect of possible rotation around the tie.

(1)P Concrete pockets shall be capable of transferring vertical actions, bending moments and horizontal shears from columns to the soil. The pocket shall be large enough to enable a good concrete filling below and around the column.

(1) Pockets expressly wrought with indentations or keys may be considered to act monolithically with the column.
 (2) Where vertical tension due to moment transfer occurs careful detailing of the overlap reinforcement of the similarly wrought column and the foundation is needed, allowing for the separation of the lapped bars. The lap length according to 8.6 should be increased by at least the horizontal distance between bars in the column and in the foundation (see Figure 10.7 (a) ) Adequate horizontal reinforcement for the lapped splice should be provided.
 (3) The punching shear design should be as for monolithic column/foundation connections according to 6.4, as shown in Figure 10.7 (a), provided the shear transfer between the column and footing is verified. Otherwise the punching shear design should be as for pockets with smooth surfaces.

The illustration is a schematic cross-sectional view of a precast “pocket” foundation—specifically Figure 10.7(a), labeled “with keyed joint surface.” It shows how a reinforced‐concrete column is seated into a recess in a cast-in-place footing, with forces and moments transferred through a grout or concrete infill and friction against the pocket walls.

Overall arrangement  
• The footing is depicted as a large rectangular block, represented by solid outlines. Diagonal dashed lines extend from the bottom corners up to the outer edges of the pocket, indicating the footing’s spread or “cruciform” influence lines.  
• A vertical concrete pocket (shown in red shading) is cast into the footprint of the footing. This pocket has relatively thick sidewalls and a U-shaped profile that surrounds three sides of the base of the column. The red color highlights the in-situ grout or concrete fill placed after the precast element is positioned.  

Column and pocket geometry  
• A square or rectangular precast column is lowered into the pocket, leaving an annular gap “s” (dimension callout) between its faces and the inner faces of the hardened pocket walls.  
• The embedment depth lₛ is indicated on the left side of the pocket, measured from the top of the footing down to the level where the keyed interlock begins. The requirement l ≥ 1.2·h from the accompanying text refers to the minimum embedment length relative to the column–pocket height.  
• The top edge of the pocket wall is shown flush with the footing surface, providing a reference datum for the vertical position of the column and grout.  

Reinforcement detailing  
• Both lateral pocket walls are shown heavily reinforced with vertical bars, depicted as dotted shafts with periodically cross-hatched rectangles representing ties or deformed bar segments. These reinforce against lateral pressures, transfer of F₁ forces along the walls, and potential punching shear at the pocket bottom.  
• Additional reinforcement must anchor into the column base and the pocket walls as per notes (3), ensuring continuity and adequate anchorage for transfer of axial and shear loads.  

Loads and transfer mechanism  
• A downward vertical force Fᵥ is shown acting through the column’s centroid.  
• A horizontal shear force Fₕ is applied at the column top, arrowed to the right, simulating lateral loads (wind, seismic, or eccentric gravity).  
• A moment M is indicated by a curved arrow about the column’s base, depicting overturning or rotational demand.  
• The forces and moment are resisted by a combination of:  
  – Compressive bearing between the column base plate and grout in the pocket (F₁),  
  – Frictional resistance along the interface walls (limited by µ ≤ 0.3), and  
  – Shear capacity of the concrete in the pocket region and punching capacity of the slab under the column.  

Notation callouts  
• “s” denotes the uniform side clearance for grout/filling.  
• “lₛ” denotes the development or embedment length over which compressive forces are transferred.  
• Keyed joint surface refers to intentional roughening or projecting keys in the pocket walls to improve mechanical interlock and limit slip.  

This image, in combination with the accompanying text, illustrates the structural design considerations for pocket foundations, emphasizing embedment depth, friction limits, reinforcement detailing, and shear/punching resistance.

(1)P This section provides additional requirements for lightweight aggregate concrete (LWAC). Reference is made to the other Sections (1 to 10 and 12) of this document and the Annexes.
 Note. Headings are numbered 11 followed by the number of the corresponding main section. Headings of lower level are numbered consecutively, without connection to sub-headings in previous sections. If alternatives are given for Expressions, Figures or Tables in the other sections, the original reference numbers are also prefixed by 11.

(1)P All clauses of the Sections 1 to 10 and 12 are generally applicable, unless they are substituted by special clauses given in this section. In general, where strength values originating from Table 3.1 are used in Expressions, those values have to be replaced by the corresponding values for lightweight concrete, given in this section in Table 11.3.1.
 (2)P Section 11 applies to all concretes with closed structure made with natural or artificial mineral lightweight aggregates, unless reliable experience indicates that provisions different from those given can be adopted safely.
 (3) This section does not apply to aerated concrete either autoclaved or normally cured nor lightweight aggregate concrete with an open structure.

Below is a structured, detailed description of Table 11.1 from EN 206-1, suitable for ingestion into a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store. This description highlights the key fields, their relationships, and the normative context in which they are used.

1. Table identity  
   • Title: “Density classes and corresponding design densities of LWAC according to EN 206-1”  
   • Purpose:  
     – Classify lightweight-aggregate concrete (LWAC) by its bulk density.  
     – Provide representative design densities for plain and reinforced LWAC (with normal reinforcement ratios) to calculate self-weight or permanent loading.  
     – Support two approaches:  
       1. Use tabulated target densities directly in design.  
       2. Calculate the reinforcement’s contribution to overall density analytically.  

2. Column overview  
   The table is arranged in six columns, each corresponding to a “density class” label: 1,0 / 1,2 / 1,4 / 1,6 / 1,8 / 2,0. These labels roughly mirror the aggregate’s density in kg/m³ divided by 1 000, rounded to one decimal place.  

   For each class, three key density values are provided:  
   A. “Density (kg/m³)” — the bulk density range of the fresh or hardened LWAC itself.  
   B. “Density (kg/m³) Plain concrete” — a reference density for plain LWAC with nominally no reinforcement.  
   C. “Density (kg/m³) Reinforced concrete” — a reference density for LWAC containing a typical reinforcement percentage.

3. Row‐by‐row data  
   1. Density class 1,0  
      • LWAC density range: 801–1000 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 1050 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 1150 kg/m³  
   2. Density class 1,2  
      • LWAC density range: 1001–1200 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 1250 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 1350 kg/m³  
   3. Density class 1,4  
      • LWAC density range: 1201–1400 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 1450 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 1550 kg/m³  
   4. Density class 1,6  
      • LWAC density range: 1401–1600 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 1650 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 1750 kg/m³  
   5. Density class 1,8  
      • LWAC density range: 1601–1800 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 1850 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 1950 kg/m³  
   6. Density class 2,0  
      • LWAC density range: 1801–2000 kg/m³  
      • Plain concrete design density: 2050 kg/m³  
      • Reinforced concrete design density: 2150 kg/m³  

4. Contextual notes (from EN 206-1 clauses)  
   – These design densities assume “normal percentages of reinforcement.” If a project uses atypical reinforcement ratios, the engineer can calculate the reinforcement’s mass contribution explicitly rather than rely on the tabulated “reinforced” values.  
   – As an alternative design check, the target density of the composite concrete (including aggregate and reinforcement) may be specified directly in project specifications, rather than selecting a class.  
   – The same density classes feed into other EN 206-1 provisions. For example, the tensile strength modifier η₁ in formula (11.1) depends on the upper bound of the class density (ρ). Specifically:  
     η₁ = 0,40 + 0,60·(ρ/2200)  

5. Usage guidance for RAG  
   – Index entries by “density class” and corresponding numeric ranges.  
   – Tag “plain” vs. “reinforced” densities to distinguish design‐load applications.  
   – Link density class to tensile‐strength coefficient η₁ via the class upper‐limit ρ.  
   – Retain context pointers to EN 206-1 clauses that allow calculation of reinforcement contribution and specification of target densities.

(1)P In EN 206-1 lightweight aggregate is classified according to its density as shown in Table 11.1. In addition this table gives corresponding densities for plain and reinforced concrete with normal percentages of reinforcement which may be used for design purposes in calculating self-weight or imposed permanent loading. Alternatively, the density may be specified as a target value.
 (2) Alternatively the contribution of the reinforcement to the density may be determined by calculation.
 (3) The tensile strength of lightweight aggregate concrete may be obtained by multiplying the fct values given in Table 3.1 by a coefficient:
 η1 = 0,40 + 0,60ρ /2200
 (11.1)
 where
 ρ is the upper limit of the density for the relevant class in accordance with Table 11.1

Table 11.3.1 summarizes the key tensile- and compressive-deformation parameters for lightweight aggregate concrete (LWAC) across the spectrum of strength classes f_ck, from 12 MPa up to 80 MPa.  Its structure can be broken down into four main blocks:

1. Strength classes and tensile-strength parameters  
   – Column 1 “f_ck (MPa)”: characteristic cylinder strength classes for LWAC (12, 16, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 70, 80).  
   – Column 2 “f_ctm (MPa)”: mean axial tensile strength, f_ctm, for each class.  
   – Column 3 “f_ctk,0.05 (MPa)”: 5 %-fractile (characteristic lower) tensile strength.  
   – Column 4 “f_ctk,0.95 (MPa)”: 95 %-fractile (characteristic upper) tensile strength.  

   Example entries (rounded):  
     • f_ck=12 MPa → f_ctm=1.3 MPa; f_ctk,0.05=1.0 MPa; f_ctk,0.95=1.7 MPa  
     • f_ck=40 MPa → f_ctm=3.3 MPa; f_ctk,0.05=2.5 MPa; f_ctk,0.95=3.8 MPa  

2. Peak compressive strain ε_lc1  
   – Column 5 “ε_lc1 (×10⁻³)”: strain at peak stress, calculated from  
       ε_lc1 = k · f_cm/(E_ci·η_E)  
     where  
       · f_cm ≈ f_ck + 8 MPa,  
       · E_ci is the initial (secant) modulus for normal-density concrete (from Table 3.1),  
       · η_E = (ρ/2200)² adjusts E_ci for lightweight density ρ, and  
       · k = 1.1 for sanded LWAC, k = 1.0 for other LWAC.  
   Typical ε_lc1 values increase with strength class (e.g. 2.0 ×10⁻³ at 12 MPa; 2.7 ×10⁻³ at 80 MPa).  

3. Stress–strain curve shape factors (see EN 1992-1-1 Figures 3.2–3.4)  
   – Columns 6–7 “see Figure 3.2”: dimensionless parameters defining ascending and first descending branch shapes.  
   – Columns 8–9 “see Figure 3.3” and “|ε_lc2| ≥ |ε_cu2|”: characteristic second-branch strain ε_lc2 (×10⁻³) and minimum required ultimate strain.  
   – Columns 10–11 “see Figure 3.4” and “|ε_lc3| ≥ |ε_cu3|”: characteristic third-branch strain ε_lc3 (×10⁻³) and minimum required ultimate strain.  

   In practice, for a given f_ck, one reads off the shape factors in Figures 3.2–3.4 and uses the tabulated ε_lc2/ε_lc3 to ensure the post-peak softening tail of the stress–strain law meets the ductility requirements.  

4. Associated design notes (not in tabular columns)  
   – Secant modulus E_lcm for LWAC may be estimated by multiplying the normal-density values (Table 3.1) by η_E = (ρ/2200)² (clause 11.2).  
   – For high-precision deflection or crack analyses, ISO 6784 compressive tests should be carried out to determine E_lcm directly.  
   – A default coefficient of thermal expansion of LWAC is 8 ×10⁻⁶ /K (unless national annexes specify otherwise).  

By capturing both the statistical tensile-strength data and the compressive‐stress–strain shape parameters, Table 11.3.1 provides all the numerical inputs needed to model LWAC behavior in limit-state and serviceability analyses, with density correction for both stiffness and peak strain.

(1) An estimate of the mean values of the secant modulus Elcm for LWAC may be obtained by multiplying the values in Table 3.1, for normal density concrete, by the following coefficient:
 ηE = (ρ/2200)2
 (11.2)
 where ρ denotes the oven-dry density in accordance with EN 206-1 Section 4 (see Table 11.1).
 Where accurate data are needed, e.g. where deflections are of great importance, tests should be carried out in order to determine the Elcm values in accordance with ISO 6784.
 Note: A Country’s National Annex may refer to non-contradictory complementary information.
 (2) The coefficient of thermal expansion of LWAC depends mainly on the type of aggregate used and varies over a wide range between about 4⋅10-6 and 14⋅10-6/K
 For design purposes where thermal expansion is of no great importance, the coefficient of thermal expansion may be taken as 8⋅10-6/K.
 The differences between the coefficients of thermal expansion of steel and lightweight aggregate concrete need not be considered in design.

The table reproduced below is “Table 11.6.1N” from Eurocode 2 (or a national annex thereto). It gives recommended values of the minimum shear stress parameter vₗ,min (in MPa) as a function of the effective depth of a member, d, and the characteristic cylinder compressive strength of the concrete, f_ck. In the standard notation of Clause 11.6, vₗ,min is the lower‐bound shear resistance term used in Expression (11.6.2) for lightweight concrete members:

 vₗ,min = 0.30 · k^(3/2) · f_lck^(1/2)

where k = 1 + √(200/d) ≤ 2.0. In practice, vₗ,min may be tabulated as below once k and f_lck are fixed.

------------------------------------------------------------
Table 11.6.1N: Values of vₗ,min for given values of d and f_ck  
Effective depth d (mm)  →    200    400    600    800    ≥ 1000  
Characteristic strength f_ck (MPa) ↓  
   20 MPa               0.36   0.29   0.25   0.20    0.22  
   30 MPa               0.44   0.35   0.31   0.28    0.27  
   40 MPa               0.50   0.39   0.35   0.32    0.31  
   50 MPa               0.56   0.44   0.39   0.36    0.34  
   60 MPa               0.61   0.48   0.42   0.39    0.37  
   70 MPa               0.65   0.52   0.46   0.42    0.40  
   80 MPa               0.70   0.55   0.49   0.45    0.43  
------------------------------------------------------------

Key observations:

1. Axes and Layout  
 - Rows are grouped by concrete strength f_ck from 20 MPa up to 80 MPa in 10 MPa increments.  
 - Columns are for member effective depths d = 200, 400, 600, 800 mm and ≥ 1000 mm.  
 - Each cell is the minimum shear stress vₗ,min in MPa.

2. Trend with f_ck (horizontal slices)  
 - For a fixed depth, vₗ,min increases with f_ck, roughly in proportion to √f_ck.  
 - At d = 200 mm, vₗ,min goes from 0.36 MPa (20 MPa concrete) up to 0.70 MPa (80 MPa).  
 - The percentage increase from 20 to 80 MPa is on the order of +94%.

3. Trend with depth d (vertical slices)  
 - For a fixed f_ck, vₗ,min generally decreases as d increases from 200 mm to around 600 mm, illustrating the size effect (larger sections tend to have lower nominal shear strengths).  
 - Beyond about 600 mm, the reduction in k (since k = 1 + √(200/d)) becomes smaller, so vₗ,min levels out or even slightly rebounds.  
 - Example at f_ck = 50 MPa: vₗ,min drops from 0.56 MPa at 200 mm to 0.39 MPa at 600 mm and further to 0.36 MPa at 800 mm, then to 0.34 MPa for ≥ 1000 mm.

4. Use in Shear Design (Clause 11.6)  
 - In lightweight concrete without shear reinforcement, the design shear resistance is computed as:  
    V_Rd,c = [C_Rd,c · η₁ · k · (100 ρ_l f_lck)^(1/3) + k₁ σ_cp] · b_w d  
    ≥ (vₗ,min + k₁ σ_cp) · b_w d  
   where η₁ is a modification factor (Clause 11.1), ρ_l is reinforcement ratio, σ_cp is average axial stress, C_Rd,c and k₁ are code constants.  
 - Here vₗ,min is the term ensuring a minimum shear capacity even if the statistical or empirical formula would predict a smaller value.

5. Practical Implications  
 - Designers lookup vₗ,min for their chosen concrete grade and section depth to ensure the shear design formula does not drop below this floor value.  
 - National Annexes may specify different tabulated values or a different coefficient in the defining equation; the values above reflect the “recommended” default (C_Rd,c = 0.15/γ_c, k₁ = 0.15).

By capturing these values in a vector‐store or database, a retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) system can quickly furnish the appropriate minimum shear stress needed during automated design checks or code‐compliance reports.

The figure is a three-dimensional sketch of a rectangular wall segment (“plain wall”), shown in oblique perspective so that both its front face and one side face are visible. It is intended to illustrate the geometry and loading for the simplified computation of the axial resistance of a plain‐concrete wall when subjected to a uniaxial eccentric axial force.

1. Geometry of the wall segment  
   • Shape: A solid rectangular prism with overall width labelled b (running left–right across the front face) and overall depth or height labelled hw (running vertically on the side face). In practice b × hw is the gross cross‐sectional area.  
   • Edges: All twelve edges of the prism are drawn with solid lines; hidden central axes are shown with a dashed line.  
   • Faces:  
     – Front face: a rectangle of width b and thickness into the page (not explicitly dimensioned).  
     – Side face: a rectangle of height hw and the same thickness.  

2. Centroid axis  
   • A dashed line is drawn longitudinally through the mid-plane of the prism (parallel to the axis of the concrete wall). This represents the centroidal axis of the cross‐section.  

3. Applied load NEd and eccentricity e  
   • NEd: On the top broad face of the prism, a solid arrow pointing straight down indicates the axial design load, NEd. The arrow is drawn slightly offset from the centroidal dashed axis.  
   • e: The horizontal (in-plane) distance between the line of action of NEd and the centroidal axis is marked by a smaller arrow labelled e. This distance is the uniaxial eccentricity in the direction of hw.  

4. Dimensional call-outs  
   • b: On the front face, a pair of short arrows at the mid-height mark the overall width, b.  
   • hw: On the near side face, a pair of arrows running from the bottom corner to the top edge indicate the overall depth or “height” of the section, hw.  

5. Caption and context reference  
   • Although the figure itself does not carry a formal caption, it is clearly the graphical counterpart to the text’s Equation (12.2):  
        NRd = η · fcd · b · hw · (1 – 2e/hw)  
     which gives the design axial resistance of a rectangular section under an axial load with eccentricity e.  
   • The surrounding text (not shown in the drawing) explains that plain‐concrete stress–strain relations are taken from clause 3.1.7, that temperature and shrinkage deformations may be neglected when adequate curing and detailing are provided, and that this simplified method must not be less conservative than a full stress–strain analysis.  

Overall, the image serves as a clear, dimensioned reference for engineers: it defines the section dimensions (b, hw), locates the eccentric axial load NEd relative to the centroid (through e), and underpins the derivation of the simplified axial‐resistance formula for plain walls.

The table reproduced here (Table 12.1) forms part of the shear-resistance check in plain (unreinforced) concrete walls as laid out in Eurocode 2.  In conjunction with Eqs. (12.3) and (12.4) in the standard—where  
    σ_cp = N_Ed / A_cc  
    τ_cp = k · V_Ed / A_cc  
and the coefficient k (typically k = 1.5 unless your National Annex specifies otherwise)—the factor β from Table 12.1 modifies the effective shear area to account for how many edges of the wall are laterally restrained.  

Layout of Table 12.1  
• Columns  
 – “Lateral restraint”: describes which edges of a rectangular wall panel are held laterally (i.e. prevented from moving sideways) by adjacent slabs or walls.  
 – “Sketch”: a schematic plan-view of the panel. Labels used are  
  • A = Floor slab (providing lateral restraint),  
  • B = Free edge (no lateral restraint),  
  • C = Transverse wall (providing lateral restraint).  
  Arrows show the clear height l_w (vertical dimension) and the span b (horizontal dimension) of the panel under consideration.  
 – “Expression for β”: a formula giving β as a function of the aspect ratio b / l_w, sometimes in piecewise form when the ratio exceeds a given limit.  

• Rows  
 1. Restraint along two edges  
 – Only the top and bottom edges are held by floor slabs (A); the two vertical edges are free (B).  
 – β is expressed as a function of b / l_w to reflect the way shear distributes when only two opposite edges are braced.  
 2. Restraint along three edges  
 – The top and bottom edges are supported by slabs (A) and one vertical edge by a transverse wall (C); the remaining vertical edge is free (B).  
 – A different b / l_w–dependent formula for β applies, recognizing the extra support.  
 3. Restraint along four edges  
 – All four edges (top, bottom, left and right) are braced—top/bottom by slabs (A), both verticals by transverse walls (C).  
 – The expression for β typically has two branches: one for b / l_w below some threshold (so β increases with b/l_w), and one for b / l_w above that threshold (where β is capped at a constant).  

Footnotes and special cases  
• The table assumes that within the clear height l_w there are no openings, or that any openings do not exceed 1/10 of the wall area. Where there are larger or more frequent openings, each unbraced segment between openings must be treated separately, using its own b and l_w.  
• If, beyond slabs, the wall is tied rigidly at top and bottom into adjacent in-situ concrete (with continuous reinforcement such that bending moments at the edges can be fully transferred), the β-values from this table may be reduced by a factor of 0.85.  
• The β-values should be increased if the transverse bracing elements (walls, stiffeners or recesses) themselves are not fully rigid.  
• A transverse wall qualifies as a bracing wall only if its total thickness (in the direction into the page of the sketch) is at least 0.5·h_w, where h_w is the full wall thickness, and if it spans the same clear height l_w.  

How to use β in the shear check  
1. Calculate the axial stress σ_cp = N_Ed / A_cc and the basic shear stress τ_cp = k·V_Ed / A_cc.  
2. Look up the appropriate β from Table 12.1 using the panel’s lateral‐restraint pattern and its aspect ratio b / l_w.  
3. In Eq. (12.4), multiply V_Ed by β (i.e. use k·β·V_Ed/A_cc) to get the factored shear stress.  
4. Verify τ_cp ≤ f_cd (the design compressive strength in shear), provided that ultimate tensile strength of concrete suffices to avoid brittle failure.  

This table thus provides a quantitative adjustment for the number and stiffness of lateral restraints that help carry shear in plain-concrete walls, ensuring safe design under combined axial and shear loading.

(1) In plain concrete members account may be taken of the concrete tensile strength in the ultimate limit state for shear, provided that either by calculations or by experience brittle failure can be excluded and adequate resistance can be ensured.
 (2) For a section subject to a shear force VEd and a normal force NEd acting over a compressive area Acc the absolute value of the components of design stress should be taken as:
 σcp = NEd / Acc τcp = kVEd / Acc
 (12.3)
 (12.4)
 Note: the value of k for use in a Country may be found in its National Annex. The recommended value is 1,5.
