sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The table under review is Table A.1 from Annex A of EN 1992-1-1, entitled “Reduced deviations.” It specifies the maximum permissible geometrical and positional deviations for concrete elements—deviations within these limits permit use of reduced partial safety factors (e.g. γs, red1) for reinforcement when a quality control system is in place (see A.2.1).

1. Table layout  
   - The first column (“h or b (mm)”) defines characteristic cross-section dimensions of the element, either depth (h) or width (b), expressed in millimetres. Three size bands are given:  
     • ≤ 150 mm  
     • 400 mm  
     • ≥ 2 500 mm  

   - The second and third columns fall under the overarching heading “Reduced deviations (mm).” These are subdivided into:  
     • “Cross-section dimension ±Δh, Δb (mm)”: the maximum absolute deviation allowed in either the depth or width of the concrete section.  
     • “Position of reinforcement +Δc (mm)”: the maximum positive deviation allowed in the cover or location of reinforcement measured from the nominal position.  

2. Numerical values  
   - For small sections (h or b ≤ 150 mm):  
     • Cross-section tolerances ±5 mm  
     • Reinforcement position tolerance +5 mm  

   - For intermediate sections (h or b = 400 mm):  
     • Cross-section tolerances ±10 mm  
     • Reinforcement position tolerance +10 mm  

   - For large sections (h or b ≥ 2 500 mm):  
     • Cross-section tolerances ±30 mm  
     • Reinforcement position tolerance +20 mm  

3. Notes and interpolation  
   - Note 1: Linear interpolation between the tabulated size bands may be used for any intermediate cross-section dimension not explicitly listed. For example, at h = 1 000 mm one could interpolate between the 400 mm and 2 500 mm rows to compute ±Δh.  
   - Note 2: In beams (where one dimension only is critical for design), the requirement applies to the controlling direction; the other horizontal dimension need only be measured for inspection, not enforced at reduced tolerances.  

4. Context of use in EN 1992  
   - These reduced deviations feed into Clause A.2.1(1). If a QC system ensures that “unfavourable deviations of cross-section dimensions are within the reduced deviations given in Table A.1,” then the designer may apply a reduced partial safety factor for reinforcement (γs, red1, typically 1,10).  
   - The same table is referenced when evaluating cover tolerances (+Δc) to determine whether reduced material factors for concrete (γc, red1, recommended 1,40) and reinforcement are permissible under national annex provisions.  
   - By tying geometry control directly into safety factor reductions, the code encourages more rigorous site tolerances and inspection regimes in order to gain design economy.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The illustration, reproduced as “Figure A.1: Cross-section deviations,” consists of two simple line-drawings (a) and (b) that together explain how geometric tolerances in a rectangular concrete element affect its overall dimensions and its effective depth (the distance from the top of the element to the centroid of the tensile reinforcement).

1) Sub-figure (a): “Cross section”  
- A filled-in rectangle represents the nominal cross section of, for example, a strip footing, pad footing or slab.  
- Across the top edge of the rectangle there is a double-headed horizontal arrow, annotated “b ± Δb,” indicating that the actual width of the section may deviate by ±Δb from the design width b.  
- Along the left side of the rectangle there is a double-headed vertical arrow, annotated “h ± Δh,” indicating that the actual overall depth (or height) of the section may deviate by ±Δh from the design depth h.  
- The drawing is entirely schematic, with bold outlines to emphasize the “as-built” section and arrowheads touching precisely the outside edges of the rectangle.

2) Sub-figure (b): “Position of reinforcement (under-estimation of effective depth)”  
- Immediately to the right of the rectangle from sub-figure (a), a thin vertical line is drawn, representing the inside face of the concrete element.  
- A dashed vertical line is drawn some distance to the right of that face, and a pair of horizontal arrows span the gap between the thin solid line and the dashed line. That gap is labeled “a = h – d.” This expression defines the distance a by subtracting the effective depth d of the reinforcement from the overall depth h of the section.  
- The dotted line implies that, if the reinforcement sits at a greater-than-intended cover or if the overall depth is under-measured, the true effective depth d could be smaller than assumed, so that a (the “lost” depth) is the amount by which the centroid of the tensile reinforcement is further from the top than expected.  

Together, these two sketches emphasize the impact of dimensional deviations (∆b and ∆h) and of inaccuracies in locating the reinforcement on the actual section properties used for strength calculations. In the context of ANNEX A.2.2 (1) of the Eurocode, if such critical dimensions (in particular the effective depth d) are measured or controlled so that they never exceed the permitted negative deviations, designers may apply reduced partial‐safety factors (γs,red2 and γc,red2) when verifying ultimate limit‐state resistance. The figure underlines why “measurement in the finished structure” or “reduction by deviations” of those dimensions is a prerequisite for using the tighter safety margins set out in the national annexes.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The fragment reproduced above is a portion of “Table C.1: Properties of Reinforcement” from the Eurocode annex. It defines the minimum mechanical and geometric requirements for two broad product‐forms of steel reinforcement—(1) bars and de-coiled rods, and (2) wire fabrics—each subdivided into three quality grades (A, B and C). In addition, a “Requirement or quantile value” column specifies the statistical limits (i.e. maximum percentage of specimens allowed to fall below the characteristic values) or tolerances that apply to each property.  

1. Heading and Structure  
   • The left-most column (Product form) identifies the reinforcement type:  
     – Bars and de-coiled rods (grades A, B, C)  
     – Wire fabrics (grades A, B, C)  
   • The right-most column lists the “Requirement or quantile value” in percent, meaning the fraction of test results permitted to deviate unfavourably from the characteristic value.  

2. Characteristic Yield Strength, fyk (MPa)  
   • Applicable to all product forms and grades.  
   • Specified range: 400 to 600 MPa.  
   • Quantile value: 5 %. This means no more than 5 % of test specimens should have yield strength below the declared fyk.  

3. Minimum Value of k = ft/fyk  
   • ft is the tensile strength at maximum load, fyk is the characteristic yield strength.  
   • Bars & rods:  
     – Grade A: k ≥ 1.05  
     – Grade B: k ≥ 1.08  
     – Grade C: k ≥ 1.15 but < 1.35  
   • Wire fabrics: same thresholds for grades A, B and C.  
   • Quantile value: 10 %.  

4. Characteristic Strain at Maximum Force, εuk (%)  
   • Indicates ductility: strain at peak tensile load.  
   • Bars & rods:  
     – A: εuk ≥ 2.5 %  
     – B: εuk ≥ 5.0 %  
     – C: εuk ≥ 7.5 %  
   • Wire fabrics: identical requirements.  
   • Quantile value: 10 %.  

5. Bendability  
   • Bars & de-coiled rods: must pass the Bend/Rebend test in EN 10080 or EN ISO 15630-1 (no visible cracking after the first bend).  
   • Wire fabrics: not applicable (denoted by “–”).  

6. Fatigue Strength  
   • Bars & rods: not specified in this table (“–”).  
   • Wire fabrics: f fatigue ≥ 0.3·A·fyk, where A is the cross-sectional area of a single wire.  
   • Quantile: “Minimum,” meaning every specimen must satisfy the fatigue criterion.  

7. Mass Tolerance of Individual Bar (%)  
   • Controls geometric accuracy via mass per metre.  
   • For nominal bar size ≤ 8 mm: ± 6.0 %.  
   • For nominal bar size > 8 mm: ± 4.5 %.  
   • Quantile value: 5 %.  

Overall, Table C.1 provides a clear framework for specifying and verifying reinforcement steel by linking mechanical thresholds (strength, ductility, fatigue) and dimensional tolerances to statistical acceptance criteria. National Annexes may adjust the recommended quantiles or characteristic values to reflect local production and quality-control capabilities.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The table shown, “Table C.2N: Properties of reinforcement,” is an informative extraction from Annex C of EN 1992-1-1 (the Eurocode for concrete), giving recommended characteristic and quantile values for two broad product forms—“Bars and de-coiled rods” and “Wire Fabrics”—each subdivided into quality classes A, B and C. In addition, the last column of the table gives the percentage quantile or requirement level that defines the characteristic value.  

1. Table structure  
  – Header row:  
     • “Product form” (first column) lists the property being specified (e.g. fatigue stress range or minimum relative rib area) and any subdivisions (e.g. nominal bar size ranges).  
     • Under “Bars and de-coiled rods” are three subcolumns labelled A, B and C (quality classes).  
     • Under “Wire Fabrics” are likewise three subcolumns A, B and C.  
     • The far right column, “Requirement or quantile value (%)”, gives the percentage level associated with each characteristic value or minimum property.  

2. Fatigue stress range (β·fyk)  
  Description: the endurance limit of reinforcement under cyclic loading to 2×10^6 cycles, expressed as a fraction β of the characteristic yield strength fyk, used for fatigue design.  
  – Bars and de-coiled rods:  
     • Class A – no value given in the table (not recommended for fatigue‐critical applications).  
     • Class B – β·fyk ≥ 150 MPa.  
     • Class C – no value given.  
  – Wire Fabrics:  
     • Class A – β·fyk ≥ 100 MPa.  
     • Classes B and C – blank (no recommendation).  
  – Requirement/quantile value: 10 %  
     • This means that at least 90 % of test results should exceed the stated fatigue stress range characteristic value.  

3. Minimum relative rib area (fR,min)  
  Description: applicable only to deformed bars and rods; measures the ratio of ribbed surface area to nominal circumference, which directly affects bond to concrete.  
  – Subdivision by nominal bar diameter (φ):  
     • 5 – 6 mm: fR,min = 0.035  
     • 6.5 – 12 mm: fR,min = 0.040  
     • > 12 mm: fR,min = 0.056  
  – Wire Fabrics (all classes): not applicable (blank).  
  – Requirement/quantile value: 5 %  
     • Implies that at least 95 % of individual tests on a production batch must meet or exceed the minimum relative rib area.  

4. Notes and national‐annex references  
  – The table’s recommended values may be overridden or modified by a country’s National Annex.  
  – The “Requirement or quantile value” column signals the percentage of test results that may fall below the characteristic value (e.g. 10 % for fatigue, 5 % for rib area), in accordance with EN 10080 procedures for evaluation of test results.  
  – Complementary rules governing bond and fatigue may be found in Expressions (C.1N) and (C.2N) of EN 1992-1-1, and in national‐annex tables C.2N and C.3N.  

In summary, Table C.2N provides designers and specifiers with minimum characteristic performance levels for fatigue resistance and bond geometry of reinforcing steels, classified by product form and quality class, together with the statistical quantile levels required for conformity.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The table reproduced above is identified as “Table C.3N – Absolute limits on test results” and appears in the context of Annex C (informative) to EN 1992-1-1. Its purpose is to define absolute acceptance limits for mechanical properties of reinforcing steel when assessed against the long-term characteristic value (denoted Cᵥ). These limits are intended to ensure that each test unit both meets minimum quality requirements and does not greatly exceed the upper bounds that could indicate atypically stiff or hard material, except where no upper limit is deemed necessary.

Structure of the table  
• Title row: “Table C.3N. Absolute limits on test results.”  
• Column headers:  
  – Performance characteristic  
  – Minimum value  
  – Maximum value  

Three performance characteristics are listed in the left-hand column, each with corresponding minimum and maximum permissible values expressed as multipliers of the long-term characteristic value Cᵥ:

1. Yield strength, fᵧₖ  
   • Minimum: 0.97 × minimum Cᵥ  
   • Maximum: 1.03 × maximum Cᵥ  
   Interpretation: No test result should show a yield stress below 97 % of the declared characteristic value, nor above 103 % of the declared characteristic value.

2. K (ratio of yield to tensile strength or another defined quality parameter)  
   • Minimum: 0.98 × minimum Cᵥ  
   • Maximum: 1.02 × maximum Cᵥ  
   Interpretation: The characteristic ratio K must remain within ±2 % of the declared characteristic.

3. Ultimate strain, εᵤₖ  
   • Minimum: 0.80 × minimum Cᵥ  
   • Maximum: Not applicable  
   Interpretation: The elongation at maximum force must be at least 80 % of the characteristic value; there is no upper bound set because excessively high ductility generally does not compromise safety.

Contextual notes from the annex and related clauses:  
– Cᵥ denotes the long-term characteristic value for each parameter (see EN 10080 and national annex guidance).  
– A test unit passes if all individual results lie within these limits; the mean of the unit must also satisfy M ≥ Cᵥ + a, with “a” given in the national annex (recommended values: 10 MPa for fᵧₖ, zero for K and εᵤₖ).  
– These absolute limits complement the long-term quality levels described in Table C.1 and ensure consistency and traceability in factory production control.  

Use in RAG/vector indexing  
• Key fields: “Table C.3N,” “Yield strength fᵧₖ,” “K ratio,” “Ultimate strain εᵤₖ,” “Minimum limit,” “Maximum limit.”  
• Typical query examples:  
  – “What are the absolute test limits for yield strength of reinforcement?”  
  – “Is there an upper limit for the ultimate strain εᵤₖ?”  
  – “How does Table C.3N relate K values to characteristic values?”  
• Embedding summary: “Defines absolute lower and upper acceptance multipliers for yield strength, K-ratio and ultimate strain of reinforcing steel, expressed in relation to the declared long-term characteristic value Cᵥ (0.97–1.03 for fᵧₖ, 0.98–1.02 for K, ≥0.80 for εᵤₖ).”

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The figure is a schematic sketch of the “equivalent-time method” for calculating relaxation losses in a prestressing tendon, taken from Figure D.1 of EN 1992-1-1.  It plots tendon stress σ on the vertical axis against real time t on the horizontal axis, and illustrates what happens over two consecutive loading stages (indexed i – 1 and i).

1. Axes and key instants  
 – Horizontal axis: time, marked with two successive load‐application instants tᵢ₋₁ and tᵢ.  
 – Vertical axis: tensile stress σ in the tendon.

2. Stress levels at each stage  
 – σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁺ (upper dashed line) is the stress “just after” the load increment applied at tᵢ₋₁.  
 – σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁻ (middle dashed line) is the stress “just before” the next load increment (i.e. at the end of the relaxation period that began at tᵢ₋₁).  
 – σₚ,ᵢ⁺ (lower dashed line) is the stress “just after” the load increment at tᵢ.  (A further σₚ,ᵢ⁻ level, not explicitly shown, would lie below the decay curve that follows.)

3. Instantaneous jumps and relaxation curves  
 – At t = tᵢ₋₁: the stress leaps instantaneously from σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁻ (the pre-load level) up to σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁺.  This vertical step is shown by a solid vertical line.  
 – For tᵢ₋₁ < t < tᵢ: the tendon stress decays under relaxation.  This is the solid, gently downward-sloping curve that falls from σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁺ at tᵢ₋₁ to meet σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁻ at t = tᵢ (just before the next load application).  
 – At t = tᵢ: a second instantaneous load increment produces another vertical jump, this time from σₚ,ᵢ₋₁⁻ up (or down, depending on sign conventions) to σₚ,ᵢ⁺.  This is again indicated by a short vertical line.  
 – For t > tᵢ: the stress again decays, now shown as the dotted (or lighter) curve leaving the σₚ,ᵢ⁺ level.

4. Interpretation in the context of Annex D  
 – The sequence of “+” and “–” superscripts tracks stress just after (+) and just before (–) each loading stage.  
 – The equivalent-time method replaces a series of real time intervals and stress changes by an “equivalent” single time at which one would observe the same total relaxation loss.  Mathematically, all previous relaxation increments ∑∆σₚ,j map onto one equivalent time tₑ, and the relaxation function ϕ(t,t₀) is evaluated from that reference point.  
 – In design calculations (see clause D.1 (3) and EN 1992-1-1 subclause 3.3.2), the total loss ∑∆σₚ is computed by superposing the losses of each stage, or by using tₑ in a closed‐form expression for tendon relaxation.

5. Graphic conventions  
 – Dashed horizontal lines mark the constant stress levels immediately before or after load increments.  
 – Solid curves denote stress variation under relaxation over the first interval [tᵢ₋₁, tᵢ].  
 – Dotted (or lighter) curves denote the analogous decay after the second load increment at tᵢ.  
 – Vertical solid lines at tᵢ₋₁ and tᵢ represent the instantaneous elastic stress changes due to the applied prestress actions.

Overall, the diagram concisely captures how prestressing strand stress is built up in discrete steps and then reduced by time-dependent relaxation, and how the equivalent-time concept lumps successive stages into a single reference for simplified computation.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The table reproduced above—“Table E.1N: Indicative strength classes”—is an informative aid linking exposure classes (from EN 1992-1-1, Table 4.1) to recommended minimum concrete strength classes (EN 206). Its principal purpose is to ensure that the concrete chosen has adequate mechanical capacity and impermeability for a given exposure condition, thereby providing the required durability against corrosion or other forms of damage.  

Structure of the table  
1. Two main headings run across the top:  
   • Corrosion  
   • Damage to concrete  

2. Under “Corrosion” three sub-categories of environmental attack are defined, each with its standardized exposure classes and corresponding indicative strength:  
   a. Carbonation-induced corrosion  
      – XC1 → C20/25  
      – XC2 → C25/30  
      – XC3 → C30/37  
      – XC4 → (no value given—implies a higher class may be necessary or refer to national annex)  
   b. Chloride-induced corrosion (e.g. from de-icing salts)  
      – XD1 → C30/37  
      – XD2 → C35/45  
      – XD3 → (no value—see national annex or project specification)  
   c. Chloride-induced corrosion from sea-water (marine environment)  
      – XS1 → C30/37  
      – XS2 → (no value—often requires specialist design or higher class)  
      – XS3 → C35/45  

3. Under “Damage to concrete” two categories address non-corrosive deterioration:  
   a. No risk of damage (dry, non-aggressive environment)  
      – X0 → C12/15  
   b. Freeze/thaw attack (with or without de-icing salts)  
      – XF1 → C30/37  
      – XF2 → C25/30  
      – XF3 → C30/37  
   c. Chemical attack (acid, sulphate or other aggressive chemicals)  
      – XA1 → C30/37  
      – XA2 → C30/37  
      – XA3 → C35/45  

Key observations and usage notes  
• The classes XC1–XC4, XD1–XD3, XS1–XS3, XF1–XF3 and XA1–XA3 correspond to progressively more aggressive environments. As the exposure severity increases, so does the recommended minimum concrete class.  
• The notation Cxx/yy refers to the characteristic cylinder strength xx MPa (and cube strength yy MPa) at 28 days, per EN 206. For example, C30/37 indicates 30 MPa cylinder strength, 37 MPa cube strength.  
• Some cells are left blank (e.g. XC4, XD3, XS2) because under those most severe conditions simply increasing the strength class may not be sufficient; additional measures (special cements, admixtures, coatings or fibre reinforcement) may be required. Users should consult their National Annex or project specifications for those cases.  
• The values in this table are indicative only. A National Annex may prescribe different “indicative” classes, or require additional testing (e.g. water permeability, rapid chloride migration) before deeming a given class acceptable.  
• In all cases the chosen strength class must not only satisfy the structural requirements (ultimate and serviceability limit states) but also provide the cover and crack control necessary to resist the specified exposure conditions.  

By cross-referencing exposure class and strength class in this way, designers can quickly select a concrete grade that meets both structural and durability requirements without having to perform long durability-specific calculations for each project phase.

sections: 2.9 Detailing of members and particular rules

content:
The illustration (captioned “Figure H.1: Definition of global bending and shear deformations (1/r and γ respectively) and the corresponding stiffnesses (EI and S respectively)”) consists of two side-by-side, hatched-fill schematics of a slender, wall-type bracing element (shown with two square window-like cutouts) mounted on a rigid foundation. Both diagrams are drawn to convey the difference between bending deformation and shear deformation in a global (whole-member) sense, as referenced in Annex H of EN 1992-1-1 (Eurocode 2).

Left-hand diagram (Global bending deformation):  
- The element is initially indicated by a dashed rectangular outline; its deformed shape is shown by a solid, curved profile.  
- A large downward-curving arrow at the top indicates an applied moment M.  
- A vertical dashed axis through the original, undeformed centroidal line is shown; a second, slightly curved dashed line follows the deformed centroid.  
- An arrow labeled “1/r = M/EI” projects from the deformed shape toward the curvature, signifying that the global radius of curvature (r) is related to the bending moment (M) and the flexural stiffness (EI) of the member.  
- The foundation is hatched with a stipple pattern to denote rigid support.

Right-hand diagram (Global shear deformation):  
- As before, a dashed rectangle outlines the undeformed member; its sheared form is shown as a parallelogram-like distortion of the same profile.  
- A horizontal force FH is applied at mid-height, indicated by a thick right-pointing arrow labeled “FH.”  
- The displaced top edge remains parallel to the foundation but is offset horizontally; the diagonal of the deformation highlights the shear strain γ.  
- An arrow at the top, labeled “γ = FH/S,” points to the shear angle (γ), showing that it equals the applied horizontal force (FH) divided by the shear stiffness (S) of the member.  
- A couple moment “FH h/2” is sketched with a curved arrow at mid-height, and a vertical dimension line marks the total height “h” between foundation and top of the member.  
- The same dashed centroidal axis is shown, now displaced by shear across the height.

Together, these two schematics visually differentiate (a) bending, characterized by member curvature and flexural rigidity EI, and (b) shear, characterized by angular distortion γ and shear rigidity S. The use of window-shaped cutouts, hatching and dashed “undeformed” outlines ensures clarity in illustrating the global deformation modes that underpin the criteria for neglecting or including second-order effects in structural analysis.

(1) For the purpose of this section flat slabs may be of uniform thickness or they may incorporate drops (thickenings over columns).
 (2) Flat slabs should be analysed using a proven method of analysis, such as grillage (in which the plate is idealised as a set of interconnected discrete members), finite element, yield line or equivalent frame. Appropriate geometric and material properties should be employed.

This schematic defines the “column strip” (outer zones adjacent to columns) and the “middle strip” (the central zone) in both principal directions. It forms the basis for distributing bending moments from an elastic analysis: negative (hogging) moments concentrate in the column strips (around the black-square supports), while positive (sagging) moments are placed into middle strips. By assigning fixed fractions of lx and ly to those strips—column strip width = ly/2 (split equally at each side) and middle strip width = lx – (ly/2) in x-direction, and similarly ly/2 in y-direction—the designer can apportion the total moments accordingly. Captioned “Figure I.1: Division of panels in flat slabs,” this layout embodies the code guidance on how to subdivide panels longitudinally and transversely for moment-distribution in flat-slab design.

The purpose of the table is to show, in a simplified form, how total bending moments obtained from an elastic analysis of a flat slab panel should be allocated between the column strips and the middle strips in both negative-moment regions (over supports) and positive-moment regions (mid-span).

      The “column strip” refers to the region of the slab immediately adjacent to and centered on each column line (width generally taken as 0.5 lx or equal to the width of a drop, if used).  
    – Row 2 (Middle Strip)  
      · Negative moments: 40 – 20 %  
      · Positive moments: 50 – 30 %  
      The “middle strip” is the remainder of the panel width between the two adjacent column strips. Its width is adjusted so that the combined widths of column strip plus middle strip equal the full panel span dimension (lx).

  • Footnote

    – Emphasizes that for each moment type (negative or positive), the percentage apportioned to column strip plus the percentage apportioned to middle strip must total 100 %.

Contextual application:

  1. The slab panel (bounded by four supports) is divided longitudinally and transversely into frames; each panel’s stiffness in the elastic analysis is based on gross cross-sections.  
  2. For vertical loads, full panel width stiffness is used; for horizontal loads, only 40 % of panel width stiffness is used to reflect joint flexibility in flat slab construction.  
  3. Total bending moments from the analysis are distributed across the slab width. Negative moments (hogging) concentrate near column centerlines, whereas positive moments (sagging) occur at mid-span.  
  4. The simplified apportionment factors in Table I.1 assign more of the negative moment (60 – 80 %) to the stiffer column strips, with the remainder (20 – 40 %) to the middle strip. For positive moments the split is more even (column strip 50 – 70 %, middle strip 30 – 50 %).  
  5. If drop panels wider than one-third the span are used, the column strip width may be taken as the drop width, and the middle strip is correspondingly reduced.  
  6. At edges and corners without perimeter beams designed for torsion, bending moments transferred to columns are capped at the sectional resistance of a rectangular block of concrete (0.17 b e d^2 fck), and the positive mid-span moment is reduced accordingly.

In summary, Table I.1 provides clear percentage ranges for splitting bending moments between column and middle strips in flat slab panels, ensuring that structural designers can quickly allocate design moments in an elastic analysis to the appropriate reinforcement regions.

(1) The structure should be divided longitudinally and transversely into frames consisting of columns and sections of slabs contained between the centre lines of adjacent panels (area bounded by four adjacent supports). The stiffness of members may be calculated from their gross cross-sections. For vertical loading the stiffness may be based on the full width of the panels. For horizontal loading 40% of this value should be used to reflect the increased flexibility of the column/slab joints in flat slab structures compared to that of column/beam joints. Total load on the panel should be used for the analysis in each direction.
 (2) The total bending moments obtained from analysis should be distributed across the width of the slab. In elastic analysis negative moments tend to concentrate towards the centre lines of the columns.
 (3) The panels should be assumed to be divided into column and middle strips (see Figure I.1) and the bending moments should be apportioned as given in Table I.1.
 Note: When drops of width > (ly/3) are used the column strips may be taken to be the width of drops. The width of middle strips should then be adjusted accordingly.
 (4) Where the width of the column strip is different from 0,5lx as shown in Figure I.1 (e.g.) and made equal to width of drop the width of middle strip should be adjusted accordingly.
 (5) Unless there are perimeter beams, which are adequately designed for torsion, moments transferred to edge or corner columns should be limited to the moment of resistance of a rectangular section equal to 0,17 bed 2 fck (see Figure 9.9 for the definition of be). The positive moment in the end span should be adjusted accordingly.

Where there may be significant variation in the permanent load between bays, γG should be taken as 1 for the unloaded bays.
 iii) the effects of this particular loading may then be applied to other critical bays and supports in a similar way.
 (2) The restrictions with regard to the transfer of moments to edge columns given in 5.11.2 should be applied.

It appears in an informative annex (J.4) of a concrete‐design code and shows, in turn, a strut‐and‐tie idealization (a) and two possible reinforcement‐detailing layouts (b) and (c).

This table, extracted from National Annex NA.2.1 of NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014/NA:2024, defines the partial safety factors (γ-factors) to be applied in the ultimate limit state design of concrete structures. In the Eurocode design philosophy, material strengths are reduced by these partial factors to derive design values:

• γC is the partial factor applied to characteristic concrete strength when determining its design compressive (fcd) or tensile (fctd) resistance.  
• γS (reinforcing steel) is the partial factor applied to the yield strength of ordinary reinforcing bars.  
• γS (prestressing steel) is the partial factor applied to the characteristic strength of prestressing tendons or strands.  

Table NA.2.1N — Partial factors for materials for ultimate limit states  
  
 γC for concrete | γS for reinforcing steel | γS for prestressing steel  
---|---|---  
1.50 | 1.15 | 1.15  
1.50 | 1.15 | 1.15  
1.20 | 1.00 | 1.00  

Key observations and intended use:

1. Default (rows 1 & 2):  
   – γC = 1.50: This is the standard partial factor for concrete in ultimate limit states when no special reduction is invoked.  
   – γS (reinf) = 1.15, γS (prestress) = 1.15: Both ordinary reinforcement and prestressing steel are subject to the same safety margin.  

   The duplication of the 1.50/1.15/1.15 line likely corresponds to two distinct cases in the main standard (for example, different reliability classes or loading combinations) but, in practice, both use identical factors.

2. Reduced factors (row 3)  
   – γC = 1.20, γS = 1.00: These lower values may be used if all the conditions for enhanced quality control and reduced material variability are met (see NA.A.2.2). Typical requirements include:  
     • Rigorous factory or site production control,  
     • Measurement of actual geometry and concrete strength in the finished structure,  
     • Assessment of reduced deviations through non-conflicting complementary information (NCCI).  

3. Application notes  
   – These factors enter directly into design equations: fcd = fck/γC for concrete compressive zones, fyd = fyk/γS for steel.  
   – The designer selects the appropriate row based on national choices, project-specific quality assurance levels, and whether reduced factors have been authorized in the National Annex.  
   – No distinction is made between reinforced and prestressed steel in the first two rows—both use 1.15. Only when reduced factors apply do they share γS = 1.00.

By embedding this table in a RAG-enabled vector store, one can quickly retrieve the correct partial factors for ultimate limit state checks, understand the conditions under which reduced factors apply, and ensure that any design follows the nationally determined parameters mandated by the Norwegian National Annex.

The table is a concise mapping between characteristic cylinder compressive strength values (f ck,cyl in MPa) and the corresponding strength-class designations used in Eurocode 2 (NS-EN 1992-1-1 and its National Annex). It is laid out in three horizontal tiers:

1.   Header row (“Cylinder strength (MPa)”):
     •  Eleven discrete target cylinder strengths: 12, 20, 25, 30, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 95.  
     •  These are the 28-day characteristic compressive strengths f ck,cyl measured on standard concrete cylinders.

2.   Second row (“Strength class normal weight concrete and heavy aggregate concrete”):
     •  Introduces the notation “Bxx” (where “xx” equals the f ck,cyl value) for normal-weight or heavy-aggregate mixes.  
     •  Only applies where cylinder strength is ≥ 20 MPa. Thus:  
       –  20 MPa → B20  
       –  25 MPa → B25  
       –  30 MPa → B30  
       –  35 MPa → B35  
       –  45 MPa → B45  
       –  55 MPa → B55  
       –  65 MPa → B65  
       –  75 MPa → B75  
       –  85 MPa → B85  
       –  95 MPa → B95  

3.   Third row (“Strength class lightweight aggregate concrete”):
     •  Introduces the notation “LBxx” for lightweight-aggregate concrete classes.  
     •  Covers a somewhat different range—beginning at 12 MPa and capping at 75 MPa—reflecting typical lightweight mixes. Specifically:  
       –  12 MPa → LB12  
       –  20 MPa → LB20  
       –  25 MPa → LB25  
       –  30 MPa → LB30  
       –  35 MPa → LB35  
       –  45 MPa → LB45  
       –  55 MPa → LB55  
       –  65 MPa → LB65  
       –  75 MPa → LB75  
     •  No lightweight classes are defined for 85 MPa or 95 MPa.

Key observations and usage notes:

-  “B” versus “LB” prefixes distinguish aggregate type and density:  
   •  B-classes (B20…B95) are for normal–weight or heavy aggregate.  
   •  LB-classes (LB12…LB75) are for lightweight aggregate.

-  The numeric suffix always equals the characteristic cylinder strength f ck,cyl in MPa.

-  This classification underpins numerous design verifications in EN 1992-1-1:  
   •  Partial factor γC and calculation of design strength f cd = αcc·f ck,cyl/γC.  
   •  Shear, punching, strut-and-tie models, corbel design—all refer back to f ck (cylinder or cube) and class.

-  The table is typically reproduced or referenced within national annexes to establish which strength classes may be used locally (for example, Norway’s NA adds further commentary on durability classes, reduced partial factors and exposure adjustments).

By storing this table in a RAG vector store, one can rapidly retrieve:

•  The correct class designation for a given target cylinder strength.  
•  Whether a given f ck level is available for normal-weight, lightweight, or both.  
•  How to interpret class notation when reading material specifications or performing design checks in concrete structural elements.

The input table, labeled “Table NA.3.5 (901) — Design ultimate strain, εud, depending on technical class,” provides the mapping from the measured ductility of reinforcing‐steel grades to the values that designers use in ultimate‐limit‐state checks. It is part of the National Annex to Eurocode 2, giving nationally determined parameters for Norway. A detailed breakdown follows:

1. Table title and purpose  
   - Title: Design ultimate strain, εud, depending on technical class.  
   - Purpose: To assign a conservative “design ultimate strain” and corresponding “design strength at ultimate strain” for different classes of reinforcing steel, based on their measured ultimate elongation (Agt). These values feed directly into strut-and-tie, anchorage and other nonlinear detailing models where the actual post-yield capacity and ductility are critical.

2. Column structure  
   a. “Reinforcing steel technical class”  
      – Categorizes steel by ductility class, as defined in Eurocode 2 and NS-EN 10080.  
      – Four rows: three classes by minimum Agt thresholds (≥ 2.5 %, ≥ 5.0 %, ≥ 7.5 %) and one class labelled “ductile steelᵇ” for Agt > 10 %.  
   b. “The ultimate strain of the reinforcing steel, Agt”  
      – Specifies the characteristic ultimate strain (elongation at maximum load) measured in a standard tensile test.  
      – Expressed as a percentage of original length.  
   c. “Design ultimate strain, εud”  
      – The prescribed strain capacity used in design. It is lower than the full tested Agt to account for variability, partial factors, and to ensure ductile behaviour under factored loads.  
      – Values: 1.0 %, 2.0 %, 3.0 % for the three Agt thresholds, and “–” (not specified) for the very‐ductile class—implying full yield is used.  
   d. “Design strength at the ultimate strain, εud”

      – Factors: 1.01, 1.02, 1.04 for the three ductility classes and 1.00 for ductile steel (i.e. fyk/γs).

   - Row 2: Agt ≥ 5.0 % ⇒ εud = 2.0 % strain ⇒ design stress = 1.02 · fyk/γs  
     (moderate ductility)  
   - Row 3: Agt ≥ 7.5 % ⇒ εud = 3.0 % strain ⇒ design stress = 1.04 · fyk/γs  
     (high ductility)  
   - Row 4: “Ductile steelᵇ,” Agt > 10 % ⇒ no reduced εud given ⇒ design stress = fyk/γs

By prescribing both a conservative strain limit and a slightly increased design strength at that strain, the table ensures that designers can capture some of the post-yield reserve of ductile bars, while maintaining the targeted safety and serviceability margins of Eurocode 2.

This table, excerpted as Table NA.4.2 from the Norwegian National Annex to NS-EN 1992-1-1, specifies the minimum concrete cover (denoted c_min,b) needed to develop adequate bond between concrete and various types of reinforcement or prestressing elements. In practice, this minimum cover is crucial to ensure that the steel is fully anchored, that bond stresses do not cause splitting or premature failure of the concrete, and that durability requirements (especially against corrosion) are satisfied.  

1. Table title and purpose  
- Title: “Table NA.4.2 — Minimum cover, c_min,b, requirements with regard to bond”  
- Scope: Defines the minimum nominal cover for different reinforcement arrangements to satisfy bond provisions of Eurocode 2 (Eurocode 2 clause 8.9.1).  

2. Column headings  
- Left column (“Arrangement of bars”) enumerates types of reinforcement or prestressing elements.  
- Right column (“Minimum cover c_min,b”) gives cover values in millimetres, expressed as a function of element dimensions or standard multipliers.  

3. Row-by-row breakdown  
a) Single reinforcing bars (“bar”)  
  – Minimum cover = diameter of bar, but not less than 10 mm.  
  Interpretation: For small bars, cover is simply their own diameter, whereas for any bar below 10 mm dia. the cover floors at 10 mm.  

b) Bundled bars  
  – Minimum cover = equivalent diameter ϕ_n (as defined in Eurocode 2 § 8.9.1), which accounts for the bundle’s overall outer dimension.  

c) Ducts for post-tensioning tendons (“duct”)  
  – Minimum cover = the lesser of (duct diameter) or 80 mm.  
  Interpretation: If very large ducts are used, cover is capped at 80 mm to avoid unreasonably thick covers; for smaller ducts the cover equals the duct’s outer diameter.  

d) Strands (e.g. seven-wire prestressing strand)  
  – Minimum cover = the greater of (the smaller cross-sectional dimension) or (half the greater dimension), but capped at 80 mm.  
  Interpretation: For non-circular or flattened strand assemblies, the cover must accommodate the geometry by using the more onerous of those two measures—but not more than 80 mm.  

e) Tendons – two sub-cases for prestressing wires:  
  • Plain strand or plain wire: cover = 1.5 × its diameter.  
  • Indented (profiled) wire: cover = 2.5 × its diameter.  
  Interpretation: Indented wires, having greater surface area and potentially higher bond stresses, require a larger multiplier to ensure adequate concrete cover and anchorage.  

4. Notes on application and cross-references  
- The “equivalent diameter” for bundled bars is defined in Eurocode 2 Clause 8.9.1.  
- c_min,b defined here relates specifically to bond and differs from cover values required for durability or fire resistance (those may be larger). In design, the largest of all applicable minimum covers (bond, fire, durability, etc.) must be used.  
- National Annex choices: these values reflect national selection of bond-related cover; other countries may specify different multipliers in their annexes.  

5. Relevance to RAG vector stores  
- Each row can serve as a discrete retrieval unit indexed by reinforcement type (e.g., “bundled bar cover,” “duct cover”), with attributes: element type, formula for c_min,b, and any limiting caps (e.g., 80 mm).  
- Cross-reference pointers: Eurocode clause 8.9.1 for equivalent diameter; National Annex for national choices.  
- Use case: during automated design checks or QA workflows, an expert system can query “required minimum cover for indented prestressing wire” and retrieve “2.5 × diameter.”

3. Footnotes

  b) Explains that each exposure class has a minimum concrete performance category; national choices may apply.

  • This table ensures that steel reinforcement remains protected against corrosion for the intended life span, accounting for carbonation, chlorides, freeze-thaw cycles, sulfate attack, etc.  
  • Designers select the exposure class based on site conditions, choose the corresponding minimum concrete grade, then apply the cover requirements.  
  • Where bond requirements (cₘᵢₙ,ᵦ) exceed these values, the greater of the two covers must be provided.  
  • The alternative M45 option for XC2–XC4 can reduce concrete thickness in less severe wetting regimes if justified and approved in the National Annex.  

By following Table NA.4.4N, engineers achieve a balance between structural durability, material economy, and design working life requirements under the Norwegian National Annex to Eurocode 2.

The small piece of tabulated data you’ve supplied defines the national‐annex modification factor αcw as a function of the mean compressive stress in a concrete element.  In Eurocode-2 (EN 1992-1-1) this factor is used to adjust the shear resistance of a member (for example a flange in a T-section) when it is subject to axial compression.  Below is a detailed, field-by-field description intended for indexing in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store:

1. Parameter name  
   • αcw (pronounced “alpha-c-w”)  

2. Physical meaning  
   • Correction factor for shear resistance in flanges or webs under axial compression.  
   • Accounts for the beneficial (or eventually detrimental) effect of uniform compressive stress σcp on shear capacity.

3. Governing variable  
   • σcp : the mean compressive stress in the concrete section (NEd/A​c).  
   • fcd : the design value of the concrete cylinder compressive strength.  

4. Piecewise definition (three branches)  
   a) Light compression (0 < σcp ≤ 0.25 fcd)  
     – Formula: αcw = 1 + (σcp / fcd)  
     – Behavior: Linear increase from αcw=1.00 (when σcp→0) up to αcw=1.25 (when σcp=0.25 fcd).  
     – Reference: NA.6.11.aN  

   b) Moderate compression (0.25 fcd < σcp ≤ 0.50 fcd)  
     – Formula: αcw = 1.25 (constant)  
     – Behavior: Plateau at the maximum benefit of axial compression up to half of fcd.  
     – Reference: NA.6.11.bN  

   c) Higher compression (0.50 fcd < σcp < 1.00 fcd)  
     – Formula: αcw = 2.5 × (1 – σcp / fcd)  
     – Behavior: Decreases linearly from 1.25 (at σcp=0.5 fcd) down toward zero as σcp approaches full concrete capacity.  
     – Reference: NA.6.11.cN  

5. Applicable range and exclusions  
   • σcp must be strictly positive and less than fcd.  No provision is given for tension (σcp ≤ 0) or for σcp ≥ fcd (crushing).  
   • Outside these intervals, other checks (e.g. ultimate axial capacity, crushing failure) govern the design.  

6. Contextual embedding  
   • This factor appears in Clause 6.11 of the Norwegian National Annex (NA) to EN 1992-1-1.  
   • It supplements the main Eurocode provision for shear resistance (often in the strut-and-tie or shear‐force expressions), reflecting Norway’s decision to introduce a piecewise αcw.  
   • It specifically modifies the effective shear‐resisting strut capacity when axial compression is present, in accordance with EN 1992’s overall requirement to consider combined axial and shear effects (see EN 1992-1-1 §6.2.2 and NA.6.2.4).  

7. Intended use in calculation workflow  
   1. From global analysis, determine axial force NEd and sectional area Ac to compute σcp = NEd/Ac.  
   2. Normalize by fcd to find σcp/fcd.  
   3. Identify which of the three ranges applies.  
   4. Compute αcw with the corresponding formula.  
   5. Insert αcw into the shear‐resistance model (e.g. Vrds = αcw · k · (100 ρl fck)1/3 bwd).  
   6. Check that Vrds ≥ VEd; iterate on section or reinforcement if necessary.

8. Relation to broader design considerations  
   • Reinforces the code’s requirement to account for axial‐shear interaction (EN 1992-1-1 Clauses 6.2.2, 6.2.4).  
   • Complements the guidelines on asymmetry of loading, sway limitations, and surface reinforcement spalling requirements described in the general clauses and Annex J.  
   • Ensures that walls, beams, corbels or column‐beam joints subject to combined loading are checked for shear in a way that reflects real behaviour under compression.

By capturing “Parameter,” “Range,” “Formula,” “Reference,” and “Usage” in distinct fields, this description can be embedded into a RAG system to quickly retrieve the role and application of αcw when answering questions about shear design in the Norwegian National Annex to Eurocode 2.

      – N* = 10⁶; k₁ = 5; k₂ = 7; Δσ_Rsk = 120 MPa  
   5) Tendons under particularly severe conditions (e.g. small-radius bends without plastic protection or post-tensioned around acute corners):  
      – N* = 10⁶; k₁ = 5; k₂ = 5; Δσ_Rsk = 80 MPa

   – For a given tendon, select the row matching its duct material and curvature.

In summary, Table NA.6.4N provides a compact set of S–N curve parameters that are essential for the fatigue design of prestressed tendons in accordance with the Norwegian choices to Eurocode 2. It distinguishes five tendon-in-duct or tendon-curvature conditions, all calibrated at one million cycles but with differing slopes (k₁/k₂) and fatigue amplitudes Δσ_Rsk.

Its purpose is to guide designers in choosing appropriate crack-width limits so as to satisfy both durability and serviceability requirements (see EN 1992-1-1 Clause 7.3.1 and National Annex NA.7.3.1).

      • “Reinforced members and prestressed members with unbonded tendons” (left)  
      • “Prestressed members with bonded tendonsa” (right)

2.  Left-hand group (unbonded tendons or conventional reinforcement)  
    • Permanent load combination:  
      – wₘₐₓ = 0.40 mm^b  
      – Note b indicates that, for this case, “given special consideration” may apply if appearance requirements are stringent or additional durability margins are needed.  
    • Frequent load combination:  
      – wₘₐₓ = 0.30·k_c  
    • Quasi-permanent load combination:  
      – wₘₐₓ = 0.30·k_c  

3.  Right-hand group (bonded prestressing tendons)  
    • Frequent load combination:  
      – wₘₐₓ = 0.30·k_c  
    • Quasi-permanent load combination:  
      – wₘₐₓ = 0.20·k_c  
    • Decompression load combinationc:

    – k_c is a coefficient (≤ 1.0) that accounts for the ratio between the effective reinforcement area and the concrete cover, and the position of the reinforcement within the cracked section (see NA.7.3.1 note a and formula NA.901).  
    – It reduces the baseline limits (0.30 mm or 0.20 mm) when reinforcement is placed deeper or concrete cover is larger, recognizing that crack widths will be narrower under such conditions.  

5.  Notes and national choices  
    a) k_c: see national Annex for the formula k_c = c_nom / c_min,dur ≤ 1.3 (Clause NA.7.3.1(5), formula NA.901)  
    b) For permanent load combinations in reinforced members, the 0.40 mm value may be relaxed or tightened depending on visual appearance criteria or additional serviceability requirements.

    – If a permanent combination in a conventional member governs, consider 0.40 mm, but check any additional project requirements for appearance or durability that may demand a lower limit.  
    – For decompression cases, use section-specific strut‐and‐tie or tensile‐stress analyses to ensure no cracking rather than rely on a numerical wₘₐₓ.

By codifying cracks limits in this way, the table ensures a clear, repeatable approach for durability and serviceability across a variety of concrete structural elements—particularly distinguishing the more stringent requirements when prestressing is bonded versus unbonded.

The table in question is drawn from the Norwegian National Annex (NA) to Eurocode 2 (NS-EN 1992-1-1) and is designated “Table NA.7.4N — Factor K where checking if calculation of deflections may be omitted.” Its primary purpose is to give the designer a single multiplier (K) that reflects the degree of continuity or restraint in various slab-and-beam systems. Once K is known, it is applied to the code’s limit for span-to-depth ratios; if the actual span-to-effective-depth ratio is less than or equal to K·(limiting ratio from EN 1992-1-1), then a detailed deflection calculation may be omitted under serviceability limit-state checks.

1. Table title and context  
   – National Annex reference: NA.7.4N (informative)  
   – Applicable clause in main standard: 7.4 “Deflections” of EN 1992-1-1  
   – Role: Simplify serviceability checks by introducing a single factor for common structural layouts  

2. Column structure  
   • First column (“Structural System”): textual description of the type of beam or slab arrangement, including support and continuity conditions.  
   • Second column (“K”): numerical factor applied to the span/depth criterion threshold.  

3. Listed structural systems and associated K‐values  
   – Simply supported members:  
     • “Beam, one- or two-way spanning simply supported slab” → K = 1,0  
       · No continuity beyond simple supports; standard limiting ratio applies unchanged.  
   – Continuously supported members:  
     • “Continuous beam or one-way continuous slab or two-way spanning slab continuous over one long side” → K = 1,3  
       · One face of continuity increases stiffness, permitting a higher span/depth ratio.  
   – Cantilevers:  
     • “Cantilever of beam or one-way or two-way spanning slab” → K = 1,5  
       · Outward restraint at support gives greater stiffness against deflection under service loads.  
   – Flat slabs:  
     • “Slab supported on columns without beams (flat slab) (based on longer span)” → K = 1,2 (and in some interpretations a secondary value K = 0,4 for an alternate limiting condition)  
       · Absence of beams reduces edge stiffness; a moderate increase over simply supported is permitted.  
       · The dual values may be used to reflect two different span-to-depth criteria (e.g. main span vs. shorter span) or can be selected per national practice.  

4. How to apply the table in design  
   a) Identify the form of slab or beam (e.g. simply supported, continuous, cantilever, flat slab).  
   b) Read off the corresponding K-value.  
   c) Multiply the basic span-to-depth limit (from EN 1992-1-1 clause 7.4.2, typically 20 for simply supported slabs) by K.  
   d) If actual span / effective depth ≤ K × (standard limit), then deflection verification by calculation may be omitted.  

5. Relationship to other serviceability requirements  
   – Even when deflection calculations are omitted, other serviceability criteria (cracking, vibration, long-term creep) must still be satisfied in accordance with EN 1992 and EN 1990.  
   – For buildings sensitive to occupant comfort (wind or seismic sway) additional checks per EN 1990 may be required.  

6. National‐versus‐international context  
   – This table is informative (not mandatory) but reflects national experience on acceptable deflection performance.  
   – Other Eurocode National Annexes may specify different K-values or alternative methods; always check country-specific parameters in the National Annex.  

In summary, Table NA.7.4N condenses the impact of continuity and support conditions into a single modifier, K, to streamline deflection checks under the serviceability limit state of EN 1992-1-1. By classifying the structural system and applying the corresponding K, the designer can determine when a detailed deflection analysis may be safely omitted.

1. Table Title and Scope

   - Purpose: To specify the minimum mandrel diameter to be used when bending reinforcement bars or mesh after they have been welded. Bending immediately after welding can induce stress concentrations, so a larger mandrel may be required to avoid damage to bar ribs and the surrounding concrete.

2. Layout and Content  
   The table is arranged in a single data row beneath a header row labelled “Minimum mandrel diameter.” The columns are not captioned by text but by stylized line-drawings of the typical bent shapes. From left to right these sketches represent:

   •  A hook or small single-leg bent bar

   •  A U-shape (two legs with a central bend)  
   •  Another shape (for which the same values apply as for the U-shape)

3. Data Row (mandrel diameters)  
   Under the first two sketches (the single-leg and the hooked end), the table entry is simply:

     5 φ

   In other words, whatever the bar nominal diameter φ, the mandrel around which the bar is re-bent must be at least five times that value.

   Under the U-shape (third sketch), a conditional rule applies:  
     – If the overall leg length (denoted d in the sketch) is at least three times the bar diameter (d ≥ 3 φ), then the minimum mandrel diameter remains 5 φ.

The table NA.C.2N, titled “Properties of reinforcement,” is taken from the Norwegian National Annex (NA) to EN 1992-1-1 and specifies characteristic quantile values for the surface rib area of reinforcing steel in two different product forms: solid bars (and de-coiled rods) and wire fabrics. A third column gives the required percentage‐area value (the “quantile value”) that the reinforcement must meet or exceed. The table is organized in two main parts: a minimum cross-section threshold section and a nominal bar-size section.

1. Header and Column Definitions  
   – Column 1 (“Bars and de-coiled rods”): identifies categories of reinforcing bars or de-coiled rods, subdivided by either product grade or geometric characteristic.  
   – Column 2 (“Wire Fabrics”): identifies corresponding categories or thresholds for welded or woven wire fabrics used as reinforcement.  
   – Column 3 (“Requirement or quantile value (%)”): gives the minimum proportion of rib area (expressed as a percentage) that must be achieved for that category.

2. Part A – Minimum Cross-Section Thresholds  
   • Row 1: Product grades A, B, C for both solid bars and wire fabrics. No numerical requirement is listed in the third column (denoted by “–”), indicating that for these grades without further qualification, no general quantile applies or it is covered elsewhere.  
   • Row 2: For solid bars the cross‐sectional area must be “≥ 150 mm²”; for wire fabrics the corresponding threshold is “≥ 100 mm².” In both cases the required quantile value is 10.0 %. In practice, this means that at least 90 % of test specimens must have a rib area at or above the value that corresponds to a 10 % quantile.

3. Part B – Nominal Bar-Size Requirements  
   Below a dividing line the table switches focus to nominal bar diameter intervals. Here each bar‐size range is associated with a minimum required rib‐area quantile:  
   • Bars 5 – 6 mm diameter: requires a quantile value of 5.0 % and the table shows a representative rib‐area parameter of 0.035 (this number corresponds to the relative rib area or a factor used in the annex’s formulas).  
   • Bars 6.5 – 12 mm diameter: similarly require 5.0 % quantile with a representative value of 0.040.  
   • Bars larger than 12 mm: require 5.0 % quantile with a representative value of 0.056.

4. Interpretation and Use  
   – The 10.0 % quantile in Part A is higher than the 5.0 % quantile in Part B, reflecting that larger‐section bars and most wire fabrics need a more substantial rib projection to ensure bond performance.  
   – In a testing program, for each size/category at least (100 – quantile)% of samples must meet or exceed the specified rib area. For instance, in the 6 – 12 mm range at a 5 % quantile, 95 % of tested bars must have rib area at or above the tabulated 0.040 value.  
   – These requirements link directly into bond‐stress calculations and anchorage provisions in the main body of EN 1992-1-1, where rib area factors enter into formulas for development length, anchorage, and cracking control.

By capturing both cross-sectional area thresholds and bar-size–specific quantiles, table NA.C.2N ensures that reinforcing steel delivered to site in Norway will conform to a consistent minimum rib-area standard, thereby supporting reliable bond performance in concrete structures designed under Eurocode 2.

Key points and context

Durability classes M90, M60, M45, M40 correspond to different combinations of exposure severity (chloride, carbonation, freeze–thaw, etc.) and required concrete cover for a 50-year or longer design working life. 4. This table is located in an *informative* annex; while not mandatory, it captures Norwegian experience regarding realistic expected concrete performance under various durability regimes. National Annex commentary stresses that actual expected strengths depend on cement type, aggregate, mix design and local practice—and that values in Table NA.E.1N should be viewed as lower-limit guidance rather than upper-limit constraints.

 This revised National Annex, NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014/NA:2024, to NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014 Eurocode 2: Design of concrete structures – Part 1-1: General rules and rules for buildings, was adopted 2024-10-25.
 This document supersedes NS-EN 1992-1-1:2004+A1:2014/NA:2021, and the following changes have been made to the document:
 — Tables NA.4.4N and NA.4.5N: The requirement for minimum cover in the exposure classes XC2, XC3, and XC4 is reduced when using durability class M45, as an alternative to the minimum requirement M60;

 — NA.A.2.1: The material factor for concrete γC,red1 is lowered from 1,5 to 1,4, which is the recommended value in the main part;
 — Minor editorial changes have been made.
